subjective.past_medical_history: HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (genotype B). Family history: Mother had hepatitis B; no other family history of hereditary diseases.

objective.routine_investigations: Repeatedly elevated ALT and total bilirubin (37.1-43.5 umol/L); normal AFP; negative HIV and HCV antibodies. Abdominal ultrasound was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Liver elastography was normal (5.1 kPa). Serum trough concentration of tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) 2 hours post-dose by LC/MS was 67 ng/mL (confirming good adherence alongside MPR >90%). HBV reverse transcriptase direct sequencing and clonal analysis showed no tenofovir-resistance mutations (rtA194T, rtS106C, rtH126Y, rtD134E, rtL269I) and no established entecavir-resistance mutations (rtM204I/V/L, rtL180M, rtI169T, rtT184A/G/I/S, rtS202G/I, rtM250V), while other mutations (rtV173L, rtA181T/V, rtQ215S, rtI233V, rtN236T) were detected.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (genotype B) with persistent viremia on entecavir and primary non-response (<1 log10 IU/mL HBV DNA decrease after 3 months) to tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) despite verified adherence (MPR >90%, 2-hour TAF concentration 67 ng/mL) and absence of known tenofovir or entecavir resistance mutations. HIV and HCV coinfections were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Started ETV monotherapy (0.5 mg/day) in August 2018 (baseline HBV DNA 1.64 x 10^5 IU/mL); ALT normalized over 12 months, but HBV DNA persisted >10^4 IU/mL. Switched to TAF (25 mg/day) in September 2019 (HBV DNA 1 x 10^4 IU/mL), achieving a nadir HBV DNA of only 3.35 x 10^3 IU/mL over 12 months. In October 2020, therapy was changed to combination TAF (25 mg/day) plus ETV (0.5 mg/day).

raw_case_text: Patient #2, a 27-year-old Chinese man with HBeAg-positive CHB (genotype B), was admitted to our center in April 2014. His brother had hepatitis B. He did not have any other family history of hereditary diseases. His AFP level and abdominal ultrasound were normal. His liver elastography was normal (6.0 KPa). Routine blood parameters and the kinetics of HBV-specific antigens and antibodies are shown in Table 2. The detection for HIV and HCV antibody was negative for this patient. He started ETV monotherapy (0.5 mg/day) at that time (Figure 1B). Owing to virus breakthrough, resistance testing in November 2016 (using a similar method as that for patient #1) detected mutant virus populations at positions 180 and 204 (rtL180M, rtM204V/I/L). The antiviral regimen was changed to TDF (300 mg/day). This resulted in his HBV-DNA level decreasing gradually to 70.7 IU/mL in November 2018. The antiviral regimen was changed to TAF (25 mg/day) in July 2019 owing to a virus breakthrough during treatment with 300 mg/day TDF. After 10 months of TAF treatment, the HBV-DNA of this patient was determined to be 4 x 10 3 IU/mL. He also met the criteria for a primary non-response to TAF. This patient complied with his antiviral regimen; an attending physician assessed his compliance at each visit, and the MPR exceeded 90%. The results revealed a TAF serum concentration of 109 ng/ml 2 h after drug administration. The antiviral treatment was changed to a combination of TAF (25 mg/day) and ETV (0.5 mg/day) in April 2020. However, the HBV-DNA and ALT level is even higher after 3 months. Second DNA sequencing detected the same mutant virus populations at positions 180 and 204 (rtL180M, rtM204V/I/L). The antiviral treatment was changed to a combination of TAF (25 mg/day) and ETV (0.5 mg/day) in November 2020. The clinical course of this patient is shown in Figure 1B.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old Chinese man presenting for hepatology evaluation and antiviral management.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted to the center in April 2014 for evaluation and antiviral management of chronic liver disease.
subjective.past_medical_history: HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (genotype B). Family history: Brother had hepatitis B; no other family history of hereditary diseases.

objective.routine_investigations: Normal AFP; negative HIV and HCV antibodies; normal abdominal ultrasound.
objective.advanced_workup: Liver elastography was normal (6.0 kPa). Resistance testing in November 2016 and repeat DNA sequencing in 2020 detected mutant virus populations at positions 180 and 204 (rtL180M, rtM204V/I/L). Serum TAF concentration 2 hours after administration was 109 ng/mL (confirming good compliance alongside MPR >90%).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (genotype B) complicated by viral breakthrough with entecavir-resistance mutations (rtL180M, rtM204V/I/L), subsequent viral breakthrough on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and primary non-response to tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) despite verified adherence (MPR >90%, 2-hour TAF concentration 109 ng/mL). HIV and HCV coinfections were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Started ETV monotherapy (0.5 mg/day) in April 2014; following viral breakthrough with rtL180M/rtM204V/I/L in November 2016, switched to TDF (300 mg/day), reducing HBV DNA to 70.7 IU/mL by November 2018. After viral breakthrough on TDF, switched to TAF (25 mg/day) in July 2019, but HBV DNA remained 4 x 10^3 IU/mL after 10 months (primary non-response). Changed to combination TAF (25 mg/day) plus ETV (0.5 mg/day) in April 2020, with higher HBV DNA and ALT after 3 months and persistent rtL180M/rtM204V/I/L on repeat sequencing; continued/reinitiated combination TAF (25 mg/day) plus ETV (0.5 mg/day) in November 2020.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old woman was diagnosed with IgG kappa MM in May 2002, when she presented with Durie-Salmon stage III A disease with lytic destruction of the pelvis. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) performed on a bone marrow aspirate in 2006 did not reveal any high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities. Induction therapy with vincristine/doxo-rubicin/dexamethasone was followed by double autologous stem cell transplantation after conditioning with high-dose melphalan (200 mg/m2), resulting in a PR that lasted for 2 years. At first relapse, 4 cycles of bortezomib and subsequent bortezomib maintenance were administered and led to a PR for further 3 years. Third-line treatment with lenalidomide, bendamustine and dexamethasone produced only a short-lived response. Therapeutic attempts with the Hsp-90 inhibitor AUY-922 (phase I-Ib/II study) and bortezomib/dexa-methasone resulted in disease progression. Salvage treatment using multidrug combinations of two novel agents (bortezomib plus lenalidomide), alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide or melphalan) and dexamethasone also failed to induce a durable response. With high-grade plasma cell infiltration of the bone marrow (<PMC4427147_cro-0008-0189-g01_undivided_1_1.webp>), increasingly severe pancytopenia developed, causing chronic fatigue and impaired quality of life and eventually led to treatment discontinuation.
In August 2010, at the age of 68 and 8 years after primary diagnosis (<PMC4427147_cro-0008-0189-g02_undivided_1_1.webp>), we started treatment with pomalidomide (4 mg days 1-21 of a 28-day cycle) and low-dose dexamethasone (40 mg weekly) in combination with doxorubicin (4 mg days 1-4 by continuous infusion). Due to grade 3 thrombocytopenia, the pomalidomide dose was reduced to 2 mg from cycle 2 onwards, resulting in improved tolerability, serological PR and hematological improvement. However, myeloma therapy had to be stopped after six cycles due to the reactivation of a hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection (11.7 x 106 copies/ml), which the patient supposedly acquired in 1945 and which had never emerged during therapy before. Antiviral treatment with entecavir was initiated, which led to a sufficient drop in viral load (9.7 x 102 copies/ml).
Five months after the interruption of antimyeloma treatment, the patient suffered from serological disease progression and a pathological humeral fracture requiring surgical treatment (<PMC4427147_cro-0008-0189-g03_undivided_1_1.webp>). To prevent further disease progression, one more cycle of pomalidomide/doxorubicin/dexamethasone was administered. For the subsequent cycles, doxorubicin was replaced by bendamustine (40 mg/m2 days 1-2) in light of the published data reporting an increased risk of HBV reactivation in patients receiving anthracyclines. However, two cycles of the new combination regimen resulted in transfusion-dependent anemia and grade 3 neutropenia, and only stable disease was observed.
Since the patient was not eligible for treatment within one of the active clinical trials at our institution, individualized therapy was initiated, whereby pomalidomide (2 mg on days 1-21 of a 28-day cycle) was combined with bortezomib (1.3 mg/m2 day 1, 4), cyclophosphamide (250 mg days 1-3) and dexamethasone (10 mg days 1-3, weekly thereafter). As ninth-line therapy, this individualized combination regimen inhibited the progression of the bone lesions, and the patient continued to experience a good quality of life. When the symptoms of sensory polyneuropathy worsened after 18 cycles, bortezomib was reduced to 1.0 mg/m2 and the cycle length was extended to 43 days. Neuropathy improved gradually; however, we observed a steady rise in serologic disease activity. For the subsequent cycles, the pomalidomide dose was increased to 3 mg days 1-21 and the cycles were repeated on day 29, resulting in sustained PR. Due to an extended treatment-free interval after 34 cycles of pomalidomide + VCD (bortezomib/cyclophosphamide/dexamethasone), we observed an increase of serologic markers. More than 12 years after primary diagnosis and 4 years and 4 months after the first treatment with pomalidomide, regrettably, our patient succumbed to a fulminant pneumogenic septicemia in grade 1 neutropenia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old woman initially presenting with Durie-Salmon stage IIIA IgG kappa multiple myeloma with lytic pelvic destruction, later developing chronic fatigue and severe pancytopenia after multi-line therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed in May 2002 with Durie-Salmon stage IIIA IgG kappa multiple myeloma with lytic destruction of the pelvis, the patient experienced multiple relapses over 8 years despite successive therapies, culminating in high-grade bone marrow plasma cell infiltration, increasingly severe pancytopenia, chronic fatigue, and impaired quality of life requiring treatment discontinuation prior to starting pomalidomide-based therapy in August 2010 (at age 68).
subjective.past_medical_history: IgG kappa multiple myeloma diagnosed May 2002 (treated with vincristine/doxorubicin/dexamethasone + double autologous stem cell transplantation after high-dose melphalan 200 mg/m^2 [PR 2 years]; 4 cycles bortezomib + maintenance [PR 3 years]; lenalidomide/bendamustine/dexamethasone; Hsp-90 inhibitor AUY-922 and bortezomib/dexamethasone; salvage multidrug combinations). Suspected remote hepatitis B virus acquisition in 1945 (never previously emerged during prior therapies).
subjective.review_of_systems: Constitutional: chronic fatigue and impaired quality of life.

objective.routine_investigations: Increasingly severe pancytopenia prior to pomalidomide; grade 3 thrombocytopenia during cycle 1 of pomalidomide/doxorubicin/dexamethasone; transfusion-dependent anemia and grade 3 neutropenia during pomalidomide/bendamustine/dexamethasone.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspirate FISH (2006) revealed no high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities; bone marrow evaluation showed high-grade plasma cell infiltration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Relapsed/refractory IgG kappa multiple myeloma complicated by hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation (11.7 x 10^6 copies/mL) after 6 cycles of pomalidomide, doxorubicin, and low-dose dexamethasone.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: In August 2010 (age 68), initiated pomalidomide (4 mg days 1-21 of 28-day cycle, reduced to 2 mg from cycle 2 due to grade 3 thrombocytopenia), low-dose dexamethasone (40 mg weekly), and continuous-infusion doxorubicin (4 mg days 1-4), achieving serological PR and hematological improvement before stopping after 6 cycles due to HBV reactivation. Entecavir reduced HBV viral load to 9.7 x 10^2 copies/mL. Five months after interrupting myeloma therapy, she had serological progression and a pathological humeral fracture requiring surgery; received 1 more cycle of pomalidomide/doxorubicin/dexamethasone, then switched doxorubicin to bendamustine (40 mg/m^2 days 1-2) for 2 cycles (stable disease, cytopenias). Ninth-line pomalidomide (2 mg days 1-21, later increased to 3 mg) + bortezomib (1.3 mg/m^2 days 1, 4; reduced to 1.0 mg/m^2 with 43-day cycles for sensory polyneuropathy after 18 cycles) + cyclophosphamide (250 mg days 1-3) + dexamethasone (10 mg days 1-3, weekly) controlled bone lesions and maintained PR over 34 cycles. Over 12 years after primary diagnosis (4 years 4 months after starting pomalidomide), she succumbed to fulminant pneumogenic septicemia during grade 1 neutropenia.

raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old man from Cambodia presented for viral hepatitis care. Institutional Review Board approval was waived for this case report. The patient had a medical history of benign prostatic hyperplasia, supraventricular tachycardia, adenomatous polyp of the colon, spinal stenosis, essential thrombocythemia, and hemoglobin E trait. The patient was co-infected with HBV and HCV and had never received treatment for either virus. The patient did not recall any past HBV vaccination. Risk factors for HBV and HCV exposure were unknown. The patient emigrated from Cambodia, where he served in the military. He had no history of blood transfusion, or surgery in Cambodia. He had no tattoos and no history of unsafe injection practices. The patient's family had no history of liver cancer, liver disease, or cirrhosis. The patient had no history of jaundice or hospitalization for liver disease. On presentation, he had a complaint only of constant generalized weakness. He did not have nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, change in bowel pattern, hematochezia, hematemesis, or blood when brushing teeth, rash, arthralgias, unexpected change in weight, abdominal pain, or swelling. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and no evidence of end-stage liver disease, including no ascites or edema, no appreciable hepatosplenomegaly, no asterixis, no spider angiomata, no jaundice, and clear mentation. Laboratory values revealed creatinine of 1.01 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase of 43I U/l, ALT of 22 U/l, and AST of 29 U/l. AFP was 3.2 ng/ml. Complete blood count revealed white blood cell count of 5, hemoglobin of 13, and platelet count of 436. HBV DNA 1 month prior to presentation had been 120 IU/ml. The patient had detectable total HBV core antibody (anti-HBc). HBV e antibody and e antigen were not detected. The HBV surface antigen antibody (anti-HBs) titer was at 106 mIU/ml and surface antigen (HBsAg) was undetectable. HBV DNA testing was repeated upon presentation and was reported as <20 IU/ml (HBV DNA not quantifiable). HIV 1,2 Ag/Ab test was negative. HCV genotype was found to be 6c-1, and HCV viral load was 14,500,000 IU/ml. HDV RNA was undetectable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed no suspicious liver lesions and cholelithiasis without cholecystitis. A biopsy was not performed but FibroSure  (LabCorp) blood test indicated F3 fibrosis with bridging. Initial counseling related to HCV and HBV was performed. HCV genotype and HBV viral load were identified for all specimens collected during HCV treatment.
One month later, the patient was seen in follow-up. HCV genotype had been identified as HCV 6c-1.
Based on AASLD guidelines, accessed on September 13, 2016, both sofosbuvir (400 mg)/velpatasvir (100 mg) and ledipasvir (90 mg)/sofosbuvir (400 mg) are acceptable treatments for HCV genotype 6, although the evidence rating was slightly stronger for sofosbuvir (400 mg)/velpatasvir (100 mg). A prior authorization was submitted for sofosbuvir (400 mg)/velpatasvir (100 mg), but rejected by the patient's insurance with a recommendation to substitute sofosbuvir (400 mg)/velpatasvir (100 mg) with ledipasvir (90 mg)/sofosbuvir (400 mg) 1 pill once daily for 12 weeks and was approved 3 weeks later. Prior to treatment initiation, HBV viral load was found to be <20 IU/ml (Figure 1). One week following treatment initiation, the patient was seen in follow-up. He was tolerating ledipasvir (90 mg)/sofosbuvir (400 mg) well, with improvement of his generalized weakness, and complained only of mild dry mouth. HCV viral load was 19 IU/ml. One week later, the patient was called back to clinic for HBV counseling, as a new black box warning had been added to the ledipasvir (90 mg)/sofosbuvir (400 mg) package insert recommending close HBV monitoring of patients on direct-acting antiviral therapy (DAA). HBV viral load was checked and found to be 287 IU/ml (up from <20 IU/ml 1.5 and 3 months earlier) (Figure 1). HCV viral load was <15 IU/ml. A plan was made to monitor the patient every 2 weeks for clinical symptoms and virologic evidence of worsening HBV, with agreement to present to a clinic earlier if any concerning symptoms developed in the interim (e.g., nausea, vomiting, jaundice, anorexia, or extreme fatigue).
Two weeks later, the patient returned for follow-up and was found to have undetectable HCV RNA and HBV viral load of 486 IU/ml (up from 287 IU/ml) (Figure 1). Due to concern for potential fulminant HBV reactivation while on DAA therapy (Table S1 in Supplementary Material), the patient was initiated on tenofovir therapy 300 mg once daily, with a plan for an indefinite course due to advanced fibrosis. The patient was seen 2 weeks following tenofovir initiation, was doing well without complaints, and was found to have undetectable HBV DNA as well as undetectable HCV RNA. The patient completed a 12-week course of HCV treatment without further event and maintained undetectable HBV DNA and HCV RNA through 12 weeks following the end of HCV treatment at the time of this writing.
Because the patient had exhibited detectable HBV DNA in the presence of HBV surface antibody at the level above the protective threshold, there was concern for the presence of an HBV vaccine escape mutant. Serum from day 139, with HBV DNA 486 IU/ml, was sent for sequencing analysis to the Center for Disease Control, Division of Viral Hepatitis Laboratory. Complete sequence results are presented (Figure S1 in Supplementary Material). The HBV genotype was identified to be C1 (98% identical to published isolate SEA-01, GenBank KM999990). The serological subtype was identified to be adrq+. Eleven mutations were identified (Table 1), including (1) S gene/polymerase: a 6-nucleotide (nt) deletion at nt 45-50 resulting in the removal of amino acids LY from pre-S2 and PI from polymerase, (2) S gene: G145A, a known immune escape S Ag mutation, (3-5) T118M, P120T, P142T: S Ag mutations affecting the a-determinant, (6) polymerase: V173A, (7) nt 1380: frameshift mutation in 50% of reads, (8) X gene: frameshift mutation at 1,581 in 52% of reads, (9) premature stop codon at 1,619, truncating X from 154 to 71 aa, (10) core: basal core promoter mutation A1762T, and (11) core: basal core promoter mutation G1764A. A summary of the mutations and prior literature describing these mutations (Table 1; Table S2 in Supplementary Material) and a schematic of the mutations (<PMC5936758_fmed-05-00097-g002_undivided_1_1.webp>) are presented.
Written informed consent was obtained from the participant for the publication of this case report.
Hepatitis B virus e Ag/Ab testing was performed using VITROS Immunodiagnostic Products for anti-HBe, HBeAg (). For the anti-HBs test, the ARCHITECT AUSAB assay (Abbott Diagnostics) was used. ARCHITECT AUSAB is a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) for the quantitative determination of anti-HBs in human adult and pediatric serum and plasma (dipotassium EDTA, lithium heparin, and sodium heparin) and neonatal serum. For the HBsAg test, the ARCHITECT HBsAg qualitative assay (Abbott diagnostics) was used. The ARCHITECT HBsAg qualitative assay is a CMIA for the qualitative detection of HBsAg in human adult and pediatric serum and plasma and neonate serum. For the HBV core Ab test, the ARCHITECT Core assay (Abbott diagnostics) was used. The ARCHITECT Core assay is a CMIA for the qualitative detection of IgG and IgM antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc) in human adult and pediatric serum and plasma (dipotassium EDTA, lithium heparin, and sodium heparin) and neonatal serum.
Hepatitis B virus DNA quantitative assay was performed using Roche Diagnostics (Cobas AmpliPrep/Cobas TaqMan v2.0).
Hepatitis B virus DNA was amplified using modified primers that produce a linearized product of the complete genome, followed by random enzymatic shearing, barcoding, and size selection to generate a shotgun next-generation sequencing (NGS) library for the Illumina platform. NGS was done using Illumina v2 150 cycle kit. Reads (150 nt) were assembled by CLC Genomics Workbench (v 10.03, Qiagen, Aarhus) into a complete HBV genome of 3,207 nt at an average coverage of 12,414.78x.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old man from Cambodia presenting for viral hepatitis care with constant generalized weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented for viral hepatitis care with a sole complaint of constant generalized weakness. He denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, bowel habit changes, hematochezia, hematemesis, gingival bleeding, rash, arthralgias, unexpected weight change, abdominal pain, or swelling.
subjective.past_medical_history: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, supraventricular tachycardia, adenomatous colon polyp, spinal stenosis, essential thrombocythemia, and hemoglobin E trait. Treatment-naive HBV and HCV coinfection (HBV DNA 120 IU/mL 1 month prior); no recalled HBV vaccination, no history of jaundice or hospitalization for liver disease. Social/epidemiological history: Emigrated from Cambodia where he served in the military; no history of blood transfusion, surgery in Cambodia, tattoos, or unsafe injections; no family history of liver disease, cirrhosis, or liver cancer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Constitutional: constant generalized weakness; denies unexpected weight change or anorexia. Gastrointestinal: denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, change in bowel pattern, hematochezia, hematemesis, abdominal pain, or swelling. Dermatological/Musculoskeletal/Hematological: denies rash, arthralgias, or bleeding when brushing teeth.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: Normal. General/Neurological: Clear mentation; no jaundice, asterixis, or spider angiomata. Abdomen/Extremities: No appreciable hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites, no edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Creatinine 1.01 mg/dL, ALP 43 IU/L, ALT 22 U/L, AST 29 U/L, AFP 3.2 ng/mL. CBC: WBC 5, hemoglobin 13, platelets 436. HIV 1/2 Ag/Ab negative; HDV RNA undetectable. Abdominal ultrasound showed no suspicious liver lesions and cholelithiasis without cholecystitis.
objective.advanced_workup: FibroSure blood test indicated F3 fibrosis with bridging (no liver biopsy performed). Whole-genome Illumina NGS of day 139 serum (3,207 nt, average coverage 12,414.78x) identified HBV genotype C1 (98% identical to SEA-01, GenBank KM999990), serological subtype adrq+, and 11 mutations: pre-S2/polymerase 6-nt deletion (nt 45-50), S antigen immune-escape mutation G145A, a-determinant mutations (T118M, P120T, P142T), polymerase V173A, nt 1380 frameshift (50% reads), X gene frameshift at 1,581 (52% reads), premature stop codon at 1,619, and basal core promoter mutations A1762T and G1764A.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Treatment-naive HCV genotype 6c-1 (viral load 14,500,000 IU/mL) and occult/vaccine-escape mutant HBV genotype C1 (subtype adrq+, G145A and a-determinant mutations) coinfection with F3 bridging fibrosis, complicated by HBV reactivation during direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy. Baseline HBV serology showed positive anti-HBc, anti-HBs 106 mIU/mL, undetectable HBsAg, negative HBeAg/anti-HBe, and HBV DNA <20 IU/mL (120 IU/mL 1 month prior). HIV and HDV were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Treated for HCV with ledipasvir 90 mg/sofosbuvir 400 mg once daily for 12 weeks (generalized weakness improved; mild dry mouth). HCV RNA declined to 19 IU/mL at week 1, <15 IU/mL at week 2, and undetectable by week 4; concurrently, HBV DNA rose to 287 IU/mL at week 2 and 486 IU/mL at week 4. Initiated indefinite tenofovir 300 mg once daily due to advanced fibrosis, achieving undetectable HBV DNA within 2 weeks; completed 12-week HCV therapy and maintained undetectable HBV DNA and HCV RNA through 12 weeks post-treatment.

raw_case_text:
In 2013, a 36 year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B based on the elevated levels of liver enzyme and the positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at a local clinic during follow-up for flu-like symptoms. He was referred to the hepatology division, in a general hospital for further assessment of chronic hepatitis B. The liver biopsy showed septal fibrosis and infiltrating lymphocyte in his liver tissue associated with degeneration of limiting plate, and histologic activity index:METAVIR score (Thio et al.) was A2-F3. He had been living in Japan all his life and had no family histories of viral hepatitis. He denied intravenous drug use and dissolute sexual behavior in Japan, but admitted occasional sexual intercourse with men in Thailand since he was 20 years old. The screening for HIV antigen/antibody test was positive and HIV infection was confirmed by the positive Western-blot HIV antibody test. The Serological HBV genotyping test by enzyme immunoassay (EIA) in the clinical laboratory testing industry (SRL Inc. Japan) showed genotype D. However, his social history was not compatible with the risk of chronically HBV gonotype D (HBV/D) infection because HBV/D is rare throughout Japan except for some areas and not prevalent among men who have sex with men (MSM). Then, HBV-DNA genotyping was performed using obtained isolates from this patient. We cloned full-length HBV isolates and determined the complete genome sequences of 2 obtained clones as previously reported (Sugauchi et al.). Briefly, the full length of HBV genome was amplified as two overlapping fragments by using the primer set to yield a 3200 bp amplicon for fragment A and another primer set to yield a 462 bp amplicon for fragment B. The fragment A or B was transferred to pGEM-T easy vector by TA cloning. The cloned plasmids of fragment A or B were sequenced and analyzed by phylogenetic analysis using MEGA6 (Tamura et al.). The Bootscaning analysis using RDP4 software (Martin et al.) revealed the clones represented as the HBV/A2 and the HBV/G/A2 recombinant strain (Fig. 1a, b). These findings indicated co-infection of HBV/A2 and HBV/G/A2. 36 nt insertion in the core region and two stop codons in the precore region were not detected in the recombinant strain because two estimated recombination junction of HBV/G were from approximately nt.192 to nt.1795 (Fig. 1b). The HBV/A2 and the HBV/G/A2 recombinant strain were compared with other registered strains including G/A recombinants by MEGA6. <PMC5014772_40064_2016_3169_Fig2_HTML_G_1_1.webp> shows the phylogenetic tree of these strains. Our HBV/G/A2 were located near the clusters of HBV/G and G/A recombinants. Our HBV/A2 belonged to the HBV/A2 cluster.
The HIV-RNA and CD4 T cell count were 4300 copies/mL and 226 cells/muL, respectively. The HIV subtype was CRF-01 AE and no primary mutations associated with drug resistance mutations were detected. Laboratory findings were as follows: platelet count, 10.6 x 104/dL; asparate aminotransferase, 84 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase, 122 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase, 272 IU/L; gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase, 34 IU/L; hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), 93,297 IU/mL; antibodies to the HBsAg (anti-HBsAg), negative; total hepatitis B core antibodies, 11.9 S/CO; HBeAg, 42.9 S/CO; antibodies to the HBeAg (anti-HBeAg), negative; HBV-DNA, >9.1 log copies/mL; hyaluronic acid, 124 ng/mL; Type IV Collagen 7 s, 7.3 ng/mL. HBV drug resistance mutations related to lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir or tenofovir were not detected. He received antiretroviral therapy (ART) consisting of tenofovir/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) and raltegravir to treat HIV-HBV/G/A2 recombinant infection. Three months after the initiation of ART, while the HBV-DNA decreased steadily, the levels of liver enzyme increased progressively with the rapid decline of HBeAg and HBsAg. The CD4 T-cell count increased to 487 cells/muL. This presentation was consistent with HIV-HBV immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). The levels of liver enzymes improved without specific treatments. The HBV-DNA decreased to 2.5 log copies/mL after 24 months of ART.

subjective.history_of_present_illness: In 2013, during follow-up at a local clinic for flu-like symptoms, the patient was found to have elevated liver enzymes, leading to referral to the hospital hepatology division for further assessment.
subjective.past_medical_history: Lifelong resident of Japan with no family history of viral hepatitis; denied intravenous drug use and dissolute sexual behavior in Japan, but reported occasional sexual intercourse with men (MSM) in Thailand since age 20.

objective.routine_investigations: Platelets 10.6 x 10^4/dL, AST 84 IU/L, ALT 122 IU/L, ALP 272 IU/L, GGT 34 IU/L, hyaluronic acid 124 ng/mL, Type IV collagen 7S 7.3 ng/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Liver biopsy showed septal fibrosis, lymphocytic infiltration, and limiting plate degeneration (METAVIR score A2-F3). Full-length HBV genome cloning, sequencing, and phylogenetic/bootscanning analysis (MEGA6, RDP4) identified coinfection with HBV/A2 and an HBV/G/A2 recombinant strain (recombination junctions ~nt 192 to nt 1795; lacking the 36-nt core insertion and two precore stop codons). assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: HIV-1 (subtype CRF-01 AE; positive Ag/Ab screen and Western blot, HIV RNA 4,300 copies/mL, CD4 226 cells/uL) and chronic hepatitis B coinfection with HBV/A2 and HBV/G/A2 recombinant strains (HBsAg 93,297 IU/mL, anti-HBs negative, total anti-HBc 11.9 S/CO, HBeAg 42.9 S/CO, anti-HBe negative, HBV DNA >9.1 log copies/mL; commercial EIA misclassified genotype as D), with METAVIR A2-F3 liver fibrosis.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initiated antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) and raltegravir. Three months after ART initiation, he developed HIV-HBV immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)—progressive liver enzyme elevation with rapid decline in HBeAg/HBsAg, steady HBV DNA decline, and CD4 increase to 487 cells/uL—which improved without specific treatment. HBV DNA decreased to 2.5 log copies/mL after 24 months of ART.

raw_case_text:
A 69-year-old man was diagnosed with post-hepatitis B cirrhosis for 20 years and presented with 2 weeks of fever. Two weeks before his admission, he developed pyrexia without obvious predisposing causes, and his highest temperature recorded was 39.6 C, with fever ocurring mainly in the afternoons. Furthermore, the patient suffered from asthenia, anorexia, mild cough, whitish sputum, and pain in the anterior chest wall without chills or abdominal pain. He had undergone a splenectomy for hypersplenism 16 years ago. During a physical examination, his temperature was 38.8 C. There were many spider angiomas in the anterior thoracic wall and decreased respiratory sound in both lungs, combined with shifting dullness and fist percussion over the liver. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 84.36 mg/L (normal range <5 mg/L) and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) level of 69 mm/h (normal range 0-43 mm/h). Liver function tests demonstrated a slight elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 59.7 U/L, total bilirubin (TBIL) at 39.7 mmol/L, and a slight decrease of albumin at 31.4 g/L. Additionally, serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level was markedly elevated to 1210 ng/ml (normal range 0-20 ng/mL). The serum adenosine deaminase (ADA) was mildly elevated to 24.4 U/L. However, an ascitic fluid examination demonstrated that ADA was normal. Negative test results were observed for purified protein derivative (PPD) and mycobacterium TB DNA. An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) test was positive. The results of coagulation function tests expressed that prothrombin time (PT) was 19.9 s (normal range 10-15 s), the international normalized ratio (INR) was 1.71, and there was 47.7% prothrombin time activity (PTA). An ultrasound (US) of the abdomen revealed signs of cirrhosis, a filling defect in the portal vein, and a large hypoechoic lesion with an irregular border and non-uniform internal echoes in the left lobe of the liver. Abdominal CT plain scans depicted a decompensated period of cirrhosis, a lobulated and inhomogeneous mass with a slightly lower density in the left lobe, measuring 13.5 cm x 6.8 cm, and the presence of ascites and bilateral pleural effusion (Figure 1). MRI, including T1- and T2-weighted imaging and contrast-enhanced with fat saturation and subsequent subtraction, revealed signs of cirrhosis and a huge mass in the left liver lobe, characterized by slightly higher non-uniform intensity, which was not significantly enhanced in the arterial phase, and mild to moderate delayed enhancement was found in the perifocal and internal septum of the venous phase and the delayed phase. In addition, the mass presented without a capsule surrounding it. The mass was hyperintense in DWI mapping. Moreover, a filling defect in the trunk of the portal vein was observed (Figure 2). The results led us to consider primary liver cancer and main portal vein tumor thrombus combined with decompensated cirrhosis.
Although discovering a space-occupying lesion of the liver on MRI and that the AFP level in the peripheral blood was extremely elevated, the first diagnosis was probably HCC. Biopsy and histology may be considered the ultimate diagnostic tests, but needle biopsy was excluded because of a high risk of bleeding; in addition, the patient declined the procedure.
To cope with fever, the patient was initially given broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment (3.0 g of cefoperazone-sulbactam every 8 h for 6 days and 0.5 g of levofloxacin every 24 h for 3 days, followed by 0.5 g of intravenous vancomycin every 12 h and 1 g of meropenem every 8 h via intravenous drip infusion for 3 days). After 12 days, the fever persisted (the highest temperature recorded was 38.2 C.). Although there was no direct evidence of TB infection, primary hepatic TB was suspected based on clinical symptoms, and an anti-TB therapeutic diagnosis was given. The patient was treated with 0.75 g of anti-TB oral ethambutol every 24 h and 0.6 g of amikacin every 24 h via intravenous drip infusion for 10 days; after that, the patient maintained a normal temperature (36.5 C). Anti-TB treatment continued at the same dosage for the following 15 days, with supplemental isoniazid at 0.3 g/24 h. In the days and weeks following the patient's coagulopathy correction, we repeatedly offered him a biopsy, but he declined it. The patient was then discharged from the hospital.
The patient received tuberculostatic therapy with amikacin, isoniazid, and ethambutol for 6 months. The level of AFP had completely normalized upon review after stopping the medication for 20 weeks, and the imaging displayed that the mass on the left liver lobe had disappeared, the portal vein filling defect had markedly reduced, and ascites and bilateral pleural effusion reduced in the patient (Figure 3). At the 2-year follow-up, no evidence of recurrence was observed (Figure 4), and the patient had recovered well. The final diagnosis was predominantly that of hepatic TB based on the disappearance of the lesions, and the level of AFP gradually returned to normal after the patient had been given anti-TB therapy for 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old man presenting with a 2-week history of afternoon fevers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to admission, the patient developed unprovoked pyrexia occurring predominantly in the afternoons (highest temperature 39.6°C), accompanied by asthenia, anorexia, mild cough with whitish sputum, and anterior chest wall pain. He denied chills or abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Post-hepatitis B cirrhosis diagnosed 20 years prior; splenectomy for hypersplenism 16 years ago.
subjective.review_of_systems: Constitutional: afternoon fevers up to 39.6°C, asthenia, anorexia; denies chills. Respiratory: mild cough with whitish sputum, anterior chest wall pain. Gastrointestinal: denies abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: Temperature 38.8°C. Skin: Numerous spider angiomas on the anterior thoracic wall. Pulmonary: Decreased breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen: Shifting dullness and positive fist percussion over the liver.
objective.routine_investigations: CRP 84.36 mg/L (normal <5), ESR 69 mm/h (normal 0-43). LFTs: AST 59.7 U/L, TBIL 39.7 mmol/L, albumin 31.4 g/L. AFP markedly elevated at 1,210 ng/mL (normal 0-20). Serum ADA mildly elevated at 24.4 U/L. Coagulation: PT 19.9 s (normal 10-15), INR 1.71, PTA 47.7%. PPD and Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA negative; IGRA positive. Abdominal ultrasound showed cirrhosis, a portal vein filling defect, and a large irregular hypoechoic lesion with non-uniform internal echoes in the left liver lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Ascitic fluid examination: normal ADA. Plain abdominal CT: decompensated cirrhosis, 13.5 cm x 6.8 cm lobulated inhomogeneous slightly hypodense left liver lobe mass, ascites, and bilateral pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced liver MRI (T1, T2, fat-sat, subtraction, DWI): cirrhosis, large unencapsulated left lobe mass with slightly higher non-uniform intensity, minimal arterial enhancement, mild-to-moderate delayed peripheral/septal enhancement, DWI hyperintensity, and a main portal vein trunk filling defect. Needle biopsy was excluded due to high bleeding risk and patient refusal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Primary hepatic tuberculosis (predominant final diagnosis, initially mimicking hepatocellular carcinoma with main portal vein tumor thrombus given AFP 1,210 ng/mL and 13.5 x 6.8 cm mass) in a patient with decompensated post-hepatitis B cirrhosis, diagnosed clinically by positive IGRA and complete radiologic/biochemical resolution on anti-TB therapy (PPD and MTB DNA negative; biopsy declined).

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Failed 12 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefoperazone-sulbactam 3.0 g q8h x 6 days, levofloxacin 0.5 g q24h x 3 days, then IV vancomycin 0.5 g q12h + meropenem 1 g q8h x 3 days) with persistent fever up to 38.2°C. Therapeutic anti-TB trial with oral ethambutol 0.75 g q24h and IV amikacin 0.6 g q24h achieved defervescence (36.5°C) after 10 days; isoniazid 0.3 g q24h was added for 15 days and he completed 6 months of amikacin, isoniazid, and ethambutol. Twenty weeks post-treatment, AFP normalized completely, the left hepatic mass disappeared, the portal vein filling defect markedly reduced, and ascites/pleural effusions decreased; at 2-year follow-up, he remained well with no recurrence.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old, no smoker Caucasian woman was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in September 2021. In August 2021, she had undergone a right breast core biopsy, and histological examination diagnosed invasive ductal breast cancer: hormonal receptor status (ER and PgR) was positive, HER2 was not overexpressed, Ki-67 was 60%.
In September 2021, staging with 18FDG PET/CT detected breast disease, axillary and mediastinal lymph node metastases, humerus, iliac and ischium bone metastases; contrast-enhanced breast MRI and bone scintigraphy both confirmed metastatic disease.
Combination therapy with Ribociclib 600mg/die for 21 days with 28-days cycle plus Letrozole 2.5mg/day plus Triptorelin 3.75mg every four weeks was adopted as first-line treatment for this pre-menopausal, hormone receptor-positive and HER2-negative MBC. Patient had no other comorbidities and did not assume drugs before starting therapy.
Before proceeding with treatment, we evaluated infectious markers, and found hepatitis B serology positive for infection as reported below:
T0 -September 2021.
- HBsAg positive
- HBV DNA 4383 IU/mL
- HBsAb Negative
- HBcAb IgG Positive
- HBcAb IgM Negative
- HBeAg Negative
- Normal transaminases and liver function tests; no HDV coinfection.
The assessment of hepatic fibrosis by a transient elastography (fibroscan), reported a value of hepatic stiffness of 3.3 kPa and of CAP (Controlled Attenuation Parameter) of 199dB/m, indicative of absence of fibrosis and steatosis.
Following the hepatologist's recommendations, the patient started treatment with Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 245 mg/day for her diagnosis of hepatitis B HBeAb positive with the recommendation to check hepatitis B status (quantitative HBV-DNA) and liver function weekly, especially during the first month of treatment with Ribociclib.
As such, during the first cycle of treatment with Ribociclib in September 2021, we carried out weekly evaluations of HBV DNA levels, which significantly decreased (28 UI/ml) and subsequently negativized (<10 UI/ml) ( Figure 1 ).
After three cycles of treatment with Ribociclib, in January 2022, 18FDG PET plus contrast-enhanced CT and breast MRI were repeated ( <PMC10285519_fonc-13-1184952-g002_A_1_2.webp><PMC10285519_fonc-13-1184952-g002_B_2_2.webp> ). The patient achieved a complete metabolic response and a partial response of disease (PR), according to Response Evaluation Criteria for Solid Tumors [RECIST1.1 ].
Compared to September 2021, there were no areas of uptake at the 18FDG PET and there was a significant reduction of the breast site, lymph node and bone metastases in the contrast-enhanced CT and breast MRI; revaluations were performed in May 2022, when 18FDG PET, contrast-enhanced CT and breast MRI confirmed disease stability ( Figure 3 ), and in September 2022 (stable disease).
Both times, HBV DNA levels continued to be undetectable.
Most importantly, treatment was well tolerated - with hematological toxicity not more than grade 2 according to CTCAE criteria and no need for dose reduction. No febrile neutropenia or QTc prolongation were reported; no liver toxicity emerged and the patient did not experience episodes of fatigue. Moreover, despite undergoing such an intense treatment, patient's mood was constantly good; she did not ask or manifest need of psychological support and, to the date, patient shows a positive thinking and feelings of gratitude ( <PMC10285519_fonc-13-1184952-g004_undivided_1_1.webp> ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old Caucasian female presenting for pre-treatment infectious screening prior to initiating systemic therapy for newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed with hormone receptor-positive (ER and PgR positive), HER2-negative invasive ductal breast cancer (Ki-67 60%) via right breast core biopsy in August 2021, with staging in September 2021 confirming axillary and mediastinal lymph node metastases and humerus, iliac, and ischium bone metastases. Prior to starting first-line therapy with ribociclib, letrozole, and triptorelin, baseline infectious markers were evaluated in September 2021. No acute hepatic symptoms were reported.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pre-menopausal, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic invasive ductal breast cancer (diagnosed August-September 2021). Non-smoker; no other comorbidities and no medications prior to oncologic therapy.

objective.routine_investigations: Baseline infectious screening (T0, September 2021): HBsAg positive, HBsAb negative, HBcAb IgG positive, HBcAb IgM negative, HBeAg negative (HBeAb positive); normal transaminases and liver function tests; no HDV coinfection.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline quantitative HBV DNA (September 2021): 4,383 IU/mL. Transient elastography (FibroScan): hepatic stiffness 3.3 kPa, Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP) 199 dB/m (no fibrosis or steatosis). Oncologic staging (September 2021): 18FDG PET/CT, contrast-enhanced breast MRI, and bone scintigraphy confirmed right breast tumor with axillary/mediastinal lymph node and humerus, iliac, and ischium bone metastases. Re-staging (January 2022, May 2022, September 2022): 18FDG PET, contrast-enhanced CT, and breast MRI showed complete metabolic response and RECIST 1.1 partial response, followed by stable disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic HBeAg-negative (HBeAb-positive) hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection without hepatic fibrosis or steatosis (HBsAg positive, HBcAb IgG positive, HBV DNA 4,383 IU/mL, FibroScan 3.3 kPa, CAP 199 dB/m) in a patient starting CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy for metastatic breast cancer. Hepatitis D virus (HDV) coinfection was excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Per hepatology advice, initiated tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 245 mg/day alongside ribociclib 600 mg/day (21 days of a 28-day cycle), letrozole 2.5 mg/day, and triptorelin 3.75 mg every 4 weeks, with weekly HBV DNA and liver function monitoring during the first month. HBV DNA dropped to 28 IU/mL and became undetectable (<10 IU/mL) during cycle 1, remaining undetectable in May and September 2022. Treatment was well tolerated with no liver toxicity, no febrile neutropenia, no QTc prolongation, no fatigue, and hematological toxicity <= grade 2 (CTCAE) without dose reduction; she achieved complete metabolic response and sustained disease stability.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man, living in Yichang City, Hubei Province, with the diagnosis of hepatitis B virus-DNA (HBV-DNA)-positive chronic severe hepatitis, was admitted to the department of hematology in the local hospital because of intermittent fever of 1-month duration; his maximum body temperature was up to 40 C. The patient had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province a month earlier, but this clue did not raise concerns for the clinicians. The physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. The positive findings in the laboratory results included hepatic abnormality with alanine transaminase (ALT) 490 U/L (0-40 U/L), aspartate transaminase (AST) 558 U/L (0-40 U/L), total-value bilirubin (TBIL) 23.23 mumol/L (5.1-28.0), direct bilirubin (DBIL) 14.37 (0-10), total protein (TP) 51.54 g/L (65-85), albumin (ALB) 26.83 g/L (40-55), and HBV-DNA 3.19 * 104 IU/ml (<1.0 * 102 IU/ml). The results of routine blood examination were slightly disordered, with white blood cell (WBC) 3.12 * 109/L and platelets (PLT) 100 * 109/L. An enhanced CT scan was performed, which showed an enlarged spleen with sustained strengthening multinodular ( Figures 1B-D ), and angioma was suspected. No other abnormalities in bone marrow lesions were identified by CT images. The patient received a positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT), which showed a significant diffuse increase in the uptake of FDG in the splenomegaly and slightly diffuse FDG uptake in the bone marrow ( Figures 1A, E-G ). After 2 weeks of antibiotic and cortical therapy, the patient still had intermittent fever with progressive deterioration in routine laboratory examinations including WBC 0.95 * 109/L, PLT 56 * 109, ALT 524 U/L (0-40 U/L), and AST 640 U/L (0-40 U/L).
In addition, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice to confirm the previous diagnosis with an interval of 2 months, and the results showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Regarding these clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was highly suspected. After the chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), the patient was discharged from the hospital in remission. Nevertheless, he was readmitted to the hospital again for persistent fever and pancytopenia 2 months later. The patient underwent splenectomy to confirm the initial diagnosis and remove a significant burden of disease. He also received antiviral treatment with entecavir due to the history of severe hepatitis B. Subsequently, the postoperative histopathological analysis indicated diffuse proliferation of extracellular and intra-macrophage amastigotes in the spleen. At this stage, the third bone marrow biopsy was performed again, and Leishmania amastigotes were found. Eventually, the patient received lipid amphotericin B therapy and related symptomatic treatment, which showed excellent clinical improvement within 1 week of treatment, and his serum ALT and AST levels all dropped to the normal range. There was no recurrence of leishmaniasis over 1 year.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male presenting with a 1-month history of intermittent fever (up to 40 C).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed intermittent fever reaching up to 40 C 1 month prior to admission to the local hospital hematology department. After 2 weeks of antibiotic and corticosteroid therapy, intermittent fever persisted alongside progressive worsening of cytopenias and transaminitis. Following transient remission and discharge after therapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, he was readmitted 2 months later for persistent fever and pancytopenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: HBV-DNA-positive chronic severe hepatitis B. Epidemiological exposure: Resident of Yichang City, Hubei Province; worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province 1 month prior to illness onset.

objective.physical_examination: Maximum body temperature up to 40 C. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: ALT 490 U/L (0-40 U/L), AST 558 U/L (0-40 U/L), total bilirubin 23.23 umol/L (5.1-28.0), direct bilirubin 14.37 (0-10), total protein 51.54 g/L (65-85), albumin 26.83 g/L (40-55), HBV-DNA 3.19 x 10^4 IU/mL (<1.0 x 10^2 IU/mL), WBC 3.12 x 10^9/L, platelets 100 x 10^9/L. After 2 weeks of antibiotics and corticosteroids: WBC 0.95 x 10^9/L, platelets 56 x 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L (0-40 U/L), AST 640 U/L (0-40 U/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced CT showed splenomegaly with sustained enhancing multinodular lesions (initially suspected as angioma) and no bone marrow lesions. PET/CT demonstrated significantly increased diffuse FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen and slightly diffuse FDG uptake in the bone marrow. Two bone marrow aspirations and biopsies performed 2 months apart showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Post-splenectomy splenic histopathology revealed diffuse proliferation of extracellular and intra-macrophage amastigotes; a third bone marrow biopsy demonstrated Leishmania amastigotes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic severe hepatitis B virus infection (HBV-DNA 3.19 x 10^4 IU/mL) co-existing with visceral leishmaniasis (confirmed by Leishmania amastigotes on splenectomy histopathology and third bone marrow biopsy) complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), initially misdiagnosed as suspected splenic angioma and splenic lymphoma.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Failed initial 2-week antibiotic and corticosteroid therapy; transiently remitted following HLH chemotherapy before relapsing 2 months later. Underwent splenectomy and received antiviral therapy with entecavir for severe hepatitis B. Following diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis, he was treated with lipid amphotericin B and symptomatic therapy, achieving marked clinical improvement within 1 week and normalization of serum ALT and AST, with no recurrence of leishmaniasis over 1 year.

raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old mother of two children was diagnosed with HIV infection at the 8-week mark of her last pregnancy and started on a tenofovir/lamivudine/efavirenz combination antiretroviral therapy with good HIV disease control (CD4 count of 844 cells/m3 and a suppressed HIV viral load).
She presented to the department of Gynaecology 4 months post-partum with a 2-week history of metrorrhagia and intermittent epistaxis that had worsened in the preceding 4 days prior to presentation. She was treated symptomatically by transfusion of two units of blood and one unit of frozen dried plasma and vitamin K in view of elevated international normalised ratio (INR) level. Gynaecological pathology was excluded, and the Department of Internal Medicine was consulted to take over patient management since she had a deranged liver function test. She also reported significant weight loss (27 kg) over a period of 4 months with no other associated symptoms. The patient had used traditional medicine in the form of scarification but reported no history of herbal ingestion. She had no previous surgery with no family history of malignancies. Obstetric history revealed that both her pregnancies were delivered by normal vaginal delivery, with her first and second pregnancies at age 14 years and 29 years, respectively. Her last delivery was complicated by a post-partum haemorrhage requiring red cell blood transfusion with no complications thereafter. She was employed as a general worker at a pharmacy with no history of smoking but reported occasional recreational use of alcohol.
Significant findings on clinical examination revealed generalised muscle wasting, a tattoo on her right upper arm with stria on the torso and arms. She was pale, anicteric with subcentimeter epitrochlear and axillary lymphadenopathy. She had no skin bruising nor any stigmata of chronic liver disease or liver cirrhosis. Abdominal examination revealed scarification marks in the epigastric region and hepatomegaly (liver span of 18 cm) with no other palpable masses.
Blood investigations revealed severe normocytic normochromic anaemia, deranged liver function (mixed pattern), and elevated INR. Hepatitis studies revealed a picture of chronic active hepatitis B infection in view of the positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg). HBV viral load was rejected due to an insufficient blood sample submitted to the laboratory. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) was marginally elevated at 22.9 microg/L (0-10 microg/L) (Table 1). A search on the National Health Laboratory Services (NHLS) Labtrack  system revealed that blood tests done 5 years before her presentation had shown a positive HBsAg and an alanine transaminase (ALT) of 75 U/L (42-98). Importantly, the patient was not aware of this diagnosis, and neither was there any further monitoring instituted.
Abdominal ultrasonography at this presentation demonstrated an enlarged liver measuring 17.28 cm with multiple heterogeneous ill-defined lesions on the left lobe, the largest measuring 8.12 cm x 5.24 cm. No portal hypertension, free fluid, or other lesions were identified (Figure 1). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed gross hepatomegaly with multiple intrahepatic lesions, and on the arterial phase, there is intense enhancement of the lesion supplied by the left hepatic artery. The lesion is relatively isodence on the delayed phase and the venous phase. Considerations included a multifocal HCC or primary hepatic lymphoma (Figure 2(a) and (b)). Lung parenchymal nodules were also noted, which were thought to be metastatic in origin. As imaging was not definitively diagnostic in this case, an ultrasound-guided liver biopsy was performed with subsequent light microscopy and immunohistochemical stains of the liver tissue. Histology confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma (Figure 3(a)-(c)). In addition, the hepatitis B core antigen immunoperoxidase stain was positive in the adjacent liver tissue, which was consistent with active hepatitis B virus infection (Figure 3(d)-(f)).
During hospitalisation, the patient was further transfused two units of red blood cells to optimise the low haemoglobin. During counselling, it was noted that the patient was not aware of the history of HBV infection as alluded above. She was then advised to get her children and her sexual partner tested for HBV infection. She was referred to the Department of Oncology for further management, where she was assessed as having advanced stage (c) HCC with lung metastasis according to the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) algorithm.   Her treatment plan included receiving six cycles of Doxorubicin  since this is the drug available in the public hospital in South Africa. Unfortunately, the patient demised at home 2 months later following her diagnosis before initiation of chemotherapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old female presenting 4 months postpartum with a 2-week history of metrorrhagia and intermittent epistaxis (worsening over 4 days) and 27 kg weight loss over 4 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months postpartum, the patient presented to the Gynecology department with a 2-week history of metrorrhagia and intermittent epistaxis that worsened during the 4 days prior to presentation. She also reported 27 kg weight loss over 4 months with no other associated symptoms. Gynecological pathology was excluded, and Internal Medicine assumed care due to deranged liver function tests.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV diagnosed at 8 weeks of her most recent pregnancy, well controlled on tenofovir/lamivudine/efavirenz (CD4 count 844 cells/m^3, suppressed HIV viral load). Retrospective NHLS Labtrack records showed positive HBsAg and ALT 75 U/L (42-98) 5 years prior (patient unaware and unmonitored). Obstetric history: two normal vaginal deliveries (ages 14 and 29), second delivery complicated by postpartum hemorrhage requiring red blood cell transfusion. No previous surgery; no family history of malignancy. Social/exposure history: Traditional scarification (no herbal ingestion); pharmacy general worker; non-smoker; occasional recreational alcohol use; tattoo on right upper arm.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports 27 kg weight loss over 4 months with no other associated symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: General: Generalized muscle wasting, pale, anicteric; no skin bruising or stigmata of chronic liver disease or cirrhosis. Skin: Tattoo on right upper arm, striae on torso and arms, epigastric scarification marks. Lymph nodes: Subcentimeter epitrochlear and axillary lymphadenopathy. Abdomen: Hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm) with no other palpable masses.
objective.routine_investigations: Severe normocytic normochromic anemia, mixed-pattern deranged liver function tests, elevated INR. Hepatitis serology: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive (HBV viral load rejected due to insufficient sample). Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) 22.9 ug/L (0-10 ug/L). HIV CD4 count 844 cells/m^3, suppressed HIV viral load. Abdominal ultrasound: Enlarged liver (17.28 cm) with multiple heterogeneous ill-defined left-lobe lesions (largest 8.12 cm x 5.24 cm); no portal hypertension or free fluid.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: Gross hepatomegaly with multiple intrahepatic lesions demonstrating intense arterial-phase enhancement supplied by the left hepatic artery and relative isodensity on venous and delayed phases (differential: multifocal HCC vs. primary hepatic lymphoma), plus pulmonary parenchymal nodules suspected to be metastatic. Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy: Histology confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma; immunoperoxidase staining of adjacent liver tissue was positive for hepatitis B core antigen.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic active hepatitis B virus infection (HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, HBcAg-positive adjacent liver tissue, with prior HBsAg positivity 5 years earlier) complicated by advanced BCLC stage C hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with suspected pulmonary metastases (confirmed by liver biopsy), in an HIV-positive patient on antiretroviral therapy. Gynecological pathology and primary hepatic lymphoma were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Stabilized with blood products (2 units red blood cells, 1 unit freeze-dried plasma, and vitamin K initially, followed by 2 additional units of red blood cells). Counseled regarding HBV diagnosis and advised HBV testing for her children and sexual partner. Referred to Oncology for planned 6 cycles of doxorubicin chemotherapy; however, she died at home 2 months after diagnosis prior to starting chemotherapy.

raw_case_text: The patient was a 27 year old man, followed at Hassan II University Hospital of Fez for chronic hepatitis B discovered during an asthenia check-up in 2014. He had a level of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) equal to 1.26 times ULN and ULN aspartate aminotransferase (AST). The HBs Antigen was positive, Antigene HBe positive with HBe Ac negative and a viral load of 45144142 IU/ml (8.06 log IU/ml). The blood test was normal, hemoglobin=18.10dL, leukocyte=5.12*103muL, poly neutrophils=1.62*103muL, lympocytes=2.85*103muL, platelet=218*103muL, serological test for hepatitis (hepatitis C, Hepatitis D), HIV and sypilica was negative. Liver ultrasonography was normal and the fibroscan showed an elasticity of 5.6 Kpa. For reasons of financial means, the patient was out of sight. In 2017, he reconsulted with cytolysis, ALT=5.74 times ULN, AST=2.06 times ULN, a viral load of 6.63 log IU/ml. The fibroscan was redone with an elasticity measured at 10.8 Kpa. Thus a liver biopsy was performed, giving a Metavir score of A1F2. An antiviral treatment based on tenofovir was prescribed but was only started in January 2019 with an improvement of the hepatic assessment and a viral load at S24 at 260 UI/ml. In April 2020, he presented with a SARS-CoV-2 infection and reported that he was no longer on antiviral B therapy. The patient had presented with influenza-like illness with headache, myalgia and fever of 38.3 C. His liver workup was disturbed with ALT at 4.4 times ULN, AST at 2.04 times ULN, GGT at 1.4 times ULN. Cardiac, respiratory and blood counts were normal. Chest CT scan showed 2 nodules in the right upper lobe of frosted glass with minimal damage estimated at <10%. Management consisted of emergency resumption of Tenofovir in combination with low-dose azythomycin and HCQ. At d14 of his hospitalization. At d18, the ALT and AST levels were 6 times ULN and 2.74 times ULN respectively. At d21, his CT scan showed a total regression of the lesions. He was hospitalized for 35 days. At discharge, the patient's liver function tests improved with a decrease in transaminase levels from baseline from 4.4 times ULN to 3.66 times ULN and from 2 times ULN to 1.44 times ULN for ALT and AST respectively. In July 2020, the patient had a normal liver function test with a negative viral load.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male presenting with an influenza-like illness consisting of headache, myalgia, and fever (38.3 C), on a background of chronic hepatitis B.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had previously started tenofovir in January 2019 for chronic hepatitis B (achieving a week-24 viral load of 260 IU/mL), presented in April 2020 with an influenza-like illness featuring headache, myalgia, and fever of 38.3 C, and reported having discontinued his hepatitis B antiviral therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic hepatitis B discovered during an asthenia check-up in 2014 (HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, anti-HBe negative, HBV viral load 45,144,142 IU/mL [8.06 log IU/mL], ALT 1.26x ULN, AST normal; normal liver ultrasound, FibroScan 5.6 kPa; HCV, HDV, HIV, and syphilis negative). Lost to follow-up due to financial constraints; re-presented in 2017 with cytolysis (ALT 5.74x ULN, AST 2.06x ULN, viral load 6.63 log IU/mL, FibroScan 10.8 kPa, liver biopsy Metavir A1F2). Started tenofovir in January 2019 with improved hepatic tests and week-24 viral load 260 IU/mL, then stopped therapy prior to April 2020.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports headache and myalgia.

objective.physical_examination: Fever of 38.3 C; cardiac and respiratory examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline (2014): Hemoglobin 18.10 g/dL, leukocytes 5.12 x 10^3/uL (neutrophils 1.62 x 10^3/uL, lymphocytes 2.85 x 10^3/uL), platelets 218 x 10^3/uL; HCV, HDV, HIV, and syphilis negative; normal liver ultrasound. April 2020 presentation: Blood counts normal; ALT 4.4x ULN, AST 2.04x ULN, GGT 1.4x ULN. Hospital day 18: ALT 6x ULN, AST 2.74x ULN. At discharge (day 35): ALT 3.66x ULN, AST 1.44x ULN. July 2020: Normal liver function tests and negative viral load.
objective.advanced_workup: Prior staging: FibroScan 5.6 kPa (2014) progressing to 10.8 kPa (2017); liver biopsy (2017) Metavir score A1F2. April 2020 chest CT: 2 ground-glass ('frosted glass') nodules in the right upper lobe with minimal parenchymal damage (<10%). Day 21 chest CT: Total regression of pulmonary lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Acute flare/reactivation of chronic hepatitis B (Metavir A1F2, following antiviral discontinuation) concurrent with SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia with <10% right upper lobe involvement). Hepatitis C, hepatitis D, HIV, and syphilis had been excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Managed with urgent resumption of tenofovir combined with low-dose azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ). Transaminases peaked at hospital day 18 (ALT 6x ULN, AST 2.74x ULN) before improving; day 21 chest CT showed total regression of pulmonary lesions. Discharged after 35 days of hospitalization with improved transaminases (ALT 3.66x ULN, AST 1.44x ULN); by July 2020, liver function tests normalized and HBV viral load was negative.

raw_case_text: A 60-year-old man was referred to our hospital for raised serum creatinine. The patient had abdominal pain for 15 days, which was mild, vague and non-radiating. It was followed by bilateral pedal edema in a day and in next three days followed by sudden onset bilateral foot drop with numbness. Patient gave history of nausea, vomiting, skin rash, anorexia and malaise since 20 days. He had weight loss of 10 kg in last 20 days. The past medical history was unremarkable. Alcohol consumption and drug abuse were absent. On physical examination, temperature was 38.4 C, blood pressure was 160/100 mm Hg, pulse rate 84/min and respiratory rate 20/min. Pedal edema was pitting, bilateral. Macular skin rashes around both ankles were present. Testicular tenderness was present. There was sensory and motor involvement in bilateral tibia and peroneal nerve distribution. Funduscopic examination showed grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy. Laboratory examination revealed a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dl, white blood cell count of 24000/microl, platelet count of 485000/microl. Serum creatinine was 2.4 mg/dl, blood urea nitrogen 102 mg/dl, potassium 5.0 mEq/l, albumin 3.1 g/dl, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U/l, alanine aminotransferase 20 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 131 U/l and total cholesterol 198 mg/dl. Prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times were normal. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria, with two to three oval fat bodies per high-power field. Protein excretion was 3.4 g/day. Bence jones proteinuria, urine immunoelectrophoresis showed non selective proteinuria. On admission, HBsAg, HBeAg and anti-HBc IgM were positive. Anti-HBs, anti-HBe, anti-HCV and anti-HIV were negative. Serum HBV-DNA level (PCR) was 582917 copies/ml. ANA, anti-dsDNA, RF, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, and cryoglobulins were negative. Serum C3 and C4 complement levels were normal. Chest x-ray and electrocardiography were normal. The nerve conduction study was compatible with axonal and demyelinating polyneuropathy in bilateral lower limbs. A kidney biopsy was performed due to nephrotic range proteinuria and revealed membranous nephropathy (MN). All glomeruli were mildly enlarged. Capillary lumina were open and lined by thickened membranes and there was spikes on the external side of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) (Jones stain). Mild uniform matrix accentuation with normal cell distribution was noted. Tubules were moderately degenerated. Interstitial area was moderately prominent for edema with leucocyte infiltration. Immunofluorescence study, showed significant granular IgG deposition along the membranes of capillary in a diffuse pattern (Figure 1). There was no immunofluorescent staining for fibrinogen, IgA, or IgM. Congo-red staining for amyloid was negative. A liver biopsy was not performed. Doppler study for renal vessels was normal and there were no microaneurysms characteristic of PAN. Prednisolone (60 mg/day), plasmapheresis (5courses) and entecavir (0.5 mg/ every second day) were started. At 2 months follow up, patient improved in the form of grade 3/5 power in both lower limbs with sensory improvement. Twenty-four hours proteinuria decreased to 800 mg/day and serum creatinine was 1.5 mg/dl with no pedal edema.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male referred for elevated serum creatinine, with a 20-day history of nausea, vomiting, skin rash, anorexia, malaise, and 10 kg weight loss, 15 days of abdominal pain, bilateral pedal edema, and sudden-onset bilateral foot drop with numbness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Twenty days prior to presentation, the patient developed nausea, vomiting, skin rash, anorexia, malaise, and a 10 kg weight loss. Fifteen days prior to presentation, he developed mild, vague, non-radiating abdominal pain, followed 1 day later by bilateral pedal edema, and 3 days later by sudden-onset bilateral foot drop with numbness. He was referred for evaluation of elevated serum creatinine.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history. No history of alcohol consumption or drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports nausea, vomiting, skin rash, anorexia, malaise, 10 kg weight loss over 20 days, and lower limb numbness.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: Temperature 38.4 C, blood pressure 160/100 mmHg, pulse rate 84/min, respiratory rate 20/min. Funduscopy: Grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy. Skin/Extremities: Bilateral pitting pedal edema; macular skin rashes around both ankles. Genitourinary: Testicular tenderness. Neurological: Bilateral foot drop with sensory and motor involvement in bilateral tibial and peroneal nerve distributions.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC: Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, WBC 24,000/uL, platelets 485,000/uL. Biochemistry: Serum creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, BUN 102 mg/dL, potassium 5.0 mEq/L, albumin 3.1 g/dL, AST 27 U/L, ALT 20 U/L, ALP 131 U/L, total cholesterol 198 mg/dL; PT and PTT normal. Urinalysis: Proteinuria with 2-3 oval fat bodies/HPF; 24-hour urine protein 3.4 g/day; non-selective proteinuria on urine immunoelectrophoresis (Bence Jones proteinuria noted). Serology: HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc IgM positive; anti-HBs, anti-HBe, anti-HCV, and anti-HIV negative. Autoimmune/complement: ANA, anti-dsDNA, RF, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, and cryoglobulins negative; C3 and C4 normal. Chest X-ray and ECG normal. Renal Doppler ultrasound normal with no microaneurysms.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum HBV-DNA (PCR): 582,917 copies/mL. Nerve conduction study: Compatible with bilateral lower limb axonal and demyelinating polyneuropathy. Kidney biopsy: Membranous nephropathy (MN) with mildly enlarged glomeruli, open capillary lumina lined by thickened membranes, external GBM spikes (Jones stain), mild uniform matrix accentuation, moderate tubular degeneration, and interstitial edema with leukocyte infiltration; immunofluorescence showed diffuse granular IgG deposition along capillary membranes (negative for fibrinogen, IgA, IgM); Congo red stain negative for amyloid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Acute hepatitis B virus infection (HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc IgM positive; HBV-DNA 582,917 copies/mL) complicated by HBV-associated membranous nephropathy (nephrotic-range proteinuria 3.4 g/day, biopsy-confirmed), bilateral axonal and demyelinating polyneuropathy (bilateral foot drop), ankle macular rash, and testicular tenderness. Hepatitis C, HIV, systemic lupus erythematosus, ANCA-associated vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, renal amyloidosis (negative Congo red), and polyarteritis nodosa (no renal microaneurysms on Doppler) were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initiated on prednisolone 60 mg/day, 5 courses of plasmapheresis, and entecavir 0.5 mg every second day. At 2-month follow-up, lower limb motor power improved to grade 3/5 bilaterally with sensory improvement, 24-hour proteinuria decreased to 800 mg/day, serum creatinine improved to 1.5 mg/dL, and pedal edema resolved.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old woman had abdominal pain, diarrhea and fever in July 2006. Because of persistent symptoms, she was hospitalized in August 2006. A cobblestone-like appearance was seen in the sigmoid colon upon colonoscopy. On the basis of the results of detailed examination, she was diagnosed as having colonic CD. Since she had severe CD with a Crohn's disease activity index (CDAI) of 373 and needed prompt and effective treatment, treatment with IFX at 5 mg/kg and 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) at 30 mg/day was initiated in September 2006. Laboratory findings at the initiation of treatment included an aspartate transaminase (AST) level of 22 IU/l, an alanine transaminase (ALT) level of 22 IU/l and negative HBsAg. She was not tested for anti-HBsAb and anti-HBcAb. At week 10 of IFX therapy, symptoms were alleviated (CDAI: 56), and remission was successfully induced. IFX was administered at weeks 0, 2 and 6 and every 8 weeks thereafter, and remission was successfully maintained. Colonoscopy about 1 year after the initiation of treatment revealed colonic mucosal healing with scarring. However, about 1 year after the initiation of IFX therapy, she began to experience delayed-onset hypersensitivity reactions to IFX such as fever and joint pain. We thus considered switching biologic therapy from IFX to ADA. On October 8, 2010, 4 years and 1 month after the first administration of IFX, the 30th and final administration of IFX was given, and her hepatic function was normal (AST 16 IU/l, ALT 21 IU/l). On December 12, 2010, hepatic function test immediately before the first administration of ADA revealed mild hepatic dysfunction (AST 61 IU/l, ALT 54 IU/l). Since no abnormal hepatic function had been found before and the cause was unknown, she received 160 mg of ADA on that day and was followed up thereafter. On December 17, 2010, although hepatic enzyme levels were still high, she received 80 mg of ADA.
On January 4, 2011, since she felt generalized malaise with an AST of 322 IU/l and an ALT of 527 IU/l, she was hospitalized for detailed examination and treatment (<PMC3934813_crg-0008-0044-g01_undivided_1_1.webp>). Examinations revealed HBsAg of 250 IU/ml and HBV DNA of >9.0 log copies/ml. HBV genotype was type C, and anti-hepatitis C virus antibody (anti-HCVAb) was negative (table 1). Virological testing of a sample obtained from her husband revealed negative results for HBsAg and anti-HBcAb and no detection of HBV DNA. Sexual transmission of HBV from her husband and others was ruled out. Abdominal echo and computed tomography examination showed no evidence of chronic hepatic disorder. Liver biopsy revealed mild fibrosis (A2/F1). These findings supported the presence of hepatic disorder due to HBV. Although no data on HBV DNA and anti-HBcAb before onset were available, her clinical course suggested de novo hepatitis B due to reactivation of HBV related to the treatment with IFX and 6-MP.
On January 5, 2011, antiviral treatment with ETV at 0.5 mg/day was initiated. Treatment with ADA was suspended after the first two administrations, but treatment with 6-MP was continued. Ten sessions of granulocytapheresis were conducted to maintain remission of CD. AST and ALT levels peaked at 440 IU/l and 624 IU/l, respectively, on January 14, 2011, and then decreased gradually over time. On March 29, 2011, hepatic function returned to normal (AST 30 IU/l, ALT 24 IU/l). Since negative HBV DNA results were obtained in June 2011, treatment with ADA was reintroduced (<PMC3934813_crg-0008-0044-g02_undivided_1_1.webp>). Since then she has continued treatment with ETV and has maintained normal levels of AST, ALT and HBV DNA without recurrence of hepatitis B. 10 months after treatment with ETV, her anti-HBsAb turned positive. She has also continued ADA and has maintained mucosal integrity and clinical remission without gastrointestinal symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old female with colonic Crohn's disease presenting with generalized malaise and markedly elevated liver transaminases.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had received infliximab (IFX) and 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) for colonic Crohn's disease since September 2006 (baseline AST 22 IU/L, ALT 22 IU/L, HBsAg negative; anti-HBsAb and anti-HBcAb not tested), developed delayed-onset hypersensitivity reactions (fever and joint pain) to IFX after 1 year and received her 30th and final IFX dose on October 8, 2010 (AST 16 IU/L, ALT 21 IU/L). Immediately before starting adalimumab (ADA) on December 12, 2010, liver enzymes were mildly elevated (AST 61 IU/L, ALT 54 IU/L); she received ADA 160 mg on December 12 and 80 mg on December 17 despite persistently elevated liver enzymes. On January 4, 2011, she developed generalized malaise with AST 322 IU/L and ALT 527 IU/L and was hospitalized.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe colonic Crohn's disease diagnosed in August 2006 (presented July 2006 with abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever; cobblestone-like sigmoid colon on colonoscopy; CDAI 373), treated with infliximab 5 mg/kg (weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks; 30 total doses through October 2010) and 6-mercaptopurine 30 mg/day, achieving remission (CDAI 56 at week 10; mucosal healing with scarring on 1-year colonoscopy). Delayed hypersensitivity reactions to IFX (fever, joint pain). Switched to adalimumab in December 2010. Epidemiological note: Husband tested negative for HBsAg, anti-HBcAb, and HBV DNA.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports generalized malaise.

objective.routine_investigations: September 2006 baseline: AST 22 IU/L, ALT 22 IU/L, HBsAg negative. October 8, 2010: AST 16 IU/L, ALT 21 IU/L. December 12, 2010: AST 61 IU/L, ALT 54 IU/L. January 4, 2011 admission: AST 322 IU/L, ALT 527 IU/L, HBsAg 250 IU/mL, anti-HCVAb negative. Peak on January 14, 2011: AST 440 IU/L, ALT 624 IU/L. March 29, 2011: AST 30 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of chronic hepatic disorder.
objective.advanced_workup: HBV DNA >9.0 log copies/mL; HBV genotype C. Abdominal CT showed no evidence of chronic hepatic disorder. Liver biopsy revealed mild fibrosis (A2/F1).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: De novo hepatitis B due to HBV reactivation (HBsAg 250 IU/mL, HBV DNA >9.0 log copies/mL, genotype C, liver biopsy A2/F1) associated with infliximab and 6-mercaptopurine therapy for colonic Crohn's disease. Hepatitis C (anti-HCVAb negative) and sexual transmission from her husband (HBsAg, anti-HBcAb, and HBV DNA negative) were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initiated entecavir (ETV) 0.5 mg/day on January 5, 2011; adalimumab was suspended after two doses while 6-MP was continued, and 10 sessions of granulocytapheresis were performed to maintain Crohn's remission.
