Month 49: Creatinine 2.05 mg/dL, eGFR 35 mL/min, proteinuria increased from 970 mg/24 h to 5,200 mg/24 h, total protein 6.6 g/dL, albumin 56%, alpha-2-globulin 17%, gamma globulin 12.2%, total cholesterol 94 mg/dL, calciuria 3 mmol/24 h, phosphaturia 0.88 g/24 h, PTH 95.7 pg/mL, albumin-corrected calcium 2.3 mmol/L, phosphorus 2.6 mg/dL, vitamin D 8.7 ng/mL. Months 54-57: Creatinine 2.15 mg/dL, eGFR 32 mL/min, proteinuria decreased to 1.9 g/24 h.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial HBV DNA: May 2010 8.620 x 10^3 IU/mL; January 2011 47.900 x 10^3 IU/mL; month 4 235 x 10^3 IU/mL; month 15 <20 IU/mL; month 30 <20 IU/mL; month 38 >170,000 x 10^3 IU/mL; month 39 6.960 x 10^3 IU/mL; month 41 351 x 10^3 IU/mL; month 49 0.047 x 10^3 IU/mL; month 54 completely undetectable. Liver elastometry (FibroScan, month 39): Moderate fibrosis (patient declined liver biopsy). Kidney allograft biopsy (month 49): Tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and arterial fibro-intimal thickening without signs of graft rejection; anti-HLA antibodies negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic HBeAg-positive hepatitis B with moderate liver fibrosis (FibroScan) and post-renal-transplant HBV viral rebound (>170,000 x 10^3 IU/mL), subsequently complicated by tenofovir/everolimus-associated nephrotoxicity and heavy proteinuria (5,200 mg/24 h; biopsy showing tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and arterial fibro-intimal thickening). Allograft rejection and anti-HLA antibodies were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Started entecavir 0.5 mg weekly post-hemodialysis (January 2011), spaced to every 10 days at month 15 (<20 IU/mL), and increased to 0.5 mg daily post-transplant. For viral rebound at month 38, added tenofovir 245 mg every 48 h, then switched after 3 months to tenofovir monotherapy 245 mg daily. Following renal decline and proteinuria at month 49, tenofovir was reduced to 245 mg every 48 h and everolimus was replaced with mycophenolic acid 360 mg twice daily. By month 54, HBV DNA completely disappeared, renal function stabilized (creatinine 2.15 mg/dL, eGFR 32 mL/min), and proteinuria declined to 1.9 g/24 h by month 57.

raw_case_text: Case 5: A 56-year-old man with a history of HBV presented with stage IV melanoma involving the liver (multiple tumors, largest = 6.4 cm), pancreas, kidney, bones and mediastinal lymph nodes. At the time of ipilimumab administration, the patient's serum AST was 61 IU/L (normal range = 8-48) and ALT was normal at 25 IU/L. His bilirubin was mildly elevated at 1.57 mg/dL (0.1-1.2). Serologies revealed the following: HBsAg negative; HBV DNA undetectable by polymerase chain reaction (PCR); HBc reactive; HBV surface antibody negative, suggesting an inactive carrier state. The patient did not have a liver biopsy, so it is unclear if he had fibrosis at the time of ipilimumab administration. The patient completed a total of 3 cycles of ipilimumab, along with concurrent administration of entecavir for prophylaxis against HBV reactivation. Though his liver function tests remained normal throughout therapy, the final cycle of ipilimumab was withheld due to clinical decompensation consisting of progressive fatigue and pain due to bone and liver metastases. The patient died of progressive melanoma shortly after receiving his third cycle of ipilimumab therapy, at which time hepatic transaminases were within normal limits.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male with stage IV metastatic melanoma and a history of HBV infection presenting for ipilimumab therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with stage IV melanoma involving the liver (multiple tumors, largest 6.4 cm), pancreas, kidney, bones, and mediastinal lymph nodes and was evaluated prior to ipilimumab initiation. During immunotherapy, he experienced clinical decompensation with progressive fatigue and pain secondary to bone and liver metastases.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Stage IV metastatic melanoma involving liver, pancreas, kidney, bones, and mediastinal lymph nodes.
subjective.review_of_systems: Experienced progressive fatigue and pain due to bone and liver metastases during therapy.

objective.routine_investigations: At ipilimumab initiation: AST 61 IU/L (normal 8-48 IU/L), ALT 25 IU/L (normal), total bilirubin 1.57 mg/dL (normal 0.1-1.2 mg/dL). HBV serologies: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc reactive, HBsAb negative. Throughout therapy and at death: Liver function tests and hepatic transaminases remained within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: HBV DNA PCR: Undetectable at ipilimumab initiation. (No liver biopsy performed; fibrosis status unknown.)

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Inactive HBV carrier state (HBsAg negative, anti-HBc reactive, HBsAb negative, HBV DNA undetectable) in a patient with stage IV metastatic melanoma undergoing ipilimumab immunotherapy.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Completed 3 cycles of ipilimumab with concurrent entecavir prophylaxis against HBV reactivation, without LFT elevation or HBV flare. The fourth cycle of ipilimumab was withheld due to progressive fatigue and metastatic pain, and the patient died of progressive melanoma shortly after cycle 3 with normal hepatic transaminases.

raw_case_text: Case 6: A 60-year-old man presented with stage IV melanoma including multiple subcutaneous metastases. He had previously undergone adjuvant therapy with interferon alfa (IFNalpha) after surgical resection of his primary lesion, as well as radiation therapy after resection of a local recurrence. Prior therapies for metastatic disease included high-dose IL-2, talimogene laherparepvec and dacarbazine with disease progression after each. Two months prior to the initiation of ipilimumab, the patient's serum AST and ALT were within normal limits with a reactive Hepatitis B e-Antibody (anti-HBe), nonreactive Hepatitis B e-Antigen (HBeAg), and HBV viral load of 43,100 IU/mL. Without intervening therapy, HBV viral load fell to 2,950 IU/mL ten days later. Tenofovir therapy was initiated. After four days of treatment the patient's viral load was 41 IU/mL. Four cycles of ipilimumab were administered, which were well-tolerated and produced no LFT abnormalities. One month later, HBV viral load was undetectable. The patient expired four months after initiation of ipilimumab from progressive melanoma. Of note, this case was previously reported in detail but summarized here to expand the current case series.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male with stage IV metastatic melanoma presenting for ipilimumab immunotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with stage IV melanoma with multiple subcutaneous metastases after progressing on multiple prior systemic therapies and underwent pre-treatment evaluation 2 months prior to starting ipilimumab, revealing active HBV viremia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage IV melanoma with multiple subcutaneous metastases; prior surgical resection of primary lesion with adjuvant interferon alfa (IFNalpha), resection of local recurrence with radiation therapy, and high-dose IL-2, talimogene laherparepvec, and dacarbazine for metastatic disease (with progression after each).

objective.routine_investigations: Two months prior to ipilimumab: AST and ALT within normal limits; anti-HBe reactive, HBeAg nonreactive. During 4 cycles of ipilimumab: No LFT abnormalities.
objective.advanced_workup: HBV viral load: 43,100 IU/mL 2 months prior to ipilimumab, decreasing to 2,950 IU/mL 10 days later without intervening therapy; decreased to 41 IU/mL after 4 days of tenofovir and became undetectable 1 month later.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic HBeAg-negative (anti-HBe reactive) hepatitis B virus infection (baseline HBV viral load 43,100 IU/mL) in a patient with stage IV metastatic melanoma.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initiated on tenofovir therapy, achieving rapid viral suppression (41 IU/mL at day 4; undetectable at 1 month). Tolerated 4 cycles of ipilimumab with no LFT abnormalities. Died 4 months after ipilimumab initiation from progressive melanoma.

raw_case_text: Case 8: A 56-year-old Venezuelan man with HBV, who had previously received adjuvant IFNalpha after resection of a primary melanoma (cKIT mutant), presented with metastatic disease including pancreatic and splenic metastases. Prior to the initiation of ipilimumab, the patient's HBV DNA level was 9560 IU/mL with normal liver function tests. The patient stated that he had a liver biopsy in South America which was within normal limits; however this was not confirmed by repeat liver biopsy, although his radiographic imaging from the US does not show evidence of fibrosis. The patient was administered entecavir 0.5 mg daily, after which the viral load fell to 454 IU/mL. Ipilimumab was initiated 2 weeks later and entecavir was continued. The patient's viral load became undetectable, and his LFTs remained within normal limits throughout the course of treatment. Although he completed 4 cycles of ipilimumab without significant complications, post-therapy radiologic scans demonstrated progressive disease. He was subsequently treated with temozolomide, then nilotinib, again without hepatic complications.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old Venezuelan male with metastatic melanoma and HBV infection presenting for ipilimumab immunotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with metastatic melanoma involving the pancreas and spleen and underwent pre-treatment HBV evaluation prior to initiating ipilimumab.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection; reported a prior normal liver biopsy in South America (unconfirmed by repeat biopsy). History of cKIT-mutant melanoma status post primary resection and adjuvant interferon alfa (IFNalpha). Epidemiological context: Venezuelan male.

objective.routine_investigations: Prior to ipilimumab: Normal liver function tests; LFTs remained within normal limits throughout ipilimumab, temozolomide, and nilotinib therapy. Radiographic imaging in the US showed no evidence of fibrosis.
objective.advanced_workup: HBV DNA: 9,560 IU/mL prior to entecavir; decreased to 454 IU/mL on entecavir before ipilimumab initiation, and became undetectable during therapy. Post-ipilimumab radiologic scans demonstrated progressive melanoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Active hepatitis B virus infection (baseline HBV DNA 9,560 IU/mL, no radiographic fibrosis) in a patient with metastatic cKIT-mutant melanoma (pancreatic and splenic metastases).

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initiated entecavir 0.5 mg daily, lowering HBV DNA to 454 IU/mL prior to starting ipilimumab 2 weeks later while continuing entecavir. Viral load became undetectable and LFTs remained normal across 4 cycles of ipilimumab without significant complications. Due to progressive melanoma on post-therapy scans, he subsequently received temozolomide and then nilotinib, again without hepatic complications.

raw_case_text: A 38-year-old Afghan origin male presented with generalized edema. He gave the history of intravenous (IV) drug abuse. Edema started 2 weeks before admission. Urine sediment had dysmorphic red blood cells (RBCs) and serum creatinine was 1 mg/dl. The amount of proteinuria was 4560 mg/day. Secondary evaluation revealed a negative human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) tests. HBsAg was positive. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 25 mm/1st hr. Liver functions tests were within normal limits. C reactive protein (CRP) was negative. Cardiac doppler echography was normal. Kidney sonography showed right and left kidneys of 11.6x5 and 12.2x4.6 cm2 in dimensions, respectively. Other secondary evaluation tests including serologic activity of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), cryoglobulins, complement levels, antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), anti-phospholipid antibody panel tests and serum protein electrophoresis were within normal range. For further evaluation, a kidney biopsy was performed. On renal biopsy, 13 glomeruli were included, none of them was sclerotic. All glomeruli displayed mesangial proliferation accompanied by endocapillary proliferation in 1/3 of the glomeruli. The glomeruli had a lobulated pattern. On silver staining, spikes were absent, however, glomerular basement membrane (GBM) was thickened. Extracapillary proliferation was absent. Interstitial inflammation, fibrosis and tubular atrophy were absent, however, tubular cells showed significant degenerative changes and RBC casts were observable. On immunofluorescence (IF) study of 9 obtained glomeruli, linear band-like intra-capillary wall deposits of IgG were observed (3+ on a scale of 0 to 3+ intensity). Also, there was 1+ of C3 deposition, while C1q, IgA and IgM were not found. There was also 1+ positivity of IgG in the mesangial area. Granular deposits of IgG along the GBM were absent. The morphologic lesions and the IF study was mostly consistent with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), type I. The patient was treated with 50 mg/day prednisolone. Two months after starting the treatment and during the third periodic check up, patient complained of urinary frequency and dysuria. Primary evaluation revealed a serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dl and a bacteriuria in urine analysis. Clarithromycin (500 mg/twice day) was added to the regimen. One week after treatment, patient was referred to the emergency ward due to confusion and malaise. Except for the previously mentioned drugs (prednisolone and clarithromycin), there was no history of other drug intake. Also, there was no history of gastro-enteritis. Primary evaluation showed a serum creatinine of 20 mg/dl. A jugular catheter was installed and hemodialysis was started. Previous treatment with 50 mg/day of prednisolone was also continued. New evaluation of biochemical parameters also showed negative HIV and HCV serologic tests. On real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) >2x107 IU/ml of viral DNA of hepatitis B was found. At this time lamivudine was added to the patient's regimen. Other serologic tests including ANCA, SLE panel test, anti-phospholipid antibodies, anti-GBM antibody and C3, C4 and CH50 levels were within normal limits. Liver function tests and coagulation panel were disturbed. General condition of the patient improved after seven hemodialysis sessions. At this stage, there was no more need for dialysis and serum creatinine gradually decreased. At this time, we decided to perform a second kidney biopsy. After correcting the coagulation profile using fresh frozen plasma, the second renal biopsy was performed. On the second kidney biopsy, of 12 obtained glomeruli, 10 showed crescents and none of the glomeruli was sclerotic. Crescents were mostly circumferential and cellular. There was peri-glomerular infiltration, too. Destruction of Bowman's capsule in some of the glomeruli was observed. Interstitial area harbored moderate inflammatory cell infiltration. Tubular casts, either RBCs or degenerated debris casts were numerous. Tubular dilatation was evident. Tubular cells showed marked degenerative changes. Vessels had normal morphology and architecture. On IF study, the findings were similar to those of the first biopsy. The interpretation was a proliferative glomerulonephritis involved endocapillary and extracapillary regions, mostly consistent with MPGN, Type I. Finally, serum creatinine returned to 1 mg/dl after two months of admission and the patient was discharged and returned to his country in stable condition and the lamivudine was continued (Figures 1  and 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old Afghan male presenting with a 2-week history of generalized edema, later re-presenting with confusion, malaise, and severe acute kidney injury.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed generalized edema 2 weeks prior to initial admission, found to have nephrotic-range proteinuria (4,560 mg/day) and dysmorphic hematuria, and was started on prednisolone 50 mg/day. Two months later, he developed urinary frequency and dysuria (creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, bacteriuria) and was prescribed clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily. One week later, he was referred to the emergency ward with confusion and malaise (serum creatinine 20 mg/dL). He denied other drug intake or gastroenteritis.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of intravenous (IV) drug abuse. Epidemiological context: Male of Afghan origin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Subsequently developed urinary frequency and dysuria at 2 months, followed by confusion and malaise 1 week later. Denied gastroenteritis or other medication intake.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: Generalized edema. Emergency re-presentation: Confusion.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: Serum creatinine 1 mg/dL, urine sediment with dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria 4,560 mg/day, ESR 25 mm/1st hr, CRP negative, LFTs normal, HIV negative, HCV negative, HBsAg positive; SLE serologies, cryoglobulins, complement levels, ANCA, antiphospholipid antibody panel, and serum protein electrophoresis normal. Kidney sonography: right kidney 11.6 x 5 cm^2, left kidney 12.2 x 4.6 cm^2. Cardiac Doppler echocardiography normal. Two-month check-up: Serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, bacteriuria on urinalysis. Emergency re-presentation: Serum creatinine 20 mg/dL; HIV, HCV, ANCA, SLE panel, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-GBM antibody, C3, C4, and CH50 all normal/negative; LFTs and coagulation panel disturbed. Two months after re-admission: Serum creatinine returned to 1 mg/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: First kidney biopsy: 13 non-sclerotic glomeruli showing mesangial proliferation, endocapillary proliferation in 1/3 of glomeruli, lobulated pattern, thickened GBM without spikes on silver stain, no extracapillary proliferation, tubular cell degeneration, and RBC casts; IF (9 glomeruli) showed 3+ linear band-like intra-capillary wall IgG deposits, 1+ C3, 1+ mesangial IgG, negative C1q/IgA/IgM. Real-time HBV DNA PCR (at re-presentation): >2 x 10^7 IU/mL. Second kidney biopsy (after FFP correction): 12 non-sclerotic glomeruli with circumferential cellular crescents in 10/12 glomeruli, periglomerular infiltration, Bowman's capsule destruction, moderate interstitial inflammation, numerous RBC/debris tubular casts, tubular dilatation, normal vessels; IF similar to first biopsy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Hepatitis B virus-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) type I complicated by severe HBV reactivation (HBV DNA >2 x 10^7 IU/mL, disturbed LFTs/coagulation) during prednisolone monotherapy and crescentic transformation (10/12 glomeruli with cellular crescents) causing acute kidney injury (creatinine 20 mg/dL). HIV, HCV, SLE, cryoglobulinemia, ANCA vasculitis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and anti-GBM disease were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initially treated with prednisolone 50 mg/day (with clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily added at 2 months for UTI). At re-presentation, underwent 7 hemodialysis sessions via jugular catheter, continued prednisolone 50 mg/day, and added lamivudine for HBV replication (plus FFP prior to second biopsy). General condition and renal function improved off dialysis; serum creatinine normalized to 1 mg/dL 2 months after admission, and he was discharged in stable condition to return to his country on continued lamivudine.

raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man from Jakarta presented with jaundice, preceded by nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 7 days. The patient initially developed a flu-like syndrome for several days (fever and chills, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia). Over several days, he experienced passing tea-colored urine with decreased urine output. His medical story included asymptomatic chronic HBV infection for 11 years and never consumed anti-viral medication. The patient was treated as acute exacerbation of chronic HBV in another hospital for 2 days, but his symptoms were not resolved and was transferred to our hospital. He does not drink alcohol. Clinical examination on admission showed the patient was alert with profound jaundice. He had abdominal upper quadrant tenderness but no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Neurological examination was normal.
Baseline laboratory assessments and changes during hospitalization are shown in Table 1. Initial laboratory tests were notable for acute kidney injury (creatinine 13.18 mg/dL, ureum 327 mg/dL, eGFR 4.06 mL/min/1.73m2), elevated total bilirubin (36.06 mg/dL), indirect bilirubin (29.06 mg/dL), and liver transaminases, accompanied with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis revealed positive bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine, but no hemoglobin was detected. Polymerase chain reaction test was negative for Covid-19. HBV serological profile showed positive HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, and anti-HBe, but negative HBeAg. HBV-DNA quantification could not be performed. He tested negative for hepatitis C, hepatitis D, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver size and parenchyma without signs of splenomegaly and ascites. Hepatic elastography revealed severe liver fibrosis (F3-F4) with median liver stiffness at 14.9 kPa.
The clinical scenario was initially interpreted as an acute exacerbation of chronic HBV. Treatment included telbivudine, cefoperazone, furosemide, ursodeoxycholic acid, and supportive management. On the second day of hospitalization, he developed altered consciousness with metabolic acidosis (pH 7.087, HCO3- 3.0 mmol/L) and oliguria (<200 mL/24 hours). Ammonia level was not measured. Further questioning to his wife revealed that his symptoms occurred 4 days after returning from a 1-year trip in Serui, Papua. At this time, rapid diagnostic test for malaria was ordered which showed positivity. Peripheral blood smear showed intraerythrocytic P. falciparum (63 parasites per 500 erythrocytes) with a high degree of parasitemia (12.6%) (Figure 1).
Diagnosis of severe malaria was made, and intravenous antimalarial artesunate with oral primaquine were administered. He was transferred to the intensive care unit, intubated, and started on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) with continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) method, and after 4 sessions we observed an initial downtrend in ureum, creatinine, bilirubin, and liver enzymes level, accompanied with improvement in eGFR. However, over the following days his renal function continued to progressively decline, and the liver injury deteriorated. Eventually, he developed pulmonary edema, septic shock, multiorgan dysfunction and died on the seventh day of hospitalization despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presenting with jaundice preceded by 7 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, flu-like symptoms, and dark urine with decreased urine output.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially developed a flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, headache, myalgia, arthralgia) followed by 7 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, progressive jaundice, tea-colored urine, and decreased urine output. He was treated at an outside hospital for 2 days for presumed acute exacerbation of chronic HBV without improvement and transferred. On hospital day 2, he developed altered consciousness, metabolic acidosis, and oliguria (<200 mL/24 hours).
subjective.past_medical_history: Asymptomatic chronic HBV infection for 11 years without prior antiviral medication. Non-drinker. Epidemiological/travel history: Resident of Jakarta; symptoms started 4 days after returning from a 1-year trip in Serui, Papua (reported by his wife on hospital day 2).
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, chills, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tea-colored urine, and decreased urine output.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Alert with profound jaundice; upper quadrant abdominal tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites; neurological examination normal. Hospital day 2: Altered consciousness and oliguria (<200 mL/24 hours).
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: Creatinine 13.18 mg/dL, urea (ureum) 327 mg/dL, eGFR 4.06 mL/min/1.73 m^2, total bilirubin 36.06 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 29.06 mg/dL, elevated liver transaminases, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis: Positive bilirubin and urobilinogen, no hemoglobin. Serology/PCR: COVID-19 PCR negative; HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc positive, anti-HBe positive, HBeAg negative (HBV DNA not performed); HCV, HDV, and HIV negative. Hospital day 2: Metabolic acidosis (pH 7.087, HCO3- 3.0 mmol/L). Abdominal ultrasound: Normal liver size and parenchyma without splenomegaly or ascites. Malaria rapid diagnostic test (day 2): Positive. Peripheral blood smear: Intraerythrocytic Plasmodium falciparum (63 parasites per 500 erythrocytes; 12.6% parasitemia).
objective.advanced_workup: Hepatic elastography: Severe liver fibrosis (F3-F4) with median liver stiffness 14.9 kPa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (12.6% parasitemia on peripheral blood smear, positive RDT, altered consciousness, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, severe hyperbilirubinemia) co-existing with chronic HBV infection (HBsAg+, IgM anti-HBc+, anti-HBe+, HBeAg-, F3-F4 fibrosis on elastography), initially misinterpreted as acute exacerbation of chronic HBV. COVID-19, HCV, HDV, and HIV were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initially treated with telbivudine, cefoperazone, furosemide, ursodeoxycholic acid, and supportive care. Upon malaria confirmation on day 2, initiated intravenous artesunate and oral primaquine, transferred to the ICU, intubated, and started on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT via CVVHDF). After an initial laboratory downtrend over 4 CRRT sessions, renal and hepatic dysfunction progressively deteriorated, culminating in pulmonary edema, septic shock, multiorgan dysfunction, and death on hospital day 7 despite CPR.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old female patient was admitted to Lanzhou University Second Hospital on October 31, 2016 because of "intermittent upper abdominal pain and discomfort for 1 month." Symptoms became worse after eating greasy food. She did not receive any treatment before the admission. Because the above symptoms gradually worsened, the patient went to the local clinic. CT of the abdomen reveals space-occupying liver lesions, which was considered more as hepatic hydatid disease. For further diagnosis, the patient visited our hospital. The patient has been a carrier of HBV since childhood and has not been tested for HBV DNA or received antiviral treatment. At the same time, her mother and siblings are both HBV carriers, and she has a history of life in a pastoral area in her childhood. Appendectomy was performed because of acute appendicitis in 2009, and postoperative recovery was fine.
Laboratory examination results were as follows: white blood cells (WBC) 3.7 x 10 9 per L, red blood cells (RBC) 4.32 x 1012 per L, platelet (PLT) 119 x 109 per L, T bilirubin (TBiL) 11.7 mumol/L (normal range: 3.8-25.8 mumol/L), direct bilirubin (DBiL) 5.4 mumol/L (0-6.8 mumol/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 359 U/L (0-50 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 200U/L (0-50 U/L). Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) was 1,210 ng/ml (0-7 ng/ml). Test of HBsAg, HBeAg, Anti-HBe and Anti-HBc were positive, while test of Anti-HBs was negative. Level of HBV DNA was 5.32 x 103 IU/ml (Normal <1.0 x 102 IU/ml). Casoni test was positive. Enhanced CT of the abdomen (<PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0001_A_1_2.webp><PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0001_B_2_2.webp>) suggested malignant liver tumor and hepatic hydatid disease, but no abnormalities were found in gastroscopy and colonoscopy.
The patient had a history of HBV infection and did not receive regular antiviral treatment, and AFP was significantly increased. Combined with imaging enhancement mode, she was diagnosed as having HCC and chronic HBV infection. In addition, considering the facts that the patient had a life history in a pastoral area, the Casoni test was positive, and the abdominal CT showed obvious calcification in the liver-occupying space, she was diagnosed as having hepatic hydatid disease.
She underwent an operation on November 10, 2016. During the surgery, we found that the liver indicated signs of cirrhosis, and that the tumor and hydatid cysts were located in the right anterior lobe, adjacent to the right and middle hepatic veins. Therefore, hepatic Segment 5, 8 segment resection, hepatic hydatid internal capsule removal, and cholecystectomy (<PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0002_a_1_4.webp><PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0002_b_2_4.webp><PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0002_c_3_4.webp><PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0002_d_4_4.webp>) were performed. She was discharged 8 days after the operation. Pathological results were infiltrating moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma of the liver, with tumor thrombus in the vessel, accompanied by hydatid infection. Chronic cholecystitis was found without cancer invasion (<PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0003_a_1_2.webp><PMC8847199_fsurg-08-816501-g0003_b_2_2.webp>). After being discharged from the hospital, she received long-term oral entecavir (0.5 mg/day) antiviral therapy and oral albendazole (0.4 g/day) for 6 months.
She underwent re-examination every 3 months after the surgery. In May 2017, the level of AFP increased to 895.5 ng/ml, and the first cycle of transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE) treatment (oxaliplatin 150 mg + epirubicin 30 mg) was given. TACE was performed 3 times on June 27, August 7, and September 20, 2017, and AFP dropped to 3.73 ng/ml. In August 2019, AFP rose to 122.5 and 246.3 ng/ml in October 2019, but there was no evidence of recurrence of HCC in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The fifth TACE treatment was performed in October 2019, and there were no obvious signs of tumor staining during the TACE. AFP decreased to 182.7 ng/ml 1 month later. In March 2020, AFP elevated to 204.3 ng/ml, and the patient was advised to continue treatment, but she refused further treatment because of economic factors. In December 2020, AFP rose to 700.7 ng/ml. The recent follow-up was done in September 2021, and the patient was fine and received oral entecavir only.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old female presenting with a 1-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain and discomfort worsening after greasy food.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed intermittent upper abdominal pain and discomfort 1 month prior to admission, worsening after eating greasy food, without prior treatment. As symptoms gradually worsened, an abdominal CT at a local clinic detected space-occupying liver lesions initially suspected as hepatic hydatid disease, prompting referral to Lanzhou University Second Hospital on October 31, 2016.
subjective.past_medical_history: HBV carrier since childhood without prior HBV DNA testing or antiviral therapy. Appendectomy for acute appendicitis in 2009 with uneventful recovery. Family/epidemiological history: Mother and siblings are HBV carriers; lived in a pastoral area during childhood.

objective.routine_investigations: CBC: WBC 3.7 x 10^9/L, RBC 4.32 x 10^12/L, platelets 119 x 10^9/L. LFTs: Total bilirubin 11.7 umol/L (normal 3.8-25.8 umol/L), direct bilirubin 5.4 umol/L (0-6.8 umol/L), ALT 359 U/L (0-50 U/L), AST 200 U/L (0-50 U/L). AFP 1,210 ng/mL (normal 0-7 ng/mL). HBV serology: HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBe, and anti-HBc positive; anti-HBs negative. Casoni test positive. Follow-up AFP: 895.5 ng/mL (May 2017) -> 3.73 ng/mL (after 3 TACE sessions) -> 122.5 ng/mL (Aug 2019) -> 246.3 ng/mL (Oct 2019) -> 182.7 ng/mL (Nov 2019) -> 204.3 ng/mL (Mar 2020) -> 700.7 ng/mL (Dec 2020).
objective.advanced_workup: HBV DNA: 5.32 x 10^3 IU/mL (normal <1.0 x 10^2 IU/mL). Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: Space-occupying liver lesions with obvious calcification and enhancement features suggestive of malignant liver tumor and hepatic hydatid disease. Gastroscopy and colonoscopy normal. Surgical pathology (November 10, 2016): Infiltrating moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma with vascular tumor thrombus, co-existing hydatid infection, cirrhotic liver parenchyma, and chronic cholecystitis without cancer invasion. Follow-up MRI (October 2019): No evidence of HCC recurrence.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic active hepatitis B virus infection (HBsAg+, HBeAg+, HBV DNA 5.32 x 10^3 IU/mL) with cirrhosis, complicated by concurrent moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma (with vascular tumor thrombus; AFP 1,210 ng/mL) and hepatic hydatid disease (positive Casoni test, calcified CT lesions, histologically confirmed).

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Underwent hepatic segments 5 and 8 resection, hepatic hydatid internal capsule removal, and cholecystectomy on November 10, 2016 and was discharged 8 days later on long-term oral entecavir 0.5 mg/day and oral albendazole 0.4 g/day for 6 months. Received 5 cycles of TACE (oxaliplatin 150 mg + epirubicin 30 mg; May, June, August, September 2017, and October 2019) for rising AFP. Declined further TACE in 2020 due to economic factors despite rising AFP (700.7 ng/mL in December 2020), and remained clinically well on oral entecavir alone at September 2021 follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old woman with a 9-year (2006) history of RA had poorly controlled disease despite treatment with synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) including methotrexate (discontinued due to significant increase of liver enzymes alanine and aspartate transferase AST/ALT > 3 ULN), sulfasalazine and etanercept (lack of adequate response to treatment). None of these drugs fully controlled the disease activity. Additionally, the patient did not receive chloroquine due to ophthalmological contraindications. Her Larsen's radiological grade was stage III. It was positive for rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (anti-CCP) were absent. In 2008 the patient was diagnosed with chronic HCV infection after abnormal liver function tests (LFT) and HCV RNA detection. The route of transmission was probably blood transfusion, which took place 25 years ago.
After three months of therapy with interferon alpha (INF-alpha) and ribavirin the HCV RNA turned to negative and anti-HCV treatment was completed after one year. Furthermore, a hepatologist recognized non-active hepatitis B infection (surface HBs antigen and HBV DNA negative, anti-HBc antibody was present). For the first time the HBV infection was diagnosed and treated in 1979 but there were no records from that period.
Because of high RA activity (DAS28 = 6.6) it was decided after consultation with a hepatologist to start tocilizumab therapy with a dose of 8 mg/kg monthly from November 2010. The hepatologist recommended regular testing of serum HBs antigen due to the risk of HBV reactivation during biological treatment.
All haematological parameters (haemoglobin, mean cell haemoglobin [MCH], mean corpuscular volume [MCV], red blood cell count [RBC], total white blood cell [WBC] count, platelet [PLT] count) and hepatic transaminase levels were in normal range before starting therapy. Liver ultrasonography revealed no abnormalities.
A significant clinical response to RA treatment was gained (DAS28 = 2.03) in December 2010. There was observed a decrease in WBC level from 6820/microl to 3160/microl after the first TCZ administration. Four times TCZ therapy was interrupted due to neutropenia, according to recommendations in Summary of Product Characteristics. In the case of lowering the number of leukocytes the dose of TCZ was reduced to 4 mg/kg. Moderate to severe neutropenia was recorded one day after a dose of TCZ (Table I). However, at the end of the 4-week dosing interval the neutrophil count usually returned to the normal level. Blood levels of folic acid, vitamin B12, ferritin, and iron were in the normal range. 
The patient was instructed to pay particular attention to avoid infections, especially after TCZ administration. From the beginning of tocilizumab therapy until now only once have urinary tract infection and symptoms of herpes labialis with a benign course been observed. LFT were performed every month and values remained in the normal range.
As well as HBV DNA measured after 2 years of TCZ therapy and HBsAg checked every month remained negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old female with a 9-year history of poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis presenting for initiation of tocilizumab therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had persistently active rheumatoid arthritis (DAS28 = 6.6; Larsen radiological stage III) refractory to synthetic DMARDs and etanercept, and underwent hepatology evaluation prior to starting tocilizumab in November 2010.
subjective.past_medical_history: Nine-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RF positive, anti-CCP negative, Larsen stage III; failed methotrexate due to AST/ALT >3x ULN, sulfasalazine, and etanercept; chloroquine contraindicated ophthalmologically). Chronic HCV infection diagnosed in 2008 (probable transmission via blood transfusion 25 years prior), cured with 1 year of interferon-alpha and ribavirin (HCV RNA negative at 3 months). Non-active hepatitis B virus infection initially diagnosed and treated in 1979 (no records; HBsAg negative, HBV DNA negative, anti-HBc positive).

objective.physical_examination: High rheumatoid arthritis disease activity (DAS28 = 6.6 prior to therapy, improving to DAS28 = 2.03 in December 2010).
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-tocilizumab baseline: Normal hematological parameters (Hb, MCH, MCV, RBC, WBC 6,820/uL, platelets) and normal hepatic transaminases; HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive; RF positive, anti-CCP negative; normal folic acid, vitamin B12, ferritin, and iron; liver ultrasonography normal. Post-tocilizumab: WBC dropped from 6,820/uL to 3,160/uL after first dose with transient moderate-to-severe neutropenia 1 day post-dose (normalizing by end of 4-week interval). Monthly LFTs and monthly HBsAg remained normal/negative over 2 years.
objective.advanced_workup: HBV DNA: Negative prior to therapy and remained negative after 2 years of tocilizumab therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Non-active/resolved hepatitis B virus infection (HBsAg negative, HBV DNA negative, anti-HBc positive) and cured hepatitis C in a patient with refractory seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (DAS28 6.6), without HBV reactivation during 2 years of tocilizumab therapy.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Started monthly intravenous tocilizumab 8 mg/kg in November 2010 with monthly HBsAg and LFT monitoring. Achieved rapid clinical response (DAS28 2.03 in December 2010). Therapy was interrupted 4 times for neutropenia and dose-reduced to 4 mg/kg for leukopenia; she had only one benign urinary tract infection and herpes labialis episode. Over 2 years of follow-up, LFTs remained normal and HBsAg and HBV DNA remained negative.

raw_case_text:
72-year-old women presented to our hospital with elevation of serum transaminases for one day on August 19, 2021. Liver chemistry showed alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 132 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 92 U/L, alkaline phosphatase(ALP) 113 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 56 U/L. She has no fatigue, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, dark urine, pale stool, itchy skin, or other symptoms. Past medical history: She underwent splenectomy and was diagnosed with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma due to splenomegaly in September 2019. She started R-CHOP regimen in November 2019. Her laboratory finding showed isolated HBcAb positive (HBcAb+/HBsAb-/HBsAg-/HBeAb-/HBeAg-), undetected (< 20 IU/ml) HBV DNA, and normal transaminases before and during chemotherapy. Complete response to chemotherapy was achieved and immunosuppressive therapy was withdrawn in June 2020 after completing 4 cycles of it. Monitoring of HBV markers and aminotransferases every 1-3 months after chemotherapy showed no change through 14 months after cessation of chemotherapy. She had no history of receiving anti-HBV drug, liver diseases and blood transfusion. She has no history of taking Chinese traditional medicine, health products or other drugs. She had no history of alcohol consumption. Physical examination didn't show any signs of liver disease (jaundice, liver palm, spider angioma, hepatomegaly, shifting dullness or edema in lower limbs). Blood tests still showed isolated HBcAb positive and undetected HBV DNA. The patient was tested negative for antibodies of hepatitis A virus (HAV) IgM, anti-hepatitis C virus (HCV) IgG, anti-hepatitis E virus (HEV) IgM and IgG. The serum Cytomegalovirus-DNA and Epstein Barr viruses-RNA were negative(<500copies/ml). Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) was borderline positive (1:100); Anti-soluble liver antigen and anti-liver-pancreas antibodies (Anti-SLA/LP), anti-mitochondrial autoantibodies (AMA), liver kidney microsomal antigen (LKM) and smooth muscle antibody (SMA) were negative. Serum immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) were normal. Ultrasonography showed markedly increased echogenicity of the liver, thickening of the gallbladder wall, and right renal cyst. Fibro Scan showed an increased CAP score (300 dB/m) and a fibrosis score of 7.1 Kpa.
On August 19, 2021, she was prescribed diammonium glycyrrhizinate enteric-coated capsules and bicyclol tablets for liver protection. One month later (September-2021), ALT level decreased to normal (27 U/L). However, AST level kept abnormal. Four months later (January-2022), HBV DNA increased to 7.8 E+01 IU/ml. Although blood test on the same day still showed isolated HBcAb positive, HBV reactivation was considered, and antiviral therapy was recommended to her. Unfortunately, she refused anti-HBV therapy. She was advised to come back to the hospital for monthly follow-up, but she did not until April 2022.
In April 2022, HBV DNA level increased significantly to 1.86 E+04 IU/ml, together with positive of HBsAg, HBeAg and HBcAb. Liver biochemistry showed ALT 20 U/L, AST 47 U/L. She was prescribed TAF immediately. One month later (May-2022), HBV DNA turn back to undetectable. Three months later (July-2022), complete response (undetectable HBV DNA, HBsAg loss and transaminase normalization) was achieved. Re-examined Fibro Scan in July 2022 showed a CAP score of 255 dB/m and a fibrosis score of 4.0 Kpa. The laboratory findings during the monitoring period are shown in  Figure 1 .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old female presenting with a 1-day finding of elevated serum transaminases.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: On August 19, 2021 (14 months after completing R-CHOP chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma), the patient presented with a 1-day elevation of serum transaminases (ALT 132 U/L, AST 92 U/L). She reported no fatigue, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, dark urine, pale stool, itchy skin, or other symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Splenectomy and diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (due to splenomegaly) in September 2019; received 4 cycles of R-CHOP from November 2019 to June 2020 with complete response. Before, during, and for 14 months after chemotherapy, labs showed isolated HBcAb positivity (HBcAb+/HBsAb-/HBsAg-/HBeAb-/HBeAg-), undetectable HBV DNA (<20 IU/mL), and normal transaminases. No history of anti-HBV drugs, liver diseases, blood transfusion, traditional Chinese medicine, health products, other drugs, or alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for fatigue, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, dark urine, pale stool, and itchy skin.

objective.physical_examination: No physical signs of liver disease (no jaundice, liver palms, spider angiomas, hepatomegaly, shifting dullness, or lower limb edema).
objective.routine_investigations: August 19, 2021: ALT 132 U/L, AST 92 U/L, ALP 113 U/L, GGT 56 U/L; isolated HBcAb positive, HBV DNA undetectable (<20 IU/mL); anti-HAV IgM, anti-HCV IgG, and anti-HEV IgM/IgG negative; serum CMV DNA and EBV RNA negative (<500 copies/mL); ANA borderline positive (1:100); anti-SLA/LP, AMA, LKM, and SMA negative; serum IgG and IgM normal. Abdominal ultrasound: Markedly increased liver echogenicity, gallbladder wall thickening, and right renal cyst. September 2021: ALT normalized (27 U/L), AST remained abnormal. April 2022: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, HBcAb positive; ALT 20 U/L, AST 47 U/L.
objective.advanced_workup: FibroScan (August 2021): CAP score 300 dB/m, fibrosis score 7.1 kPa. Serial HBV DNA: Undetectable (<20 IU/mL) in August 2021; increased to 7.8 x 10^1 IU/mL in January 2022; increased significantly to 1.86 x 10^4 IU/mL in April 2022; undetectable in May 2022 and July 2022. Repeat FibroScan (July 2022): CAP score 255 dB/m, fibrosis score 4.0 kPa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Delayed hepatitis B virus reactivation (reverse seroconversion from isolated HBcAb positivity to HBsAg+/HBeAg+ with HBV DNA 1.86 x 10^4 IU/mL) occurring 19-22 months after cessation of R-CHOP chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, on a background of hepatic steatosis. HAV, HCV, HEV, CMV, EBV, and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initially given diammonium glycyrrhizinate enteric-coated capsules and bicyclol tablets in August 2021; declined recommended anti-HBV therapy in January 2022 when HBV DNA first rose (78 IU/mL). Following overt reactivation in April 2022, immediately started tenofovir alafenamide (TAF). HBV DNA became undetectable within 1 month (May 2022); by July 2022 (3 months), she achieved complete response with undetectable HBV DNA, HBsAg loss, normalized transaminases, and improved FibroScan (CAP 255 dB/m, fibrosis 4.0 kPa).

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old male had a history of chronic hepatitis B infection and hypertension and a mild increase in glucose levels. He had been regularly followed up in a gastrointestinal outpatient clinic for chronic hepatitis B infection. Half a year before admission, a complicated liver cyst was incidentally found on liver sonography in another hospital, where computed tomography (CT)-guided biopsy of the complicated liver cyst was performed. The pathology report revealed grade 2 neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) with a mitotic figure of 7 in 10 high-power fields. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed the diagnosis of NETs with positive chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and CD 56 staining. The lesion was negative for CK-7 and hepatocellular carcinoma markers, including Hepar-1, arginase-1, and glypican-3. Metastatic NET was considered. During this period, there was no abdominal pain, flushing, or diarrhea but mild cold sweating.
He was then hospitalized in our hospital. The hemogram and biochemistry investigations were normal, including serum carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) levels (<0.6 IU/L, normal: <37 IU/L), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels (1.36 ng/mL, normal: <5 ng/mL), and alpha-fetoprotein levels (3.8 ng/mL, normal: <9 ng/mL). Serum chromogranin A levels were elevated (119.80 ng/mL, normal: <101.9 ng/mL), but adrenal function (cortisol 12.87 microg/dL, normal: 7-9AM 4.2-22.4 microg/dL, 3-5PM 3.1-16.7 microg/dL; adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) 35.10 pg/mL, normal: 7.2-63.3 pg/mL), gastrin levels (44.2 pg/mL, normal: 28-185 pg/mL), and C-peptide levels (4.5 ng/mL, 1.1-4.4 ng/mL) were all within the normal range, as were urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) (8.1 mg/day, normal: 1.9-9.8 mg/day) and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) (4.8 mg/day, normal: 2-6 mg/day) levels. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (7069.00, nonreactive: <0.9, equivocal: 0.9-10, reactive: >10), anti-HBs antibody (528.50 IU/L, nonreactive: <10), and anti-HBc antibody (0.005, non-reactive: >1.0) were all reactive but nonreactive to anti-hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibody. Subsequent abdominal CT showed a pancreatic body cystic tumor approximately 1.5 cm in size ( Figure 1A ) and a suspected pancreatic tail tumor associated with liver tumors in the right and left lobes ( Figure 1B ). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen revealed a solid mass at the pancreatic tail with numerous liver tumors favoring metastases. The pancreatic body tumor was a cyst ( Figure 2A ). Positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) with MRI also showed peripancreatic lymph node metastases ( Figure 2B ). Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) of the right lobe of the liver was performed during this admission. He was discharged 3 days after TACE.
He started to take 5 mg everolimus twice a day and 20 mg octreotide LAR every 28 days, starting from 8 days after the 1st TACE. No hepatitis B virus (HBV) prophylaxis treatment was administered. After he took everolimus for three months and octreotide 3 times, and subsequent abdominal CT showed stationary pancreatic NETs but decreased liver metastasis nodule numbers, suggesting partial response to concurrent everolimus (  <PMC8047461_fendo-12-639967-g003_A_1_2.webp><PMC8047461_fendo-12-639967-g003_B_2_2.webp> ). Therefore, he underwent laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy three and half months after the initial treatment of everolimus. The pathology report revealed grade 2 NETs of the pancreas with direct invasion of the spleen. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that tumor cells were positive for CD56, chromogranin A, synaptophysin and beta-catenin on the membrane and negative for insulin. Ki-67 index was 15% (  Figures 4A, B ). The postoperative course was uneventful, and he was discharged 7 days after the surgery.
He continued everolimus 5 mg twice a day and octreotide 20 mg every 28 days after the operation. No HBV prophylaxis treatment was administered as before. Two and half months after the surgery, he underwent abdominal CT for follow-up, which disclosed no evidence of local recurrence at the pancreas and regression of the liver tumor where previous TACE was performed; the other liver metastases appeared as stable disease.
Approximately 2 weeks after the last abdominal CT, he had general weakness with an icteric look and then coma. He visited another hospital abroad, and was initially hospitalized there; hepatic failure progressed there. Four days later, he was transferred back to our hospital and admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). The hemogram and biochemistry study showed coagulopathy but no thrombocytopenia (international normalized ratio (INR) 2.9, platelet count 22,6000/microL), jaundice (total bilirubin 11.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.9 mg/dL), abnormal liver function test (aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 824 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 636 U/L), azotemia (blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 21.2 mg/dL, creatinine 5.87 mg/dL) or elevation in ammonia level (408 microg/dL). The HBV DNA level was 1.832509 million cps/ml, and the anti-hepatitis B e antibody was reactive, so entecavir was prescribed. Anti-hepatitis C antibody, CMV-IgM, HIV antigen, EB-VCA IgM, and RPR were all nonreactive. Acute hepatitis B flare-up-related fulminant hepatic failure was diagnosed since other possible causes of hepatic failure were excluded. However, general tonic clonic seizures occurred in the ICU, but brain CT showed no obvious lesions. Five days after hepatic failure was apparent, pulseless ventricular tachycardia occurred. The patient expired after failed resuscitation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male with chronic hepatitis B and metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor initially presenting with mild cold sweating, and later presenting with acute general weakness, jaundice, and coma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six months before initial admission, routine liver sonography incidentally detected a complicated liver cyst biopsied as metastatic grade 2 neuroendocrine tumor (NET), during which he had mild cold sweating without abdominal pain, flushing, or diarrhea. Following right-lobe TACE, everolimus (5 mg twice daily) and octreotide LAR (20 mg every 28 days) without HBV prophylaxis, and laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy, he continued everolimus and octreotide. Approximately 2 weeks after his 2.5-month postoperative follow-up CT, he developed general weakness, jaundice, and coma; initially hospitalized abroad with progressive hepatic failure, he was transferred back to the ICU 4 days later.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic hepatitis B virus infection (followed regularly in GI clinic), hypertension, and mildly elevated glucose. Metastatic grade 2 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (status post TACE and laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy/splenectomy; receiving everolimus 5 mg BID and octreotide LAR 20 mg q28d without HBV prophylaxis).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initially reported mild cold sweating; denied abdominal pain, flushing, or diarrhea. Later developed general weakness.

objective.physical_examination: At acute decompensation/ICU admission: Icteric appearance, coma, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the ICU.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: Normal hemogram and biochemistry; CA 19-9 <0.6 IU/L (<37), CEA 1.36 ng/mL (<5), AFP 3.8 ng/mL (<9); chromogranin A elevated at 119.80 ng/mL (<101.9); cortisol 12.87 ug/dL, ACTH 35.10 pg/mL, gastrin 44.2 pg/mL, C-peptide 4.5 ng/mL (ref 1.1-4.4), urinary VMA 8.1 mg/day, 5-HIAA 4.8 mg/day; HBsAg reactive (7,069.00), anti-HBs reactive (528.50 IU/L), anti-HBc reactive (0.005), anti-HCV nonreactive. ICU admission: INR 2.9, platelets 226,000/uL (reported as 22,6000/uL), total bilirubin 11.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.9 mg/dL, AST 824 U/L, ALT 636 U/L, BUN 21.2 mg/dL, creatinine 5.87 mg/dL, ammonia 408 ug/dL; anti-HBe reactive; anti-HCV, CMV-IgM, HIV antigen, EBV-VCA IgM, and RPR nonreactive.
objective.advanced_workup: Staging abdominal CT, MRI, and FDG-PET/MRI: 1.5 cm pancreatic body cyst, solid pancreatic tail mass, peripancreatic lymph node metastases, and bilateral hepatic metastases. Biopsies (liver cyst and surgical distal pancreatectomy/splenectomy): Grade 2 pancreatic NET with direct splenic invasion (7 mitoses/10 HPF, Ki-67 15%; positive CD56, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, membrane beta-catenin; negative insulin, CK-7, Hepar-1, arginase-1, glypican-3). ICU admission: Quantitative HBV DNA 1,832,509 copies/mL; brain CT showed no obvious lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Acute hepatitis B flare-up causing fulminant hepatic failure (HBV DNA 1,832,509 copies/mL, AST 824 U/L, ALT 636 U/L, total bilirubin 11.1 mg/dL, INR 2.9, ammonia 408 ug/dL, coma, acute kidney injury) during everolimus therapy without HBV prophylaxis in a patient with chronic hepatitis B and metastatic grade 2 pancreatic NET. HCV, CMV, HIV, EBV, syphilis (RPR), and intracranial lesions were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Entecavir was initiated upon ICU admission. Despite intensive care, he developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures followed by pulseless ventricular tachycardia 5 days after hepatic failure became apparent and expired after failed resuscitation.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old female was admitted to the Clinical Hospital No. 1 of Sechenov University on August 16, 2019 because of weakness, recurrent extended abdominal pain, and an increase in body temperature up to 39 C. The patient had a medical history of untreated viral hepatitis B (inactive carriage) for over 20 years. The first symptoms presented 2 weeks before admission.
Physical examination of the patient revealed pallor of the skin and moist tongue that was furred with a white coating. The lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. The heart sounds were muffled at auscultation with a pulse rate of 72 beats/min. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, and the liver size was within normal limits. Splenomegaly was found during percussive estimation of the spleen, with dimensions of 13x10 cm. The spleen protruded from the costal arch within 7 cm, the surface of which was elastic and smooth during palpation.
The patient had no family history of cancer, addiction to alcohol, tobacco, or drugs, or known allergies. Signed consent of the patient for the examination and treatment was obtained.
Complete blood count and metabolic panel included: hemoglobin 98 g/L, red blood cells 3.95x1012 cells/L, platelet count 110x109 cells/L, white blood cells 2.8x109 cells/L, ferritin 1080 ng/mL, ferrum 5 mmol/L, total protein 71.6 g/L, albumin 37.1 g/L, total bilirubin 13.2 mmol/L, AST 27 IU/L, ALT 40 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 269 IU/L.
Coagulogram data included: plasma fibrinogen 5.51 g/L, prothrombin index (PTI), 74%, international normalised ratio (INR) 1.17, and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 0.97.
Ultrasonography and computed tomography (CT) of the abdominal organs revealed normal size of the liver and intrahepatic bile ducts. The hepatic parenchyma included multiple calcifications of up to 1 cm in diameter. The portal vein was 11 mm in diameter, and its linear blood flow velocity was estimated to be 12 cm/s. The gallbladder was normal. The spleen was enlarged to 135 mm x 75 mm x 155 mm. Its parenchyma included calcifications up to 0.5 cm in diameter and active specific tissue. The splenic vein diameter was 11 mm, and its linear blood flow velocity was 12 cm/s. No free liquids were detected in the abdominal cavity. These observations were indicative of splenomegaly, portal hypertension, and no lymphadenopathy.
During EGD, atrophic gastritis of the antrum was observed. Esophageal or gastric varicose veins were not detected. Liver fibrosis was estimated by FibroScan indicating 1st degree fibrosis (stage F1 on the METAVIR scale). The serological study showed the reactivation of chronic hepatitis (titer of HBsAg 6819 IU/mL DNA HBV [+]); therefore, antiviral therapy, including entecavir 1 mg x1 time per day, was prescribed.
The etiology of splenomegaly remained unclear. Symptoms, fever, laboratory changes (pancytopenia), and enlargement of the spleen during reactivation of viral replication indicated the presence of a lymphoproliferative disease. Based on this fact, during the follow-up examination, bone marrow biopsy was performed. Cytological examination revealed insignificant lymphoproliferation. There were no pathological changes or lymphocytosis shown in the myelogram. There were no mutations in the JAK2 V617F, MPL 515, and 12ex genes detected by polymerase chain reaction assays.
Antibodies to platelet levels were 260% (reference range up to 200), soluble glycocalicin 70%, immunochemical examination of blood and urine demonstrated decreased IgM concentration up to the low end of the normal range, and inflammatory dysproteinemia was found.
On August 22, 2019, the patient's condition significantly deteriorated due to the onset of acute pain in the abdomen, weakness, and an increase in body temperature up to 38.5 C. The patient was urgently transferred to the Surgery Department.
On physical examination, the patient's condition was found to be severe, accompanied by skin dryness and a coated tongue. Vesicular respiration was defined throughout the lung fields, and no wheezing was detected. The respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min. Heart sounds were rhythmic with a pulse rate of 122 beats/min and blood pressure of 110/75 mmHg. The abdomen was distended and painful on palpation. There was muscle tension over the entire surface of the abdominal cavity. The patient had no stool, passage of flatus was normal. The entire left half of the abdominal cavity was occupied by the spleen, which was painful and found to have solid consistency during palpation. The spleen had increased in size by 2 cm in 3 h during dynamic monitoring. Ultrasonography and CT of the abdominal organs revealed that the portal vein was 16 mm in diameter and contained an occlusive thrombus. The dimensions of the spleen were 260x111 cm. The splenic vein diameter was 18 mm, and its linear blood flow velocity was 3 cm/s. Due to the threat of rupture of the spleen due to acute thrombosis of the portal vein, an emergency splenectomy was performed. The removed spleen was approximately 380x210x170 mm in size (<PMC8200168_JBM-12-431-g0001_undivided_1_1.webp>). Histological and immunohistochemical examination of the operating material enabled the identification of splenic marginal zone lymphoma.
The postoperative period was uneventful, lab-based indicators normalized, and the patient's condition improved. The patient was prescribed antitumor therapy (rituximab 375 mg/m2 of body surface once a week for 4 weeks) and anticoagulant therapy (rivaroxaban 20 mg once a day for 6 months). The patient was discharged on the 8th day after surgery. Blood test indicators were as follows: RDW, 16.9%; neutrophils, 63.7%; and platelet count, 99 x 109/L. During anticoagulant medication, thrombocytopenia and hypocoagulation persisted. Ultrasonography and CT of the abdominal organs confirmed that there were no free liquids in the abdominal cavity, portal vein diameter was estimated at 18 mm, and partial recanalization with parietal thrombi was determined.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old female presenting with a 2-week history of weakness, recurrent abdominal pain, and fever up to 39 C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to admission on August 16, 2019, the patient developed weakness, recurrent extended abdominal pain, and fever up to 39 C. On August 22, 2019, her condition acutely deteriorated with severe abdominal pain, weakness, fever up to 38.5 C, abdominal distension with guarding, and rapid splenic enlargement (2 cm increase over 3 hours), prompting urgent transfer to Surgery.
subjective.past_medical_history: Untreated inactive viral hepatitis B carriage for over 20 years. No family history of cancer; no alcohol, tobacco, or drug addiction; no known allergies.
subjective.review_of_systems: On August 22, reported absence of stool with normal passage of flatus.

objective.physical_examination: Admission (August 16): Pale skin, moist tongue with white furred coating, lungs clear bilaterally, muffled heart sounds (pulse 72 bpm), soft non-tender abdomen with normal liver size, splenomegaly 13 x 10 cm protruding 7 cm below the costal arch (elastic, smooth). Deterioration (August 22): Severe condition, dry skin, coated tongue, vesicular breath sounds without wheezing (RR 20/min), rhythmic heart sounds (pulse 122 bpm), BP 110/75 mmHg, distended painful abdomen with diffuse muscle tension, firm painful spleen occupying the entire left hemiabdomen and enlarging 2 cm in 3 hours.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old Filipino man was diagnosed with HBV infection in 1994 in the Philippines. He remained without symptoms until 25 years later, when he presented to our institution sent by his primary care provider for positive HBsAg. His only pertinent history was heavy alcohol intake years prior to presentation which was reduced to 1 to 3 glasses of wine daily.
His work up revealed AST 29 U/L, ALT 47 U/L, hemoglobin of 16.8 g/dL, and platelets of 289 cells/UL. Blood chemistry demonstrated a creatinine of 0.89 mg/dL, BUN of 10 mg/dL, and sodium of 145 mEq/L. Alpha fetoprotein (AFP) was 2.9 ng/mL. Initial hepatitis work up revealed HBsAg reactive, HBcAb reactive, and HBeAg and HBeAb non-reactive with HBV DNA viral load of 36 IU/mL indicating chronic active hepatitis B, but also HBsAb 590 mIU/mL. Given the contradictory nature of the results, a repeat testing was obtained, which again showed HBsAg reactive, HBcAb reactive, HBeAg and HBeAb non-reactive, HBV DNA 73 IU/mL, and HBsAb 706 mIU/mL. The confirmed coexistence of HBsAg and high titers of HBsAb indicated immune escape variants.
Ultrasound imaging of the abdomen revealed irregular liver margins suggestive of cirrhosis. In accordance with AASLD guidelines, hepatic cirrhosis was diagnosed by imaging. Routine screening for HIV returned non-reactive and the clinical concern for lactic acidosis was low. Co-infection with hepatitis C or D was ruled out by nonreactive serologies. Hepatitis B virus genotype and basal core promoter (BCP)/precore mutation were sent to reference laboratory and came back as "not detected" perhaps due to inadequate viral load. Repeat BCP was deferred due to viral suppression and minimal evidence of clinical impact.
Treatment of naive s-variant chronic HBV and immune active disease, was initiated with entecavir 1 mg daily. Viral suppression was achieved within 2 months of therapy with undetectable HBV DNA <10 IU/mL and sustained to the time of this report at 18 months. He remains asymptomatic and adherent (Table 1).

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Started entecavir 1 mg daily, achieving viral suppression (HBV DNA <10 IU/mL) within 2 months, sustained at 18 months of follow-up, with the patient remaining asymptomatic and adherent.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old woman presented to outpatient clinic with complaints of severe fatigue and malaise. Her physical examination, past medical history and family history were normal. Laboratory values were as follows: Complete blood count within normal limits, glucose: 115 mg/dl, BUN, creatinine, lipid panel, electrolytes, alkaline phosphatase, gama glutamil transferase and bilirubin levels were all within normal ranges. AST: 16 U/L, ALT: 10 U/L, HBsAg: Positive, HBeAg: Negative, AntiHBe: positive and HBV DNA: 46.010 IU/ml. Abdominal ultrasound showed a single 15 x 10 mm sized hemangioma in the right lobe of liver and splenomegaly (135 mm). In liver biopsy with modified Ishac scoring system, hepatitis activity index was 5 and fibrosis score was 3. She was diagnosed with CHB and PEG IFN alpha-2a 180 mug treatment once weekly was iniated.
At two month of PEG IFN alpha-2a therapy, our patient complained of bilateral tinnitus and hearing loss. At this stage, otorhinolaryngologist was consulted and audiological examination was found to be normal. Then, PEG IFN alpha-2a treatment was continued. Audiological examination was repeated every week. HBV DNA levels were undetectable at first, third and sixth month of treatment but at 6 month, symptoms of tinnitus and hearing loss got worsened and bilateral sensorineural ototoxicity was detected in audiological examination. Thus, PEG IFN alpha-2a was stopped. One month later, bilateral ototoxicity completely reversed and audiological exam returned to normal.
Lamivudine 100 mg once daily was planned whenever HBV DNA level exceeds 2000 IU/ml. However, HBV DNA remained negative during six month follow-up. She is now symptom free and continues to be followed.

Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive. Abdominal ultrasound: Single 15 x 10 mm hemangioma in the right hepatic lobe and splenomegaly (135 mm).

Liver biopsy (modified Ishak scoring system): Hepatitis activity index 5, fibrosis score 3. Audiological examinations: Normal at month 2 of therapy; detected bilateral sensorineural ototoxicity at month 6; returned to normal 1 month after stopping PEG-IFN alpha-2a.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Initiated PEG-IFN alpha-2a 180 ug once weekly, achieving undetectable HBV DNA by month 1 (maintained at months 3 and 6). At month 6, PEG-IFN alpha-2a was discontinued due to worsening bilateral tinnitus, hearing loss, and confirmed bilateral sensorineural ototoxicity; ototoxicity completely reversed within 1 month with normal audiometry. Lamivudine 100 mg once daily was planned if HBV DNA exceeded 2,000 IU/mL, but HBV DNA remained negative over 6 months of follow-up and she remained symptom-free.

raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old female was admitted in October 2021 due to recurrent rashes of varying sizes with residual pigmentation on both lower extremities for one year. She had previously received low-dose steroids, but saw no improvement. Subsequently, her rash spread to the limbs and back, accompanied by knee joint pain and numbness in the dorsal foot after physical exertion. In January 2021, she tested positive for hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBsAg) with HBV-DNA of 8.64*107IU/mL, and then she received entecavir treatment. In July 2021, laboratory evaluations showed RF positivity with a significantly decreased complement C4. The blood free light chain kappa/lambda ratio was 5.675 (elevated), and cryoglobulin was positive. Bone marrow flow cytometry revealed abnormal plasma cells (CD38+, CD19+, CD138+, ckappa+, CD20-, CD56-, CD117-, clambda-) accounting for approximately 0.25% of the nucleated cells. Her HBV-DNA levels decreased below the detection limit. Her ANA, dsDNA, and ANCA were negative. The urine protein was 0.1g/day and serum creatinine was 61mumol/L. The cryoglobulin tested positive, and immunofixation of the cryoglobulin revealed a monoclonal IgM kappa and polyclonal IgG, consistent with type II mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (as shown in  <PMC11099222_fimmu-15-1390958-g002_C_3_4.webp> ). Skin biopsy suggested leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Renal biopsy revealed MPGN with hemosiderin deposits in the mesangial area and thrombus-like material deposition in a few glomerular capillary lumens, consistent with cryoglobulin-related renal damage (as shown in  <PMC11099222_fimmu-15-1390958-g002_A_1_4.webp> ). Immunofluorescence showed IgG (+/-), C3 (2+), IgM (1+), kappa (2+), and lambda (+/-) in the mesangial area and capillary wall, while Fib, IgA, C1q, and Alb were negative. Electron microscopy showed electron-dense deposits in the mesangial area (as shown in  <PMC11099222_fimmu-15-1390958-g002_B_2_4.webp> ). She then received entecavir, along with a steroid combined with intravenous cyclophosphamide regimen. However, her purpura reappeared as the glucocorticoid was tapered. Subsequently, she underwent three sessions of plasmapheresis, followed by 2 doses of rituximab (1g per infusion), after which her rash almost disappeared. One month later, her methylprednisolone was reduced to 20mg/day and was subsequently tapered.
In May 2022, She presented with recurrent widespread non-blanching purpura, anemia, inflammation, and persistently high levels of RF and low C4. Her cryoglobulin levels significantly increased, while CD19+ cells remained undetectable. No pathogenic mutations related to Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia in the MyD88 and CXCR4 genes. As there was no life-threatening organ damage, she continued antiviral treatment and methylprednisolone (10mg qd).
In September 2022, she developed ulceration on her lower limb and experienced difficulty walking due to pain. She then started orelabrutinib treatment (150mg qd), and her fresh rash completely disappeared two days later. A week later, her ulcerated wound healed, and she was able to walk normally again. She continued taking orelabrutinib for 3 months but discontinued in December 2022 due to a COVID-19 infection. One week after discontinuation, her rash recurred and she also exhibited signs of fatigue and arthralgia. She then resumed orelabrutinib three weeks later at a lower dosage (50mg qd), and the symptoms improved within 3 days. In April 2023, her hemoglobin was 92g/L, CRP was 9.17, and urine protein was 0.33g/day with stable serum creatinine but significantly low level of C3 (0.304g/L) and C4 (<0.066g/L). Her serum cryoglobulin remained at a high level, including IgG at 2.36g/L and IgM at 2.84g/L. The levels of HBsAg, HBcAb, RF-IgG, and RF-IgM were higher in the cryoglobulins than those in the cold supernatant. (Detailed in  Table 1 ) The bone marrow flow cytometry showed abnormal B lymphocytes accounting for approximately 0.27%, and abnormal plasma cells for 0.82% of the nucleated cells, suggesting no improvement in abnormal clonal cells. We have summarized the clinical course in  <PMC11099222_fimmu-15-1390958-g002_D_4_4.webp> .

Definitive Diagnosis: Hepatitis B virus (HBV)-associated type II mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis with cryoglobulinemic MPGN. Autoimmune vasculitis/SLE (ANA, dsDNA, ANCA negative) and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (MYD88/CXCR4 negative) were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Continued entecavir alongside corticosteroids and IV cyclophosphamide, but purpura recurred during steroid taper. Treated with three sessions of plasmapheresis and two 1 g rituximab infusions with near-complete rash resolution; methylprednisolone was tapered to 20 mg/day and then 10 mg daily. Discontinued orelabrutinib in December 2022 due to COVID-19 infection, with rash, fatigue, and arthralgia recurring 1 week later; resuming orelabrutinib at 50 mg daily 3 weeks later improved symptoms within 3 days, though high cryoglobulins, hypocomplementemia, and clonal bone marrow cells persisted in April 2023.

raw_case_text:
A 68-year-old man was evaluated with jaundice and signs of encephalopathy at the emergency department. He had a history of Crohn's disease (for which he underwent an ileocecal resection and was currently in remission without any medication) and a stable CHB infection since 2005. The transmission route was identified as men who have sex with men, although the precise date of transmission was unknown. HBV had been adequately suppressed with antiviral therapy; initially with entecavir which was subsequently switched to tenofovir disoproxil (TDF) 4 years ago. Notably, in 2005, HBeAg seroconversion occurred, persisting as negative in the following years. However, an HBeAg seroreversion was observed during tenofovir administration. The most recent HBeAg quantification was performed 3 years ago and showed that the patient was HBeAg-positive, anti-HBe-negative. Five years ago, liver stiffness measurement showed F2-3 liver fibrosis (8.8 kPa, FibroScan , Echosens, France). Two months ago, TDF was stopped since his treating physician proposed TDF cessation as he had been stable for multiple years (based on ALT and HBV DNA levels; HBeAg and HBsAg levels were not quantified, but he was assumed to be HBeAg negative). Follow-up appointments were scheduled for every 3 months.
At the emergency department, he complained about reduced alertness and jaundice for a couple of days and general malaise for 1-2 months. He did not use any new medication (including herbal supplements) or alcohol in the weeks before presentation. Emergency room vitals included a blood pressure of 157/93 mm Hg, heart rate of 101 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, and temperature of 37.5 C. Physical examination was notable for jaundice, bilaterally crepitation in the lung bases, and tenderness around the umbilicus. He was also noticeably slow in his reaction. The toxicology screen was negative for drugs, and paracetamol levels were low.
Laboratory results are displayed in Table 1. These showed elevated liver enzymes, international normalized ratio, and HBV DNA load of 7.1E8 IU/mL. Abdominal ultrasound showed liver steatosis, but no signs of cirrhosis, ascites, or portal hypertension. Acute liver failure due to HBV reactivation was considered. Antiviral therapy (TDF) was restarted, and broad-spectrum antibiotics as well as N-acetylcysteine were administered. During admission, liver function worsened, international normalized ratio increased, and encephalopathy progressed for which the patient was intubated. The clinical course is depicted in <PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F01_undivided_1_1.webp>.
After 3 days, the patient was transferred to a liver transplantation unit. HBV serum makers showed an elevated HBV DNA load and a positive HBeAg. Viral co-infections (HIV, hepatitis A virus, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis D virus, hepatitis E virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus) were excluded, and serum alfa-1-antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, ANA, cANCA, pANCA, antibodies against smooth muscle, anti-SLA, anti-mitochondrial antibodies were all within the normal range.
Four days after admission, the encephalopathy progressed and the liver function deteriorated further. The patient fulfilled both the King's College and the Clichy criteria for transplantation in the setting of acute liver failure. Consequently, the patient was put on the high-urgency liver transplantation waiting list. The next day, a liver (donation after brain death) became available, and the patient was successfully transplanted. Postoperative, prophylaxis with hepatitis B immunoglobulins 5,000 IE/day (Hepatect) was started next to antiviral therapy.
The liver explant showed a mottled, nutmeg appearance without signs of nodularity (<PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F02_undivided_1_1.webp>). Histological findings (<PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F03_a_1_5.webp><PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F03_b_2_5.webp><PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F03_c_3_5.webp><PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F03_d_4_5.webp><PMC11052559_crg-2024-0018-0001-538342_F03_e_5_5.webp>) showed confluent hepatocyte necrosis throughout the parenchyma, accompanied by moderate lobular infiltration and periportal ductular reaction. The portal/periportal regions showed lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with interface activity. There were no signs of significant fibrosis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for HBsAg. Thus, histological findings showed signs of acute liver failure which could be consistent with an HBV reactivation without signs of advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.
One day after the transplantation, the liver enzymes increased. CT abdomen showed infarction of liver segment 6 and stenosis of the hepatic artery, suggesting allograft dysfunction. The liver function improved in the following days, but the kidney function worsened (creatinine of 454 mumol/L) for which continuous veno-venous hemofiltration was started. Five days postoperative, inflammation parameters increased (C-reactive protein: 150 mg/L, leukocytes: 32 x 109/L, temperature: 36.8 C) and a CT showed signs of acute pancreatitis, for which supportive management was initiated.
Seventeen days posttransplantation, the patient became progressively hemodynamically unstable, which was caused by intra-abdominal bleeding. The patient was hemodynamically supported at the ICU. A re-laparotomy was performed and showed peripancreatic necrosis, bile duct injury, and bleeding from the vena cava inferior due to a dissolved suture caused by pancreatic necrosis. Hemostasis could not be achieved, the bleeding was packed with gauzes, and the patient was returned to the intensive care unit. Total blood loss was 15 L. Postoperatively, the patient developed multi-organ failure due to ischemia of the liver, stomach, head of the pancreas, cecum, sigmoid, kidneys, and parts of the small intestine. This all resulted from hemorrhagic shock due to the vena cava bleeding. Supportive treatment was stopped because there was no prospect of recovery, and the patient died. The CARE Checklist has been completed by the authors for this case report, attached as online supplementary material (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000538342).

Definitive Diagnosis: Acute liver failure secondary to hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation following TDF cessation. Plan & Clinical Outcome: Restarted TDF and administered broad-spectrum antibiotics and N-acetylcysteine. Liver function, INR, and encephalopathy worsened, requiring intubation and transfer to a liver transplant unit on day 3.
