assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Active chronic hepatitis C (HCV viral load 24,597 IU/mL) concurrent with recurrent MRSA tricuspid valve endocarditis (admission blood cultures and day 6 sternal abscess I&D cultures positive for MRSA) complicated by septic pulmonary emboli, sternal osteomyelitis, and mixed Type II cryoglobulinemic leukocytoclastic vasculitis with suspected renal and ischemic colonic involvement (multidisciplinary consensus favored endocarditis-driven cryoglobulinemia over active HCV or vancomycin reaction). ANCA-associated vasculitis and infectious colitis (C. difficile, H. pylori, enteric PCR) were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Vancomycin was switched on day 2 to IV daptomycin and ceftaroline (days 3-13 until blood cultures were negative for 72 hours), then narrowed to daptomycin monotherapy to complete 6 weeks of IV therapy from blood culture clearance. Underwent sternal abscess incision and drainage on day 6. Hematochezia resolved with conservative bowel rest by day 15. Discharged on hospital day 52 with complete resolution of cutaneous vasculitis, normalized serum creatinine (0.99 mg/dL), and no further hematochezia. Hepatitis C antiviral therapy was deferred to outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old male with a past medical history of substance use disorder, bilateral lower extremity ulcers, chronic hepatitis C infection for 6 years, and poor compliance with medical care presented to the ED with complaints of abdominal distention and scrotal swelling. The patient reported that symptoms started two weeks before his presentation and had progressively worsened. Patient also complained of bilateral non-healing lower extremity wounds which he had for a year. In terms of the hepatitis C, it was diagnosed six years prior to this presentation. Patient denied being on any treatment plan, with no adequate follow up with any physician. On examination, the abdomen was grossly distended with positive fluid wave, suggesting ascites. There was a 3+ pitting edema extending from the scrotum to the bilateral lower extremity ulcers with draining a foul-smelling purulent discharge. The lower extremity ulcers had sparce open lesions each noted to be superficial with fibro-granular wound beds, with mild odor, and serous discharge noted.
Initial vital signs revealed a temperature of 98.7 F, BP 129/70 mmHg, Pulse 71 bpm, RR 18 breaths per minute with oxygen saturation of 100%. Labs revealed hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dl (Normal: 12-16 g/dl) with platelet count of 78 K (Normal: 130-400 K). Urinalysis revealed large blood with 0-2 RBCs, negative nitrite, trace leukocyte esterase with 0-2 WBCs, and 100 mg/dl protein. A repeat urinalysis revealed large blood with 2-4 RBCs, positive nitrite, trace leukocyte esterase with 0-2 WBCs, and >300 mg/dl protein. CMP showed creatinine of 4.3 mg/dl with a baseline creatinine of 0.8 mg/dl a year prior, and BUN 55 mg/dl. A CT abdomen and pelvis confirmed a new-onset cirrhotic liver with abdominal ascites (See <PMC9195058_jchimp-12-02-053f1_undivided_1_1.webp>). A hepatitis panel was ordered, and it was negative for hepatitis A, and B, but positive for Hepatitis C virus. HIV was also negative. The patient was started on Furosemide, Octreotide, and Nadolol. He also received antibiotics and his wounds were managed.
The next day, the patient developed leukopenia with WBC of 4.5, with worsening hemoglobin and platelet count of 11.1 g/dl and 47 x 109/L respectively. His renal function continued to worsen with creatinine 4.76 mg/dl, and BUN 63 mg/dl. Patient underwent ultrasound-guided paracentesis, with 1.5 L of fluid removed. A renal ultrasound was performed which showed nonspecific increased echogenicity. His ascites and lower extremity ulcers improved significantly on the treatment regimen however, renal function continued to decline precipitously.
Given worsening renal function and cirrhosis, a possible diagnosis of the hepatorenal syndrome was made. Patient was started on Albumin infusion with no significant improvement in renal function. Hence, the nephrology team was consulted, and a renal biopsy was recommended. Patient was started on dialysis and the renal biopsy was subsequently performed.
Renal biopsy results showed mild focal mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with co-dominant deposits of IgA and C3. Serum complement levels were also lowwithC3 of 66 (normal: 82-185),C4 count of 11 (normal: 15-53), and lowtotal complement levels <10 (normal: 31-60). Patient hadHCVviral load count of 156,000 IU/mL and HCV genotype of 1a. Serum cryoglobulin levels were ordered, but due to a lab error itwas not resulted. These findings, together with the patient's clinical presentation, suggested a picture of mixed cryoglobulinemia secondary to HCV over hepatorenal syndrome as the cause of the patient's presenting symptoms. Patient was managed with Methylprednisone 1 g IV for 3 days and discharged with a plan for outpatient hemodialysis three times per week, as well as outpatient gastroenterology follow up to initiate Hepatitis C virus treatment. Patient was also encouraged to follow up outpatient to start treatment with Rituximab.
After being discharged from the hospital, patient was noted to have followed up with his dialysis appointments. We also scheduled the patient with our medicine clinic for a visit. Prior to the scheduled time of his clinic visit, the patient was called to confirm his appointment by a clinic staff. A family member responded to the call and confirmed that the patient passed away due to suspicions of drug overdose.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old man presenting with a 2-week history of progressive abdominal distension and scrotal swelling, and a 1-year history of bilateral non-healing lower extremity wounds.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to emergency department presentation, the patient developed abdominal distension and scrotal swelling that progressively worsened. He also reported bilateral non-healing lower extremity wounds present for 1 year.
subjective.past_medical_history: Substance use disorder, bilateral lower extremity ulcers (1 year), untreated chronic hepatitis C diagnosed 6 years prior with no regular medical follow-up and poor compliance with medical care. Baseline serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL 1 year prior.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: temperature 98.7°F, blood pressure 129/70 mmHg, pulse 71 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 100%. Abdomen grossly distended with positive fluid wave (ascites). 3+ pitting edema extending from the scrotum to the bilateral lower extremities, with sparse superficial open lower extremity ulcers showing fibro-granular wound beds, mild odor, serous drainage, and foul-smelling purulent discharge.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: Hb 12.1 g/dL (ref 12-16), platelets 78 K (ref 130-400 K), creatinine 4.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL), BUN 55 mg/dL. Next day: WBC 4.5, Hb 11.1 g/dL, platelets 47 x 10^9/L, creatinine 4.76 mg/dL, BUN 63 mg/dL. Initial urinalysis: large blood, 0-2 RBCs, negative nitrite, trace leukocyte esterase, 0-2 WBCs, 100 mg/dL protein; repeat urinalysis: large blood, 2-4 RBCs, positive nitrite, trace leukocyte esterase, 0-2 WBCs, >300 mg/dL protein. Low complements: C3 66 (ref 82-185), C4 11 (ref 15-53), total complement <10 (ref 31-60); serum cryoglobulin was not resulted due to lab error. Negative hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and HIV serologies. Renal ultrasound showed nonspecific increased echogenicity.
objective.advanced_workup: CT abdomen and pelvis confirmed new-onset hepatic cirrhosis with abdominal ascites. Ultrasound-guided paracentesis removed 1.5 L of ascitic fluid. Renal biopsy revealed mild focal mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with co-dominant IgA and C3 deposits.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Decompensated cirrhosis and acute renal failure secondary to suspected HCV-associated mixed cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis (favored over hepatorenal syndrome given biopsy-proven focal mesangial proliferative GN with IgA/C3 deposits, hypocomplementemia, and lack of response to albumin). Confirmed active hepatitis C infection with positive HCV panel, HCV viral load 156,000 IU/mL, and HCV genotype 1a. HAV, HBV, and HIV were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Treated with furosemide, octreotide, nadolol, antibiotics, wound care, and 1.5 L paracentesis, with marked improvement in ascites and lower extremity ulcers. Albumin infusion failed to improve precipitously declining renal function, requiring initiation of hemodialysis. Following renal biopsy, received IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days and was discharged on thrice-weekly outpatient hemodialysis with planned outpatient gastroenterology follow-up for HCV treatment and rituximab. He attended dialysis appointments but died prior to his scheduled clinic visit due to suspected drug overdose.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old African American male with chronic HCV presented to Johns Hopkins Dermatology with an intensely pruritic rash on his hands, legs, and trunk of 4 weeks duration. The eruption began approximately 10 days after receiving the Tdap vaccine (Adacel ; Sanofi Pasteur, Swiftwater, PA, USA). On physical exam, he had violaceous, flat-topped, 3- to 6-mm discrete and coalescing papules on his dorsal hands, back, chest, abdomen, buttocks, and lower extremities (Figure 1(a) and (b)). Examination of buccal mucosal surfaces revealed slight hyperpigmentation without evidence of Wickham striae. There was no evidence of nail involvement.
A clinical diagnosis of LP was confirmed when punch biopsy of a representative skin lesion was obtained. Histopathology revealed a dense lichenoid infiltrate of lymphocytes with colloid bodies along the dermal-epidermal junction (Figure 2(a)). There was epidermal hyperplasia with orthokeratosis, focal hypergranulosis, and a saw-toothed rete-ridge pattern with Max Joseph spaces (Figure 2(b)). The patient's daily medications included glimepiride 2 mg, metformin 500 mg, loratadine 10 mg, omeprazole 320 mg, simvastatin 40 mg, triamterene-hydrochlorothiazide 75-50 mg daily, ferrous sulfate 325 mg, methadone, and a fluticasone inhaler 100 mug/actuation. As-needed medications included clonazepam 0.5 mg, oxycodone/acetaminophen, and an albuterol inhaler 90 mug/actuation. Laboratory testing revealed transaminase elevation (aspartate transaminase (AST): 79 U/L, alanine transaminase (ALT): 56 U/L), elevated alpha-2-macroglobulins (356 mg/dL), low apolipoprotein A-1 (81 g/L), low albumin (3.4 g/dL), and a microcytic anemia with low serum iron (24 microg/dL). Serum studies were positive for anti-HCV antibody and HCV RNA was elevated at 6.198 log IU/mL. HCV FibroSURE fibrosis score was 0.83 and necroinflammatory activity score was 0.59, indicating fibrosis stage F4, cirrhosis, and moderate necroinflammatory activity. Rapid plasma reagin and human immunodeficiency virus were both negative.
The patient was treated with 60-mg intramuscular Kenalog and topical clobetasol 0.05% ointment. Significant improvement was noted on his 8-week follow-up visit.

As-needed medications: clonazepam 0.5 mg, oxycodone/acetaminophen, and albuterol inhaler 90 mcg/actuation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports intense pruritus. Home medications documented in past medical history.

objective.physical_examination: Violaceous, flat-topped, 3- to 6-mm discrete and coalescing papules distributed on the dorsal hands, back, chest, abdomen, buttocks, and lower extremities. Buccal mucosa showed slight hyperpigmentation without Wickham striae. No nail involvement.
objective.routine_investigations: AST 79 U/L, ALT 56 U/L, elevated alpha-2-macroglobulin 356 mg/dL, low apolipoprotein A-1 81 g/L, low albumin 3.4 g/dL, and microcytic anemia with low serum iron 24 mcg/dL. Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and HIV tests were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy confirmed lichen planus: dense lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate with colloid bodies along the dermal-epidermal junction, epidermal hyperplasia with orthokeratosis, focal hypergranulosis, and saw-toothed rete ridges with Max Joseph spaces. FibroSURE showed fibrosis score 0.83 (stage F4 cirrhosis) and necroinflammatory activity score 0.59 (moderate activity).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Tdap-triggered lichen planus in a patient with active chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and F4 cirrhosis. Confirmed by positive anti-HCV antibody, elevated HCV RNA (6.198 log IU/mL), FibroSURE F4 cirrhosis, and diagnostic skin biopsy. Syphilis (RPR) and HIV were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Treated with 60 mg intramuscular triamcinolone acetonide (Kenalog) and topical clobetasol 0.05% ointment, achieving significant clinical improvement at his 8-week follow-up visit.

raw_case_text: A 68-year-old man was referred to our hospital with a deteriorated general condition due to chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b. In this advanced stage of disease, treatment with pegylated interferon, ribavirin and a direct acting antiviral (DAA) was not indicated. Progressive cirrhosis necessitated a liver transplant 2 years later. The pre-transplant ophtalmological examination was performed 6 months before the actual liver transplantation and was completely normal. Following the transplantation, treatment with triple immunosuppression with tacrolimus, mycophenolatic mofetil and prednisolone was initiated. Tacrolimus was replaced by cyclosporine because of confusion. Three months later, the liver function had normalized with therapeutic blood levels of cyclosporine around 75 microg/l, the viral load at that moment was 130,499 IU/ml. Four months after the liver transplantation, the patient developed an acute visual loss in both eyes. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.6 in the right eye and 0.12 in the left eye. There was a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. On fundoscopy, bilateral optic disc oedema with haemorrhages at the disc margin was seen (Figure 1 (Fig. 1)). Treatment with cyclosporine A was interrupted and the dose of prednisolone was increased to 24 mg in combination with mycoplenolatic mofetil. One month later his vision was at 0.4 in the right eye and 0.25 in the left eye. The papillary oedema gradually subsided and the optic nerves became pale. Goldmann perimetry showed normal peripheral limits and central visual field testing showed a superior nasal scotoma in the right eye and an inferior nasal scotoma in the left eye. Brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) was within normal limits. A blood sample could not detect any infectious causes of an optic neuropathy, but an HCV viral load was >5 million IU/ml was measured. Patient was closely monitored, but after one month there was no visual improvement and optic pallor was progressive bilaterally; the dosage of prednisolone was increased to 2 x 32 mg. Six months after transplantation liver function tests deteriorated and the patient developed a histologically proven fibrotic cholestatic hepatitis. Antiviral therapy with peginterferon alpha 2a and ribavirin was given for one month. During that month BCVA slightly decreased and visual fields deteriorated. After this month, seven months after the liver transplant, therapy was switched to ribavirin and sofosbuvir. Afterwards visual acuity stabilized and Goldmann perimetry showed a scotoma inferior and nasal in the right eye and a narrowing of the peripheral field in the left eye. Central visual field examination showed an increase of the inferior nasal scotoma in both eyes. Ten months after the transplant, therapy was switched to daclatasvir and sofosbuvir because of the availability of DAA (direct acting antiviral) in Belgium. Prednisolone was progressively tapered and cyclosporine was reintroduced. The viral load dropped to 373 IU/ml. Over the following months, vision improved slightly to 0.7 in the right eye and to 0.5 in the left eye. The peripheral and central visual fields improved. The optic nerves had become atrophic (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)). Liver function test normalized and the viral load became undetectable. Three months after the start of daclatasvir and sofosbuvir the patient was a sustained responder and the liver test was completely normal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old man presenting initially with deteriorated general condition requiring liver transplantation, and subsequently with acute bilateral visual loss 4 months post-transplant.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Referred with deteriorated general condition that progressed to liver transplantation 2 years later. Four months after liver transplantation, he developed acute bilateral visual loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b with progressive cirrhosis (initially ineligible for pegylated interferon, ribavirin, and DAA) status post liver transplantation. Normal pre-transplant ophthalmological examination 6 months prior to surgery. Post-transplant triple immunosuppression initially consisted of tacrolimus (switched to cyclosporine due to confusion), mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone.

objective.physical_examination: Four months post-transplant: best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) 0.6 OD and 0.12 OS; right relative afferent pupillary defect; fundoscopy showed bilateral optic disc edema with disc-margin hemorrhages. One month later: BCVA 0.4 OD, 0.25 OS with subsiding papillary edema and progressive bilateral optic disc pallor (later evolving to optic nerve atrophy).
objective.routine_investigations: At 3 months post-transplant: normalized liver function tests and therapeutic cyclosporine trough ~75 mcg/L. Blood testing excluded other infectious causes of optic neuropathy. At 6 months post-transplant: deteriorating liver function tests.
objective.advanced_workup: Goldmann and central visual field testing (1 month after visual loss) showed normal peripheral limits with a right superior nasal scotoma and left inferior nasal scotoma; at 7 months post-transplant, showed right inferior nasal scotoma, left peripheral field narrowing, and enlarged bilateral inferior nasal scotomas. Brain MRI was normal. Liver biopsy at 6 months post-transplant confirmed fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Post-liver transplant recurrent chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1b infection progressing to biopsy-proven fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis (6 months post-transplant) with concurrent bilateral optic neuropathy/optic atrophy. Viral load rose from 130,499 IU/mL at 3 months post-transplant to >5 million IU/mL during visual loss. Other infectious causes of optic neuropathy and intracranial lesions (normal brain MRI) were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: At onset of visual loss, cyclosporine was interrupted and prednisolone increased to 24 mg (with mycophenolate mofetil), then increased to 32 mg twice daily after 1 month due to progressive optic pallor. Following fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis at 6 months, received peginterferon alpha-2a plus ribavirin for 1 month (during which BCVA and visual fields worsened), switched at 7 months to sofosbuvir plus ribavirin (stabilizing visual acuity), and switched at 10 months to daclatasvir plus sofosbuvir (with prednisolone taper and cyclosporine reintroduction). HCV viral load fell to 373 IU/mL and then became undetectable, LFTs completely normalized, he achieved sustained virologic response 3 months after starting daclatasvir/sofosbuvir, and vision/visual fields improved slightly (BCVA 0.7 OD, 0.5 OS) despite residual optic atrophy.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old Chinese man visited our hospital complaining of abdominal distension. He was positive for hepatitis C antibodies and showed elevated hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA (3.26E+004 IU/mL). The results of liver function tests were as follows: aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 38.2 U/L (reference range: 15-40), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 47.1 U/L (reference range: 9-50), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 92.2 U/L (reference range: 45-125), and total bilirubin 12.2 mmol/L (reference range: 0-26). Notably, both gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT) (108.5 U/L, reference range: 10-60) and alpha-fetoprotein were elevated (22.22 ng/mL, reference range: 0-20), and CA19-9 was normal (13.14 ng/mL, reference range: 0-37). EBV nucleic acid quantitative detection was 4.50E+003 copies/mL. Abdominal ultrasound showed the presence of a hypoechoic lesion in the right posterior lobe of the liver that was 41x51 mm in size. The results of a complete blood count, blood chemistry tests, and urinalysis were normal.
Gadolinium ethoxybenzyl diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed the lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images (Figure 1A and B). The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map showed that the tumor features restricted diffusion (Figure 1C). After administration of contrast material, the lesion showed hypoenhancing against the background (Figure 1D) and a heterogenic perfusion defect in the hepatobiliary phase. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (CEUS) showed hyperenhancement in the arterial phase, and after the contrast agent was rapidly cleared (<40s), the portal and delay phases showed hypoenhancement (Figure 1E and F). These findings led us to suspect a malignancy such as hepatocellular carcinoma, due to the patient's hepatitis C background. An abscess was also considered, although the patient did not have other symptoms, such as fever. After performing ultrasound-guided percutaneous tumor biopsy, examination of biopsy specimens revealed the presence of nodular cirrhosis. Histologically, the tumor consisted of poorly differentiated tumor cells along with intense lymphocytic infiltrates and interstitial fibrous proliferation (Figure 2A). Immunohistochemically, the neoplastic cells exhibited expression of cytokeratin 19 (Figure 2B) and 7 (Figure 2C) and no expression of HepPar-1 (Figure 2D). Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization produced negative results.
The patient was diagnosed with LELCC and hepatitis C-related liver cirrhosis. He underwent MWA (Figure 3) without adjuvant therapy and was given anti-HCV medication (400 mg sofosbuvir and 100 mg velpatasvir tablets once per day). Under ultrasound guidance, two microwave antenna (ECO-100C18 MWA antenna (Yigao, Nanjing, China)) were used for ablation together. First, feeding artery was ablated 4 min at 55 W. Second, tumor was ablated with 0.5cm safety margin. After ablation, ablation efficacy was evaluated by CEUS immediately.
AST and ALT were elevated at 47 U/L and 71.9 U/L, respectively, on postoperative day 1. GGT was also slightly elevated at 110.4 U/L. Pleural effusion occurred, and pleural drainage was performed on day 3 after MWA. The patient recovered and was discharged on postoperative day 7. Four months after MWA, laboratory tests showed HCV RNA < 100 IU/mL, alpha-fetoprotein 6.77 ng/mL, normal liver function, and EBV nucleic acid was not detected. MRI showed hyperintense on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, foci measuring 6.0 cm in the right posterior segment of the liver (Figure 4A and B). The ADC map did not show that the lesion features restricted diffusion (Figure 4C). The lesion exhibited mild peripheral enhancement in the arterial phase and low enhancement in venous and delay phases (Figure 4D). The patient has been followed-up with regular outpatient visits and no new lesions have occurred within 9 months after MWA (Figure 5).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old Chinese man presenting with abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient visited the hospital complaining of abdominal distension without other symptoms such as fever.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies fever.

objective.routine_investigations: LFTs: AST 38.2 U/L (ref 15-40), ALT 47.1 U/L (ref 9-50), ALP 92.2 U/L (ref 45-125), total bilirubin 12.2 mmol/L (ref 0-26), GGT 108.5 U/L (ref 10-60). Tumor markers: AFP 22.22 ng/mL (ref 0-20), CA19-9 13.14 ng/mL (ref 0-37). EBV nucleic acid quantitative detection 4.50 x 10^3 copies/mL. CBC, routine blood chemistry, and urinalysis were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 41 x 51 mm hypoechoic lesion in the right posterior lobe of the liver.
objective.advanced_workup: Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced liver MRI showed a T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense lesion with restricted diffusion on ADC, hypoenhancement against liver background, and a heterogeneous perfusion defect in the hepatobiliary phase. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) showed arterial-phase hyperenhancement with rapid washout (<40 s) and portal/delayed-phase hypoenhancement. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous tumor biopsy showed nodular cirrhosis and poorly differentiated neoplastic cells with intense lymphocytic infiltration and interstitial fibrous proliferation; immunohistochemistry was CK19+, CK7+, HepPar-1-, and EBER in situ hybridization was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Lymphoepithelioma-like cholangiocarcinoma (LELCC; EBER-negative) and hepatitis C-related liver cirrhosis. Confirmed by positive anti-HCV antibodies, elevated HCV RNA (3.26 x 10^4 IU/mL), and percutaneous liver/tumor biopsy. Liver abscess and hepatocellular carcinoma (HepPar-1 negative) were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Underwent ultrasound-guided microwave ablation (MWA) without adjuvant therapy using two ECO-100C18 antennas (feeding artery ablated 4 min at 55 W, tumor ablated with 0.5 cm safety margin; confirmed immediately by CEUS) and started oral sofosbuvir 400 mg/velpatasvir 100 mg once daily. Postoperative day 1 labs showed AST 47 U/L, ALT 71.9 U/L, and GGT 110.4 U/L; pleural effusion required drainage on day 3, and he was discharged on day 7. Four months post-MWA, HCV RNA was <100 IU/mL, AFP was 6.77 ng/mL, LFTs normalized, EBV DNA was undetectable, and MRI showed a 6.0 cm non-restricted ablation zone (T1 hyperintense, slightly T2 hyperintense, mild peripheral arterial enhancement). No new lesions appeared over 9 months of outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
In 2019, a 66-year-old woman from Luanda, Angola was referred to our service. Apart from well controlled hypertension, she was well with no other co-morbidities. Chronic HCV infection was diagnosed 10 years prior, following routine health screening. At that point, genotype analysis performed in Angola reported genotype 2a infection. At that point, she had declined pegylated interferon and ribavirin treatment given its potential toxicities. The route of acquisition of her HCV infection was unknown as no clear identifiable risk factors were evident. Her ALT was 71 IU/L (laboratory normal range 5-40 IU/L) and significant liver fibrosis was excluded with a FibroScanRliver stiffness measurement of 7.6kPa and an AST to Platelet Ratio Index (APRI) score of 0.2. Liver ultrasound was normal and HCV viral load was 9 772 784 IU/mL (Xpert, Cepheid, CA, USA). HIV and HBsAg testing, was negative. We did baseline population-based Sanger sequencing to evaluate for RAS in the NS3, NS5A and NS5B HCV genes using pan genotypic primers and the web-based geno2pheno program (Table 1). Sequences were aligned with GenBank reference sequences using BioEdit and a NS5B neighbour-joining phylogenetic tree was constructed in Mega 6.0 with 1000 bootstrap resamplings (<PMC7908326_PAMJ-36-232-g001_undivided_1_1.webp>). We assigned the sequence as a novel genotype 7b variant (accession number MT633130-MT633134). Considering the presence of extensive baseline RAS in the patient, a DAA therapy regimen was considered (Table 1).
The only available data on treatment was the single genotype 7a patient inadvertently treated in the ASTRAL-1 study. A sofosbuvir/velpatasvir combination was considered, however given the range of RAS, particularly the NS5A 93H mutation, the choice of velpatasvir posed a concern. This mutation impairs treatment response since it induces a high fold in vitro resistance to daclatasvir and velpatasvir. This has been observed to negatively influence SVR in real world experience with DAA therapy, mostly with genotype 3 HCV. An obvious lack of data of the NS5A 93H RAS in genotype 7b in addition to the range of other RAS present, influenced our decision making. Similarly and although not analogous to our patient, data observed in the retreatment MAGELLAN-1 part 2 study suggested that a 16 week duration of treatment with the NS3/NS5A DAA combination of glecaprevir and pibrentasvir, to be better than 12 weeks in patients with prior DAA failure and significant RAS. Given this, we elected to treat the patient with 16 weeks of glecaprevir and pibrentasvir combination as well as the NS5B nucleotide polymerase inhibitor sofosbuvir, all as single daily dosing. After 4 weeks on therapy, HCV viral load was recorded at <10IU/ml (HCV Xpert, Cepheid, CA, USA) and undetected at the end of treatment. Sustained virological response at 12 weeks post end of treatment (SVR12), was confirmed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old Angolan woman referred for evaluation and antiviral management of chronic viral hepatitis diagnosed 10 years earlier.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Referred in 2019 for management of a chronic hepatic viral infection originally detected 10 years earlier during routine health screening. She had previously declined pegylated interferon and ribavirin therapy due to potential toxicities and remained otherwise clinically well.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Luanda, Angola. Well-controlled hypertension with no other comorbidities. Chronic hepatitis C diagnosed 10 years prior on routine health screening (previously reported as genotype 2a in Angola; declined interferon/ribavirin). No identifiable transmission risk factors.

objective.routine_investigations: ALT 71 IU/L (ref 5-40 IU/L), APRI score 0.2. HIV and HBsAg testing were negative. Liver ultrasound was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: FibroScan liver stiffness measurement was 7.6 kPa, excluding significant liver fibrosis. Population-based Sanger sequencing of NS3, NS5A, and NS5B genes (geno2pheno, BioEdit, Mega 6.0 phylogenetic analysis) revealed extensive baseline resistance-associated substitutions (RAS), including NS5A 93H.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic hepatitis C virus infection caused by a novel HCV genotype 7b variant (GenBank accession MT633130-MT633134; previously mistyped as genotype 2a) with baseline HCV viral load of 9,772,784 IU/mL (Xpert) and extensive baseline RAS including NS5A 93H. HIV, HBV (HBsAg negative), and significant liver fibrosis were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Because NS5A 93H confers high-level resistance to velpatasvir and daclatasvir, she was treated with 16 weeks of once-daily glecaprevir/pibrentasvir plus sofosbuvir. HCV viral load fell to <10 IU/mL after 4 weeks of therapy, became undetectable at end of treatment, and achieved confirmed sustained virologic response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12).

raw_case_text: Case 1: A 65-year-old man presented with metastatic melanoma involving his lungs and mediastinal and neck lymph nodes; he had no detectable hepatic metastases. The patient had contracted HCV (genotype 1a) approximately twenty five years prior to his melanoma diagnosis, though his hepatitis was never treated. A liver biopsy performed in 2000 demonstrated periportal fibrosis without bridging as well as mild inflammatory activity. Pathologic findings from a repeat liver biopsy in 2005 were unchanged. His melanoma was initially treated with high-dose interleukin-2 (IL-2) in May 2011. After two cycles, his melanoma had regressed, but he developed obstructive jaundice secondary to cholelithiasis with gallbladder sludge, requiring a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Serologic evaluation around the time of surgery (August 2011) revealed the following: HCV viral load: 690,000 IU/mL, hepatitis A IgM negative, HBV core (HBc) IgG and IgM negative, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) negative. A liver biopsy performed during surgery revealed cirrhosis with mild, non-specific inflammation and focal hemosiderin accumulation. He received two more cycles of IL-2, but his melanoma subsequently progressed and he began treatment with ipilimumab in November 2011. During and after ipilimumab administration, hepatic transaminases remained unchanged from baseline, with grade 1 elevations. Although the patient tolerated 4 cycles of ipilimumab without drug-limiting toxicities, he experienced disease progression and was transitioned to temozolomide. After three cycles of temozolomide, HCV viral load had increased four-fold to 2,720,000 IU/mL. The patient expired sixteen months after the initiation of ipilimumab from progression of his melanoma.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old man presenting with metastatic melanoma involving the lungs and mediastinal and neck lymph nodes, later developing obstructive jaundice during systemic immunotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Presented with metastatic melanoma involving the lungs, mediastinal lymph nodes, and neck lymph nodes without hepatic metastases. After receiving two cycles of high-dose interleukin-2 (IL-2) starting in May 2011 (with initial melanoma regression), he developed obstructive jaundice secondary to cholelithiasis with gallbladder sludge requiring laparoscopic cholecystectomy in August 2011.
subjective.past_medical_history: Untreated chronic hepatitis C virus (genotype 1a) contracted approximately 25 years prior to melanoma diagnosis. Prior liver biopsies in 2000 and 2005 both demonstrated unchanged periportal fibrosis without bridging and mild inflammatory activity.

objective.routine_investigations: August 2011 serologies: negative hepatitis A IgM, HBc IgG and IgM, and HBsAg. Hepatic transaminases remained unchanged from baseline with grade 1 elevations during and after ipilimumab.
objective.advanced_workup: Intraoperative liver biopsy during August 2011 laparoscopic cholecystectomy revealed cirrhosis with mild, nonspecific inflammation and focal hemosiderin accumulation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Untreated chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1a infection with progression to biopsy-proven cirrhosis in a patient with metastatic melanoma (without hepatic metastases) complicated by obstructive jaundice from cholelithiasis/gallbladder sludge. HCV viral load was 690,000 IU/mL in August 2011 and increased four-fold to 2,720,000 IU/mL after three cycles of temozolomide. Hepatitis A and hepatitis B were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis/obstructive jaundice after 2 cycles of high-dose IL-2, then received 2 additional cycles of IL-2. Following melanoma progression, received 4 cycles of ipilimumab starting November 2011 without drug-limiting toxicities or LFT worsening, then transitioned to temozolomide for further progression. Died 16 months after initiating ipilimumab from melanoma progression.

raw_case_text: Case 2: A 56-year-old man with HCV was found to have stage IIIA cutaneous melanoma. A local recurrence in June 2010 was treated with excision and axillary lymph node dissection. Laboratory values at that time revealed an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 45 IU/L (normal range 0-40 IU/L), a normal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (0-55 IU/L), a negative HBsAg, a negative HBc IgM, a positive HCV antibody and an HCV viral load of 103,160 IU/mL. He did not receive systemic treatment for his hepatitis. Subsequent restaging scans demonstrated new metastases in lymph nodes, muscle and brain. He underwent stereotactic radiosurgery for his brain lesion followed by two cycles of temozolomide. During systemic therapy with temozolomide, the patient's hepatic transaminases rose: AST 254 IU/L, ALT 325 IU/L. Shortly thereafter, new brain and soft tissue lesions appeared. Whole-brain radiotherapy was administered, followed by initiation of ipilimumab in April 2011. Immediately prior to ipilimumab administration, hepatic transaminases had normalized (AST 29 IU/L, ALT 17 IU/L), and HCV viral load was 3,070 IU/mL. He underwent four cycles of ipilimumab without significant changes in liver function tests. The patient experienced progressive disease five months after initiating ipilimumab, at which time HCV viral load was 2,279,050 IU/mL, and AST and ALT had increased to 208 and 119 IU/L, respectively. Because of the potential for immune-related causality, corticosteroid therapy was administered, with improvement of hepatic transaminases (AST 117, ALT 36 IU/L). The patient then enrolled in a phase I clinical trial of a pan-RAF kinase inhibitor due to progression of disease, and was maintained on steroids during the course of experimental therapy. His course was marked by liver function test fluctuations (AST 35-117, ALT 28-132 IU/L) as well as adrenal insufficiency after decreasing the patient's dose of corticosteroids. Ten months after initiating ipilimumab, HCV viral load was >69,000,000 IU/mL, however, his hepatic transaminase levels subsequently normalized. Although his viral load and LFTs were discordant, the patient was approaching hospice care at this time and further investigation of the significance of these findings was postponed. Two months later, the patient died from progressive melanoma. Of note, this case was previously reported in detail but summarized here to augment the current case series.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old man presenting with stage IIIA cutaneous melanoma and local recurrence, subsequently developing distant metastases.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had stage IIIA cutaneous melanoma with local recurrence in June 2010 treated by excision and axillary lymph node dissection, followed by restaging detection of lymph node, muscle, and brain metastases, and later additional brain and soft tissue metastases.
subjective.past_medical_history: Untreated chronic hepatitis C virus infection. Stage IIIA cutaneous melanoma status post excision and axillary lymph node dissection (June 2010).

objective.routine_investigations: June 2010: AST 45 IU/L (ref 0-40), normal ALT (ref 0-55), negative HBsAg and HBc IgM. During temozolomide: AST 254 IU/L, ALT 325 IU/L. Pre-ipilimumab (April 2011): AST 29 IU/L, ALT 17 IU/L. Five months post-ipilimumab: AST 208 IU/L, ALT 119 IU/L (improved on steroids to AST 117 IU/L, ALT 36 IU/L). During subsequent experimental therapy: fluctuating AST 35-117 IU/L and ALT 28-132 IU/L, later normalizing despite viral load surge.
objective.advanced_workup: Restaging imaging revealed metastatic lesions in lymph nodes, muscle, soft tissue, and brain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Untreated chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection (positive HCV antibody; viral load 103,160 IU/mL in June 2010, 3,070 IU/mL pre-ipilimumab, 2,279,050 IU/mL at 5 months post-ipilimumab, and >69,000,000 IU/mL at 10 months post-ipilimumab with discordant normal LFTs) in a patient with metastatic cutaneous melanoma, complicated by steroid-responsive transaminitis and steroid-taper adrenal insufficiency. Hepatitis B was excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Received stereotactic radiosurgery for brain metastasis, 2 cycles of temozolomide, whole-brain radiotherapy, and 4 cycles of ipilimumab starting April 2011 (well-tolerated during cycles). Treated with corticosteroids at 5 months for suspected immune-related transaminitis with LFT improvement, then enrolled in a phase I pan-RAF kinase inhibitor trial while maintained on steroids (developing adrenal insufficiency on dose reduction). Transitioned to hospice care and died from progressive melanoma 12 months after initiating ipilimumab.

raw_case_text: Case 4: A 71-year-old man presented with metastatic ocular (choroidal) melanoma without hepatic involvement. His primary lesion had been treated thirteen years earlier with right orbital enucleation. Three years after enucleation he was diagnosed with HCV but did not require treatment. Evaluations for hepatitis A, HBV and HIV were negative. Serologic evaluation prior to initiation of ipilimumab revealed HCV viral load of 2,310,000 IU/mL and grade 1 AST and ALT. Three weeks after one cycle of ipilimumab, the patient was found to have grade 2 and 3 elevations of AST and ALT, respectively. Ipilimumab was held and high-dose prednisone was administered. HCV viral load had decreased to 408,000 IU/mL. Liver biopsy demonstrated chronic, active Scheuer grade 2 hepatitis and Scheuer stage 2 periportal fibrosis. There was no evidence of associated autoimmunity; a panel of serologic markers associated with autoimmune hepatitis (anti-nuclear cytoplasmic antibody, IgG; double stranded DNA antibody, IgG; F-actin antibody, IgG; anti-soluble liver antigen, IgG; mitochondrial M2 antibody, IgG; liver kidney microsome antibody; and anti-neuronal nuclear antibody) was negative. Extractable nuclear antigen screen was equivocal and was not pursued. His serum IgG was mildly elevated at 1630 mg/dL (normal range 694-1,618). As there was no evidence of autoimmune hepatitis, his prednisone was discontinued. Magnetic resonance imagining (MRI) of the abdomen revealed no evidence of malignancy. The patient's ALT and AST returned to grade 1, and, after a brief dose delay, ipilimumab was restarted with subsequent normalization of hepatic transaminases. Five months after initiation of ipilimumab the patient's melanoma was stable and HCV viral load was 108,000 IU/mL. Eight months after initiation of ipilimumab, however, a bronchoscopy and PET/CT scan both showed progression of disease without hepatic involvement. Shortly thereafter, serum AST and ALT became elevated (grade 1). HCV viral load measured 11 months after initiation of ipilimumab increased to 653,000 IU/mL. The patient was treated with temozolomide, which was discontinued due to thrombocytopenia. He subsequently relocated and was lost to follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old man presenting with metastatic ocular (choroidal) melanoma without hepatic involvement.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Presented with metastatic ocular (choroidal) melanoma without hepatic involvement, 13 years after treatment of his primary tumor. Three weeks after receiving his first cycle of ipilimumab, he developed elevated hepatic transaminases.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary ocular (choroidal) melanoma treated with right orbital enucleation 13 years earlier. Diagnosed with hepatitis C virus infection 3 years after enucleation without requiring antiviral treatment.

objective.routine_investigations: Negative hepatitis A, HBV, and HIV evaluations. Pre-ipilimumab: grade 1 AST and ALT. Three weeks post-cycle 1 ipilimumab: grade 2 AST and grade 3 ALT elevations (returned to grade 1, then normalized upon ipilimumab rechallenge; later grade 1 elevation at ~8 months). Mildly elevated serum IgG 1,630 mg/dL (ref 694-1,618).
objective.advanced_workup: Autoimmune hepatitis serologic panel (ANCA IgG, anti-dsDNA IgG, F-actin IgG, anti-SLA IgG, mitochondrial M2 IgG, anti-LKM, anti-neuronal nuclear antibody) was negative; ENA screen equivocal. Liver biopsy showed chronic active Scheuer grade 2 hepatitis and Scheuer stage 2 periportal fibrosis without autoimmune features. Abdominal MRI revealed no hepatic malignancy. Bronchoscopy and PET/CT at 8 months demonstrated extrahepatic melanoma progression without hepatic involvement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic untreated hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection with biopsy-proven chronic active hepatitis (Scheuer grade 2, stage 2 periportal fibrosis) in a patient with metastatic choroidal melanoma. HCV viral load was 2,310,000 IU/mL pre-ipilimumab, 408,000 IU/mL at 3 weeks, 108,000 IU/mL at 5 months, and 653,000 IU/mL at 11 months. Hepatitis A, HBV, HIV, autoimmune hepatitis, and hepatic metastases were excluded.

Plan & Clinical Outcome: Ipilimumab was held 3 weeks after cycle 1 for grade 2/3 transaminitis and high-dose prednisone was initiated, then discontinued once biopsy and serology ruled out autoimmune hepatitis. Following brief dose delay and return of LFTs to grade 1, ipilimumab was restarted with LFT normalization and stable melanoma at 5 months. After extrahepatic progression at 8 months, temozolomide was started but discontinued due to thrombocytopenia; the patient relocated and was lost to follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old man with chronic genotype-1A HCV infection complicated by compensated cirrhosis (Child-Turcotte-Pugh Score A [CTP-A], Model for End-Stage Liver Disease [MELD] 6) with radiographic and laboratory evidence of portal hypertension was evaluated for HCV treatment. He previously had been treated with multiple courses of interferon and ribavirin with end-of-treatment responses but subsequent relapses. He also had been treated with interferon, ribavirin, and a protease inhibitor, but discontinued the medications prematurely due to adverse drug effects. The patient had RYGB surgery in early 2000.
In 2014, he was treated with a combination of sofosbuvir and simeprevir. Prior to therapy, his liver enzyme levels were normal and his HCV RNA level was 29 964 IU/mL. After the first 4 weeks of treatment, HCV RNA was undetectable but it became detectable again by the 16th week of treatment. In 2015, he was treated with sofosbuvir and ledipasvir for 24 weeks. He had no detectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after completion of treatment (SVR-12) but relapsed 24 weeks later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis presenting for antiviral treatment evaluation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented for evaluation of chronic liver disease complicated by compensated cirrhosis (Child-Turcotte-Pugh Score A, MELD 6) with radiographic and laboratory evidence of portal hypertension. He had previously been treated with multiple courses of interferon and ribavirin with end-of-treatment responses followed by relapses, as well as a regimen of interferon, ribavirin, and a protease inhibitor that was discontinued prematurely due to adverse drug effects.
subjective.past_medical_history: Compensated cirrhosis (CTP-A, MELD 6) with portal hypertension. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery in early 2000. Prior unsuccessful courses of interferon/ribavirin and interferon/ribavirin/protease inhibitor.

objective.routine_investigations: Prior to 2014 therapy, liver enzyme levels were normal; laboratory evidence of portal hypertension was noted.
objective.advanced_workup: Radiographic evidence of portal hypertension was noted.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic genotype-1A hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection complicated by compensated cirrhosis (CTP-A, MELD 6) and portal hypertension, confirmed by pre-treatment HCV RNA level of 29,964 IU/mL in 2014.

Plan & Clinical Course: In 2014, he was treated with sofosbuvir and simeprevir; HCV RNA became undetectable after 4 weeks but became detectable again by week 16 of treatment. In 2015, he received sofosbuvir and ledipasvir for 24 weeks, achieving undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR-12), but relapsed 24 weeks later.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old woman with chronic genotype-1A HCV infection complicated by cirrhosis (CTP-A, MELD 6) with a history of grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy was evaluated for HCV treatment. She previously had been treated unsuccessfully with interferon and ribavirin. She had RYGB surgery in the 1990s.
In 2014, she had elevated liver enzyme levels (aspartate aminotransferase = 88 U/L, alanine aminotransferase = 76 U/L) and an HCV RNA level of 4 136 276 IU/mL. She was treated with a combination of sofosbuvir and simeprevir for 12 weeks. HCV RNA level during treatment is unknown; however, 8 weeks after completing therapy, her HCV RNA level was 3 132 997 IU/mL. Subsequently, she was treated with a combination sofosbuvir and ledipasvir, but this therapy was stopped after 11 weeks due to lack of virologic response.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis and a history of grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy presenting for antiviral treatment evaluation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented for evaluation of chronic liver disease complicated by cirrhosis (Child-Turcotte-Pugh Score A, MELD 6) with a history of grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy. She had previously undergone unsuccessful treatment with interferon and ribavirin.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cirrhosis (CTP-A, MELD 6) with a history of grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery in the 1990s. Prior unsuccessful treatment with interferon and ribavirin.

objective.routine_investigations: In 2014, elevated liver enzymes: AST 88 U/L and ALT 76 U/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic genotype-1A hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection complicated by cirrhosis (CTP-A, MELD 6) and grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy, confirmed by baseline HCV RNA level of 4,136,276 IU/mL in 2014.

Plan & Clinical Course: Treated with sofosbuvir and simeprevir for 12 weeks; on-treatment HCV RNA was unknown, and 8 weeks after completing therapy HCV RNA was 3,132,997 IU/mL. Subsequently treated with sofosbuvir and ledipasvir, which was stopped after 11 weeks due to lack of virologic response.

raw_case_text:
An 85-year-old Japanese woman visited the Tsuji Dental and Oral Surgery Clinic on September 17, 2021, complaining of pain in her buccal mucosa. She had received dental treatment at her family dentist's office in April 2021, when the dentist first indicated the presence of OLP in the buccal mucosa. Subsequently, she complained of pain in the area while eating and was referred to our clinic by her family dentist. White lesions were found on the buccal mucosae, on both sides, along with erosions on the left buccal mucosa (Fig. 1). The lesions were clinically diagnosed as OLP by an oral surgeon. Beclomethasone dipropionate 50 mug was sprayed daily on the oral mucosa twice daily for pain relief.
The patient was diagnosed with hepatitis C after receiving a blood transfusion during a hysterectomy for uterine cancer at age 55. Consequently, she regularly visited a hospital with a full-time hepatologist for 30 years (from age 55 to 85) but did not receive antiviral therapy for the HCV infection. She was taking ursodeoxycholic acid once daily as anti-inflammatory therapy for several years. The patient was diagnosed with hypothyroidism at around 65 years of age and was taking levothyroxine sodium hydrate daily. Additionally, she was diagnosed with cholelithiasis and age-related hearing loss. She did not use a hearing aid and was able to communicate. No signs of dementia were observed.
IFN therapy was recommended to the patient by her hepatologist in the past. However, she refused the treatment due to concerns about the side effects; the reason for refusal of treatment was determined using a questionnaire, owing to the age-related hearing loss (Table 1).
DAA treatment for hepatitis C was introduced in Japan in 2014. The hepatologist had recommended this treatment to the patient several times in the past, but she did not accept antiviral therapy because she could not understand the physician's explanation due to hearing loss. The patient confided that she was aware that her hearing loss was interfering with her communication abilities; yet she pretended to be able to hear for years because she did not want to interrupt the flow of conversation in the doctor's office. She said that she "could not be bothered to ask the doctor to repeat" and "did not understand the technical terms used by the doctor."
During her first visit to our hospital, the patient and her family were informed that OLP is an oral potentially malignant disorder most likely caused by HCV infection and can be cured if the virus is eliminated by antiviral therapy. She had little knowledge about the latest treatments for hepatitis C; hence, the benefits of IFN-free DAAs were explained, and treatment at a specialized facility was recommended. Consequently, DAA treatment (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks) was started at a specialized medical facility on February 4, 2022, based on Japanese guidelines for the management of HCV infection, and the HCV RNA was undetectable within 4 weeks of treatment. Table 2 shows the results of the biochemical blood tests. The Japanese medical insurance system does not allow blood tests in dental clinics; therefore, the tests were performed at other hospitals. Improvements in OLP followed by the absence of pain were observed after starting the DAA treatment (Fig. 2). The use of beclomethasone dipropionate became almost unnecessary.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 85-year-old woman presenting on September 17, 2021, with pain in her buccal mucosa while eating.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In April 2021, during dental treatment at her family dentist's office, oral lichen planus (OLP) was first identified in her buccal mucosa. She subsequently developed pain in the buccal mucosa while eating and was referred to Tsuji Dental and Oral Surgery Clinic on September 17, 2021.
subjective.past_medical_history: Japanese woman with history of hysterectomy for uterine cancer with blood transfusion at age 55, followed by 30 years of regular hepatology visits (ages 55-85) without antiviral therapy (taking ursodeoxycholic acid once daily for several years). Hypothyroidism diagnosed around age 65 (taking levothyroxine sodium hydrate daily). Cholelithiasis. Age-related hearing loss (does not use a hearing aid; previously impaired comprehension of physician explanations). No signs of dementia.
subjective.review_of_systems: HEENT: buccal mucosal pain while eating and age-related hearing loss. Home medications: ursodeoxycholic acid once daily, levothyroxine sodium hydrate daily.

objective.physical_examination: Oral examination revealed white lesions on both buccal mucosae with erosions on the left buccal mucosa (clinically diagnosed as oral lichen planus). Able to communicate without signs of dementia.
objective.routine_investigations: Biochemical blood tests were performed at outside hospitals (Table 2; exact values not specified in text).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection (originally diagnosed after blood transfusion at age 55) associated with symptomatic oral lichen planus (OLP) of the bilateral buccal mucosae.

Plan & Clinical Course: Initially treated symptomatically with topical beclomethasone dipropionate 50 ug sprayed twice daily on the oral mucosa for pain relief. After counseling the patient and her family on the link between OLP and HCV and the benefits of interferon-free direct-acting antivirals (previously declined due to side-effect concerns and hearing-loss-related communication barriers), she began an 8-week course of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir on February 4, 2022, at a specialized facility. HCV RNA became undetectable within 4 weeks of therapy. OLP lesions improved with resolution of oral pain, making beclomethasone dipropionate nearly unnecessary.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old Japanese female (height 156.0 cm; weight 73.0 kg) with HCV-associated cirrhosis (genotype Ib) visited our clinic for the treatment of cirrhosis. She was treated with the oral administration of ursodeoxycholic acid at 600 mg/day. From May 31, 2011, injection of 80 mL of Stronger Neo-Minophagen C (usually used to lower serum transaminase, 2-3 times a week) was carried out until the end of August 2019.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) was carried out on February 10, 2011, which showed unevenness of the surface of the liver with splenomegaly, and she was diagnosed with a cirrhotic state. For eradication of HCV, PEG-IFN/ribavirin therapy was performed from August 5 to December 5, 2012, but it was not effective. Thereafter, CT performed on February 6, 2018, showed ascites and pleural effusion (<PMC8138198_crg-0015-0436-g01_a_1_2.webp><PMC8138198_crg-0015-0436-g01_b_2_2.webp>) and she was diagnosed with decompensated liver cirrhosis. Furosemide and Aldactone A were administered, but pleural effusion and ascites remained. For the low albumin level, albumin infusion was carried out from March 22, 2016, to August 30, 2019 (every 2 weeks).
On August 3, 2019, a new DAA drug, SOF (NS5B inhibitor, 400 mg)/VEL (NS5A inhibitor, 100 mg), was administered until October 25, 2019 (about 12 weeks). HCV-RNA became negative on August 30, 2019. Abdominal CT performed on September 25 showed neither ascites nor pleural effusion (<PMC8138198_crg-0015-0436-g02_a_1_2.webp><PMC8138198_crg-0015-0436-g02_b_2_2.webp>).
Hepatic encephalopathy (grade I-II), which appeared on July 23, 2019 (the patient claimed cloudiness of sensation, serum ammonia level of 112 mug/dL), disappeared on October 7, 2019 (serum ammonia level of 85 mug/dL) (<PMC8138198_crg-0015-0436-g03_undivided_1_1.webp>). She stated that her consciousness was cloudy and it took many hours for the preparation of each meal just before the SOF/VEL treatment, but after the disappearance of HCV-RNA by the therapy, her consciousness became clear and she could prepare a meal in a short time. Furthermore, she also stated that the sensation of fatigue had disappeared, and it had become easier to move by the 6th week of administration of the drugs. In addition, she also showed marked improvements in the albumin level (Fig. 4) and in prothrombin time (Fig. 5). As a result, the Child-Pugh classification improved from Child B to Child A.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old female presenting for management of liver cirrhosis, later developing cloudiness of consciousness and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented for ongoing treatment of liver cirrhosis and received oral ursodeoxycholic acid 600 mg/day and Stronger Neo-Minophagen C 80 mL injections 2-3 times weekly from May 31, 2011, through August 2019, plus biweekly albumin infusions from March 22, 2016, to August 30, 2019, for hypoalbuminemia. Following progression to decompensated cirrhosis with ascites and pleural effusion in February 2018 (persistent despite furosemide and Aldactone A), she developed grade I-II hepatic encephalopathy on July 23, 2019, reporting cloudiness of sensation/consciousness, fatigue, and taking many hours to prepare each meal.
subjective.past_medical_history: Japanese female (height 156.0 cm, weight 73.0 kg) with decompensated liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) complicated by ascites, pleural effusion, hypoalbuminemia, and grade I-II hepatic encephalopathy. Prior ineffective PEG-IFN/ribavirin therapy (August 5 to December 5, 2012).
subjective.review_of_systems: Neurological/Constitutional: cloudiness of sensation/consciousness, difficulty preparing meals, and fatigue. Medications: ursodeoxycholic acid 600 mg/day, Stronger Neo-Minophagen C, furosemide, Aldactone A, albumin infusions.

objective.physical_examination: Anthropometrics: height 156.0 cm, weight 73.0 kg.
objective.routine_investigations: Low serum albumin requiring biweekly infusions; elevated serum ammonia of 112 ug/dL on July 23, 2019 (during grade I-II hepatic encephalopathy), declining to 85 ug/dL on October 7, 2019, with marked post-treatment improvements in serum albumin and prothrombin time.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT on February 10, 2011, showed liver surface unevenness and splenomegaly consistent with cirrhosis. Repeat CT on February 6, 2018, revealed ascites and pleural effusion. Follow-up abdominal CT on September 25, 2019, showed complete resolution of ascites and pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Decompensated liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) secondary to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1b infection, complicated by ascites, pleural effusion, and grade I-II hepatic encephalopathy.

Plan & Clinical Course: Treated with sofosbuvir 400 mg / velpatasvir 100 mg (SOF/VEL) for approximately 12 weeks (August 3 to October 25, 2019). HCV RNA became negative on August 30, 2019. Ascites and pleural effusion resolved on CT by September 25, 2019, and hepatic encephalopathy resolved by October 7, 2019 (ammonia decreased from 112 to 85 ug/dL), with clearing of consciousness, faster meal preparation, resolution of fatigue, and improved mobility by week 6. Marked improvements in albumin and prothrombin time upgraded her Child-Pugh classification from Child B to Child A.

raw_case_text: A 53-year-old man first visited our hospital because of liver dysfunction in 1992. The patient had no significant medical history other than diabetes. The patient was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1. His platelet count was 165,000/muL, and his albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score was -3.07, which was classified as grade 1. He refused IFN therapy due to severe adverse events and underwent regular follow-up blood tests and abdominal ultrasound sonography (US) every 3 months. The clinical course of the patient is shown in Figure 1. His platelet count gradually decreased, and the ALBI score increased. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed the emergence of esophageal varices. In 2004, he first underwent contrast-enhanced CT to screen for hepatocellular carcinoma. The CT image did not reveal any tumor in the liver; however, there was an ovoid, homogenous, highly enhancing lesion with a diameter of 28 mm at the confluence of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein (<PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F02_a_1_5.webp><PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F02_b_2_5.webp>). Based on the CT image, the patient was diagnosed with PVA. At that time, abdominal US showed limited dilatation of the portal vein due to the PVA (<PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F02_c_3_5.webp>). As the patient did not present with any symptoms, no treatments were performed, and he was scheduled for a follow-up examination. In 2006 and 2007, the esophageal varices further enlarged, and combination therapies of endoscopic variceal ligation and endoscopic injection sclerotherapy were performed twice. His platelet count further decreased, and his ALBI score increased to -1.77, which was classified as grade 2b. In 2010, contrast-enhanced CT showed the PVA with a diameter of 38 mm and an internal thrombus (<PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F02_d_4_5.webp><PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F02_e_5_5.webp>). He was treated with intravenous administration of antithrombin III (1,500 units/day) for 10 days. The internal thrombus completely disappeared; however, the diameter of the PVA increased to 43 mm 1 year later. Oral administration of warfarin was initiated to prevent recurrence of thrombosis. The diameter of the PVA continued to gradually increase. In 2014 and 2017, radiofrequency ablation was performed for hepatocellular carcinoma in segments 6 and 7 that measured 17 mm and 15 mm, respectively. In 2017, the diameter of the PVA measured 52 mm. He then decided to undergo DAA treatment. The patient was treated with elbasvir-grazoprevir for 12 weeks. HCV disappeared at treatment week 4, and no adverse events were observed during the duration of elbasvir-grazoprevir therapy. The patient continued regular follow-up after DAA treatment. HCV did not relapse, and the viral response was sustained. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no recurrence of esophageal varices. The platelet count increased, and the ALBI score decreased after achieving SVR. In 2021, his platelet count was 96,000/muL, and the ALBI score was -2.64, classified as grade 1. The diameter of the PVA remained at 52 mm (<PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F03_a_1_5.webp><PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F03_b_2_5.webp>). Abdominal US showed an anechoic lesion with no recurrence of thrombus (<PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F03_c_3_5.webp>). Using the color Doppler method, the blood flow in the aneurysm was seen as bidirectional due to the swirling of blood, which is the so-called yin-yang sign (<PMC10871735_crg-2024-0018-0001-535957_F03_d_4_5.webp>), while a flat venous flow was observed inside the aneurysm using the pulsed-wave Doppler method (Fig. 3e). Thus, the PVA did not enlarge 4 years after achieving SVR following DAA treatment. The CARE Checklist has been completed by the authors for this case report, attached as online supplementary material (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000535957).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old man presenting in 1992 with liver dysfunction.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient first visited the hospital in 1992 for liver dysfunction. He declined interferon therapy due to concern for severe adverse events and underwent regular blood tests and abdominal ultrasound monitoring every 3 months. Over subsequent years, he remained asymptomatic at the time of portal vein aneurysm (PVA) discovery but progressively developed thrombocytopenia, worsening liver function, esophageal varices, PVA enlargement with thrombosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus. No other significant medical history at initial presentation in 1992.
subjective.review_of_systems: Asymptomatic at the time of initial portal vein aneurysm detection.

objective.routine_investigations: Baseline labs (1992): platelet count 165,000/uL, ALBI score -3.07 (grade 1). Follow-up labs (2006-2007): further decline in platelet count and ALBI score worsening to -1.77 (grade 2b). Post-SVR labs (2021): platelet count 96,000/uL, ALBI score -2.64 (grade 1). Abdominal US in 2004 showed limited portal vein dilatation due to PVA; in 2021, US showed an anechoic 52-mm lesion with no thrombus, bidirectional swirling flow ('yin-yang sign') on color Doppler, and flat venous flow on pulsed-wave Doppler.
objective.advanced_workup: Upper GI endoscopy showed emerging esophageal varices that enlarged in 2006-2007 (no recurrence post-SVR). Contrast-enhanced CT in 2004 showed no liver tumor but an ovoid, homogeneous, highly enhancing 28-mm PVA at the splenic and superior mesenteric vein confluence. Repeat CT in 2010 showed PVA enlargement to 38 mm with internal thrombus, increasing to 43 mm 1 year later and 52 mm in 2017 (stable at 52 mm in 2021). Imaging in 2014 and 2017 identified hepatocellular carcinoma nodules in segments 6 (17 mm) and 7 (15 mm).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1 infection complicated by portal hypertension, esophageal varices, enlarging portal vein aneurysm (PVA) with internal thrombosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Plan & Clinical Course: Esophageal varices were treated twice in 2006-2007 with combined endoscopic variceal ligation and injection sclerotherapy. PVA thrombosis in 2010 resolved completely after 10 days of IV antithrombin III (1,500 units/day), followed by oral warfarin prophylaxis. HCC nodules in segments 6 (17 mm) and 7 (15 mm) were treated with radiofrequency ablation in 2014 and 2017. In 2017, he completed 12 weeks of elbasvir-grazoprevir without adverse events; HCV cleared at week 4 with sustained virologic response (SVR) and no relapse. By 2021 (4 years post-SVR), varices had not recurred, platelets (96,000/uL) and ALBI score (-2.64, grade 1) improved, and the PVA remained stable at 52 mm without recurrent thrombosis.

raw_case_text:
This 42-year-old male was identified by our HCV operational delivery network (ODN) re-engagement initiative in April 2020. He had previously tested positive for HCV RNA but was unaware of the diagnosis until notification by the ODN. On assessment, he was drinking around 210 units of alcohol weekly and had no clinical signs of decompensated chronic liver disease. He had no previous history of intravenous drug use, was HIV negative and had normal renal function. Further testing confirmed hepatitis C genotype 3a infection, viral load 41,687 IU/mL, with bilirubin 22 mumol/L, albumin 40 g/L, ALT 63 mumol/L, AST 73 mumol/L, AFP 6.8 ng/mL. FibroScan showed median elasticity 12.7 kPa (IQR 1.0), in keeping with cirrhosis. He planned to engage with alcohol support services to reduce his intake and, due to being treatment naive, started HCV DAA treatment with Epclusa (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir) for 12 weeks in January 2021.
Following his diagnosis, before starting treatment for his HCV, an ultrasound of the liver demonstrated a focal lesion in the right lobe. MRI confirmed a hypervascular tumour within segments 6 and 7, measuring 4.5 cm, with radiological features of HCC and invasion into the right posterior portal vein and right hepatic vein. There were no signs of portal hypertension. Staging CT confirmed the absence of distant metastases.
His Barcelona clinic liver cancer stage, with a single lesion, Child-Pugh class A5 and good performance status was early stage (A). Surgery was considered; however, indocyanine green clearance assessment of liver function was unfavourable for resection. Endoscopy demonstrated grade 1 oesophageal varices. The multidisciplinary team recommended a strategy of attempted tumour "downstaging" by systemic immunotherapy with atezolizumab and bevacizumab, alongside DAA therapy, with a plan to reassess for sufficient improvement in liver function to allow resection. Immunotherapy commenced in February 2021 for 6 planned cycles.
In March 2021, end-of-treatment HCV RNA was undetectable. The patient continued to have 4 cycles of atezolizumab and bevacizumab, with his last fourth dose occurring in late May. There was a subsequent viral relapse with viral load in June of 51,286 IU/mL. This coincided with a return to harmful levels of alcohol. Despite imaging evidence of good tumour response, his 5th cycle of immunotherapy was held due to abnormal liver function (ALT 105, AST 230, bilirubin 64) which may have been due to viral relapse, alcohol relapse, immunotherapy hepatitis or a combination thereof. Both further systemic HCC therapy and second-line DAA therapy with Vosevi (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir) were contraindicated due to hepatic decompensation (Child-Pugh B cirrhosis).
Despite no further antiviral treatment, in July 2021 his HCV RNA became undetectable. Unfortunately, he did not attend further oncology clinic appointments due to alcohol dependence. He was admitted to hospital in February 2022 with tense ascites and HCV RNA remained undetectable on two separate blood tests, confirming sustained virological response more than 24 weeks after therapy. There has been a progression of his disease and, following the best supportive care, the patient passed away at home.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 3a infection (baseline viral load 41,687 IU/mL) with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A5, FibroScan 12.7 kPa) and early-stage (BCLC A) hepatocellular carcinoma (4.5 cm, segments 6/7 with portal and hepatic vein invasion). Excluded Differentials: HIV infection (negative) and distant metastatic disease (negative staging CT).

Plan & Clinical Course: Initiated 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa) in January 2021 alongside planned 6 cycles of atezolizumab and bevacizumab (started February 2021) for tumor downstaging. End-of-treatment HCV RNA was undetectable in March 2021. After 4 cycles of immunotherapy (last dose late May), viral relapse occurred in June 2021 (viral load 51,286 IU/mL) coinciding with alcohol relapse; the 5th cycle was held for worsening LFTs (ALT 105, AST 230, bilirubin 64), and further systemic HCC therapy and second-line Vosevi were contraindicated due to Child-Pugh B decompensation. Without additional antivirals, HCV RNA spontaneously became undetectable in July 2021 and remained undetectable on two separate tests in February 2022 (confirming SVR >24 weeks post-therapy) during admission for tense ascites. Due to disease progression, he received best supportive care and passed away at home.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 67-year-old White woman who presented to the hospital with a 2-week history of bilateral knee pain following a fall at home. Her past medical history was significant for hypertension, atrial fibrillation, hypothyroidism, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (on home oxygen). Her review of systems was notable for dizziness, generalized body ache, chronic cough, and dyspnea. She denied use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Physical examination revealed bibasilar rales on lung auscultation and anasarca with bilateral lower extremity edema and ascites. The chest X-ray revealed bilateral lung infiltrates and pleural effusions. She had stage 3 acute kidney injury with an initial serum creatinine of 7.0 mg/dL, up from a normal baseline value, which peaked at 8.1 mg/dL. Serum albumin level was low at 2.5 g/dL. The urinalysis revealed a specific gravity of 1.023, pH of 5, greater than 1,000 mg/dL of protein, and moderate blood. The urine sediment demonstrated non-dysmorphic red blood cells, hyaline casts, fine granular casts, and degenerated cellular casts. The random urine total protein was measured twice and was greater than 600 mg/dL, as a result, the urine total protein-to-creatinine ratio could not be calculated. A kidney ultrasound revealed no obstructive uropathy, and the kidneys were normal in size and had normal echogenicity. 
Her clinical presentation was concerning for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and she was empirically started on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g intravenously daily for 3 days followed by 500 mg intravenously on the 4th day). Two days after presentation, she was initiated on intermittent hemodialysis for refractory volume overload and worsening metabolic acidosis. An extensive serological and immunological work up was unrevealing, including non-reactive titers for antinuclear antibody, anti-double stranded DNA antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase 3 antibodies, anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody. Complement levels were normal, rheumatoid factor screen was negative, and cryoglobulins were undetected. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed no monoclonal protein but a low serum albumin level. Her hepatitis B virus, human immunodeficiency virus, and syphilis screen were all negative. However, the HCV antibody titer was reactive, and the HCV RNA viral load was elevated at 1,7800,000 IU/mL. 
Given the unexplained kidney failure, she underwent a percutaneous kidney biopsy. The kidney biopsy included 23 glomeruli, 1 with global sclerosis. The viable glomeruli revealed a normal morphology by light microscopy (<PMC11730055_CNCS-13-001-01_A_1_5.webp>), the electron microscopy showed extensive podocyte injury with diffuse effacement of the foot process interdigitations, extensive loss of filtration slit diaphragms, and focal detachment of foot processes from the basal membrane (<PMC11730055_CNCS-13-001-01_B_2_5.webp>). The immunofluorescence microscopy revealed "fine-dusting" of IgG deposits on the cell surface of podocytes (<PMC11730055_CNCS-13-001-01_C_3_5.webp>). These features are diagnostic of a diffuse podocytopathy, namely MCD. Furthermore, the co-localization of IgG and nephrin in the dual stain was strongly suggestive of an anti-nephrin antibody-mediated process (<PMC11730055_CNCS-13-001-01_D_4_5.webp>). There was also evidence of acute tubular injury with focal tubular necrosis and mild focal acute interstitial nephritis (<PMC11730055_CNCS-13-001-01_E_5_5.webp>). Out of the 23 sampled glomeruli, only 1 glomerulus (4%) had global sclerosis, a level of sclerosis within the normal limit of age-associated glomerular obsolescence, effectively ruling out any focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. 
Following pulse methylprednisolone therapy, her kidney function recovered, and hemodialysis was discontinued after 7 daily sessions. She was discharged from the hospital on an oral course of prednisone 60 mg once daily, with an initial plan for a 16-week taper. At the time of hospital discharge, her serum creatinine was 1.6 mg/dL. Two months later, her serum creatinine was 0.83 mg/dL, and a random urine total protein to creatinine ratio was 510 mg/g. 
She was formally evaluated for her genotype 1b chronic HCV infection. She had no evidence of advanced liver fibrosis and was started on DAA for her chronic HCV infection with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir, 4.5 months after her initial presentation. At that time, she was on a tapered prednisone dose of 10 mg daily. She successfully completed a 12-week antiviral treatment course. The HCV RNA remained undetectable 1.5 years later, confirming a sustained virological response. Unfortunately, the patient was inconsistent with her clinic visits, resulting in a longer than planned prednisone taper. Six months after her initial presentation, while on prednisone 5 mg every other day, the urine total protein-to-creatinine ratio remained normal at 134 mg/g, consistent with full remission of the nephrotic syndrome. On her most recent visit with her primary care provider, almost 2 years from the time of her initial presentation, her urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio was less than 30 mg/g.
